News.title: I’m the last one left on a village street set to be demolished for Universal’s new £5bn theme park – I’m not budging
News.content:
Next

ONE resident is the final man left on a village street set to be demolished to make way for Universal Studio’s £5billion UK theme park.

Ritchie Wood is determined not to be pushed out of his rental home, as all other neighbours on his road in Kempston Hardwick have moved out.



Wood has called the once-countryside village home for 11 years, noting its friendly community and abundance in wildlife.

But over the past few months, residents have slowly been moving out of Manor Road, knowing their homes are set to be demolished.



The street now lies in what will soon be Universal’s new and only Europe-based theme park.

Speaking to the BBC, Wood said: “It’s totally changed to how it used to be – it used to be lovely. We had a nice little community here, lots of wildlife, very quiet.”

The man’s landlord has now sold the home, and Wood knows he will be asked to leave imminently.

He said: “I genuinely have nowhere to go.



“Unfortunately, I wouldn’t be able to afford anywhere in the area for the same sort of rent [I pay now].”

At first Wood was not alone – a number of residents faced the developer and refused to leave their homes.

However, despite protest, all but one packed their bags and demolition work on the homes has now begun.

The road is now closed until November 28 while lorries and diggers tear down the strip.

Wood has called the situation heartbreaking, adding the rubble of once-homes feels surreal.



In a letter sent to residents, Universal said: “We remain committed to being a good neighbour and will continue to update our local

community as our activity progresses.”

Universal United Kingdom Resort, set to open in 2031, will spread across 476 acres and feature the theme park as well as hotels, restaurants, shops and even room for possible future expansion.

While no rides have been confirmed, plans state: “[Guests will] experience blockbuster attractions, adrenaline-pumping coasters, and mind-blowing spectaculars.



“They’ll come face-to-face with incredible creatures, heroes, and villains.

“They’ll discover great food, new laughs, new ways to play, and step into immersive worlds they’ve only ever dreamed of.”

According to analysis by Universal Destinations & Experiences, the theme park could generate almost £50bn of economic value to the UK in its first 20 years.

It is also set to support 20,000 jobs, half of which would be direct employment, and the remainder supplying services to support the site.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A new train station for exclusive park use is also set to open, connecting connect Oxford to Cambridge via Milton Keynes and Bedford.



Universal and Central Bedfordshire Council have been contacted for a response.

News.title: A66 death crash joyrider’s dad, 40, faces jail today for attacking celebrant at his son’s funeral
News.content:
Next

THE dad of one of the A66 yobs who crashed into a police car killing two officers faces jail today for attacking the celebrant at his son’s funeral.

Gye Worthy, 40, flew into a rage when Paul Maull failed to mention him in the eulogy to son Cole Worthy but did reference the teen’s step-dad.



He hurled insults and then attacked him as shocked mourners looked on.

When cops raced to Teesside Crematorium, he also got into a fracas with them.



A source close to the family said that Cole’s mother Natalie McConnell was left “devastated and shocked” by the chaos.

Offshore worker Gye, lives in Acklam, Middlesbrough, where his £200,000 home was rammed on August 22 in an attack directed at his son.

It was part of an escalating gang war which exploded a short time later as Cole, 17, and four pals leapt into a VW Passat and went hunting their rivals.

Cops spotted the car which had cloned plates and gave chase briefly but abandoned it when the motor went the wrong way along the A66.

Moments later it crashed into PC Matthew Blades, 37 and PC Tom Clough, 38, killing both officers and all five occupants of the Passat.

Police said they all had links to organised crime



There is no suggestion that Gye Worthy is linked to organised crime.

He will be sentenced at Teesside JPs court today.

News.title: Burnham’s Man City gaffe is rocket fuel for Farage as he takes every opportunity to hit the PM where it hurts
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Burnham’s Man City gaffe is rocket fuel for Farage as he takes every opportunity to hit the PM where it hurts







Next

NIGEL Farage vowed to save Brexit as he kick-started Reform’s “general election campaign” in Yorkshire.

At a packed rally in Doncaster, the party leader laid into the PM and fired up activists with his greatest hits.



Reform in power would axe Net Zero, slash migration and cut welfare spending, he told the crowd.

But fundamentally, Mr Farage was there to rally the troops after a bruising 12 months.



Sting operations and rows over donations have dented Reform’s poll lead, while the road to power remains a rocky one.

Recent surveys have put Reform, Labour and the Tories almost neck-and-neck in the race for Number 10.



But Mr Farage reassured activists — some sporting Farage No10 football shirts — that the PM’s hints of reopening the Brexit wars had handed him fresh ammunition.

Leave-voting areas such as Doncaster could prove crucial at the next election, with Labour facing a battle to hold on to its Red Wall seats.

Mr Farage, in full pantomime mode, had the crowd jeering senior Labour figures in Yorkshire, including Yvette Cooper and Ed “Moribund” Miliband.

Mr Burnham, meanwhile, is no stranger to putting his foot in it — most recently with his intervention in the Manchester City case.



A tanned Mr Farage then shot off in his helicopter after the rally, promising to hit the road and get Reform campaign-ready.

Whatever happens, this is rocket fuel for a leader looking for every opportunity to hit the PM where it hurts.

News.title: Angry bird, Trump lookalike croc & bears sharing a joke lead comedy wildlife photo contest – but which is your winner?
News.content:
MAKE IT SNAPPY Angry bird, Trump lookalike croc & bears sharing a joke lead comedy wildlife photo contest – but which is your winner?







Next

THE finalists for the Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards have been revealed – and one lookalike may ruffle some feathers.

Only time will tell whether a sweary orangutan or a grinning croc with a mop of seaweed hair will snap up the prize.



The orange beast was snapped raising his middle finger – while making direct eye contact with the camera.

And one golden ball of feathers was caught with a blazing frown – and dubbed “Angry Bird” by photographer Jan Wittmer.





A total of 40 photos are vying to be top of the pecking order.

Sent in from all over the world, the collection showcases wildlife at its cutest, funniest or most outrageous situations.



The finalists were selected from a vast pool of over 10,000 entries from 112 countries – the highest number in history.

One reptilean beast emerged from a swamp with a mop of black seaweed on its head.

Photographer Paolo Torre said the caiman’s new hairdo looked like Elvis’s rock’n’roll pomapdour – but others have pointed out that the swampy strands more closely resemble Donald Trump’s comb-over.



One owl scowls like a cartoon villain from atop a branch while another appears to karate-kick the air.

Two scheming eagles may yet snatch the prize in scenes that look like a wild seashore heist.

Appearing to have just swooped into the frame, the bird claws a package under the stern beak of a watching eagle.

The photo, by Curt Lundeen, is called “Highway Robbery Get your hands off the merchandise”.

But perhaps a bird in a petal may be worth two splashing in the sea in the eyes of the judges.



The unbelievable shot shows a tiny blue-green bird bathing inside a banana blossom.

Another adorable photo shows a cow called Doris decked in bristling green plants – with the supreme quality of the camera picking up every blade.

In another bizarre showdown a huge white polar bear crouches down to gaze into the eyes of a miniscule gull.



A pic of a strutting eagle – who looked vaguely distressed – was called: “Fashion fades, feather coats are forever”.

Fiendish perspectives make one elephant appear to be poised to kick over a tiny jeep as it stomps across the desert.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The winner will be announced in December 2026.

The top prize is a once-in-a-lifetime safari trip – but various types of Nikon cameras are also up for grabs.

News.title: ‘We could be having a General Election in May’ claims Kemi Badenoch as she rules out ANY pact with Reform
News.content:
Next

KEMI Badenoch claims Britain could head to the polls as soon as next May — but has ruled out any election pact with Reform.

The Tory leader said she believes PM Andy Burnham is “going to call an election sooner than he is saying”.



She added: “All the policies he announced are for after an election.

“We could be having a general election next May.”



But asked about “reuniting the Right”, Mrs Badenoch told the BBC: “There is no deal with Reform.”

Her comments come just days before the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.



The leader will put welfare reform at the heart of their plans.

She wants to stop jobless youngsters going straight from school on to benefits.

Under-25s who have not worked continuously for six months would earn financial support.

Anyone taking part in a new “Get to Work” programme could be required to attend Jobcentres every day.



They would also have to complete work experience or training.

Those who refuse would not receive welfare.

News.title: Now Burnham is PM his words have consequences which is why it was an own goal for him to support Man City’s owners
News.content:
PM’s City ’mare







Next

ANDY Burnham is never shy of an opinion — whether it’s on buses, music or his favourite type of pub snack.

Indeed, there’s seemingly no question to which he won’t offer a folksy answer.



The problem is, he’s Prime Minister now, and his words have consequences.

Which is why it was an own goal for him to support Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owners after they were found guilty of a £1billion cheating scandal that has rocked the football world.



The rules of being in Government are clear: do not interfere with a judicial or independent regulatory process.

Football-lover Burnham has in the past forcefully stated that an independent regulator should oversee the game.



That football regulator is now in existence — having been created by the Labour Government.

The first big decision it will face?

To determine whether, in light of City being found guilty of more than 100 Premier League financial rule breaches, its owners are “fit and proper”.

At the same time, HMRC — also an arm of Government — and the police are coming under pressure to mount their own investigations into the club, who deny any wrongdoing.



By voicing his “concern” about City’s owners quitting Manchester, he risked the perception of political interference.

Indeed, No10 was yesterday forced to try to clear up after the boss, stating that “there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules”.

Separately, Burnham also appears to have misread the room on this one.

The vast majority of fans want the Premier League to throw the book at the club for not playing fair — not go easy in case the owners walk away.

Make it work

KEMI Badenoch has thrown down the gauntlet to Labour in a high-stakes battle over Britain’s soaring welfare bill.



Andy Burnham is refusing to tackle the huge sums paid to skivers, and is preparing to target pensioner income by scrapping the triple lock.

The Tory leader, by contrast, will force under-25s to work or undergo intensive training rather than instantly signing on.

Britain is desperate for strong action to instil a proper work ethic in a generation that otherwise faces life on benefits.

Kemi’s on the right track.

Debt trap

BRITAIN is stuck in a crippling debt spiral because of Government failure to bring spending under control.



Interest payments on the nation’s £3trillion overdraft have hit a 28-year high, triggering fears of a knock-on effect for mortgage bills.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

We now spend twice as much just servicing the debt as we do on defence.

Things won’t get better until Labour stops maxing out the credit card.

News.title: Nine-day-old baby died in hotel room after drinking cocaine in her mum’s breast milk – as parents avoid jail
News.content:
TOT TRAGEDY Nine-day-old baby died in hotel room after drinking cocaine in her mum’s breast milk – as parents avoid jail







Next

THE parents of a nine-day-old baby who died in a hotel room after drinking cocaine in her mum’s breast milk have avoided jail.

Baby Darcey was found dead after ingesting the Class A drug on the morning of November 11, 2023 in Newquay, Cornwall.

Darcey’s parents – Rochelle Thomas, 30, and 29-year-old Andrew Maunder – had been staying at the Hotel Victoria shortly after the birth of their daughter.



Emergency services raced to the scene but the tot was tragically pronounced dead shortly after 11am that morning, reports Cornwall Live.



In scenes of horror, the couple were reportedly found screaming in distress in their hotel room by Thomas’ mum.

Their baby was unconscious and had blood on her face.

Thomas and Maunder were subsequently arrested and each pleaded guilty to child neglect.

A sentencing hearing at Truro Crown Court on Thursday was told both parents abused cocaine.

Maunder would regularly take the Class A drug in the evenings while a toxicology report found Thomas to have taken cocaine both during and after her pregnancy.

Prosecuting, Joss Ticehurst said the pair had “put their baby daughter’s life at risk”.

Darcey was found to have blood in her system and the court heard how the baby could have fatally ingested it through breast feeding.



But Mr Ticehurst added that cocaine was also found on their clothes and fingers while a cup on the bedside table was also contaminated.

The prosecutor said Thomas admitted to her own usage of the drug just days before she gave birth.

Defending, Victoria Bastock said it was a “tragic set of circumstances” and was “keenly felt by both defendants”.

She argued the pair were due to move north to be with Thomas’ family for support and had been seeking help at the time.

But Judge Simon Carr admonished the parents as they were sentenced to two-and-a-half years in prison, suspended for three years.



“Darcey was entitled to rely on you for her protection. You entirely failed her,” he said.

“You allowed your addiction to take precedence over your baby. Not just on the day but in the months of your pregnancy.”

The judge took into account Thomas’ drug usage as a way of coping with post traumatic stress and depression.

Maunder was also noted for his remorse and poor mental health with the judge adding that nothing would be achieved by “sending you to prison” three years after the horror.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In addition to their suspended sentence, both parents have been ordered to take rehabilitation work for a year.



Additionally, Thomas will be entered into a drug rehabilitation programme for six months.

News.title: Shocking moment electric car ploughs into temple & ‘traps worshippers under vehicle’ – as three rushed to hospital
News.content:
Next

THIS is the horror moment an electric car ploughs through a temple, crushing worshippers and injuring three people.

Shocking video shows the moment an elderly driver, 78, smashes directly into a crowd who sat before a Buddhist shrine in Bangkok, Thailand.



Police were called to the Guanyin Shrine at the Thian Fah Foundation around 1pm on Thursday following reports of a major collision.

Astonishing footage shows the grey car bursting into the room where dozens of unsuspecting people sat.



Smashing directly into three individuals, other worshippers desperately jumped from its furious path.

Bystanders immediately gathered around the car, attempting to free the people as dust and debris cover the once-peaceful shrine.



In a race against time, rescue volunteers rushed to the scene and ultimately had to use a hydraulic press to free the trio from under the electric car.

Three people were rushed to hospital with one 60-year-old woman sustaining serious injuries.



The other two victims suffered minor injuries.

The security guard reportedly said around 30 people were visiting the shrine to pay their respects when the vehicle suddenly entered through the main gate at speed.

Police have launched an investigation into what caused the incident, with local media reporting the driver suffered a sudden dizzy spell behind the wheel.



The man reportedly lost consciousness and accidentally pressed the accelerator, causing the vehicle to plough into people who were paying respects inside the 68-year-old shrine, the Bangkok Post reports.

According to The World Health Organisation, Thailand ranks near the top globally for percapital roadmortalitiess each year.

The Guanyin stature – which symbolises unconditional compassion, mercy, and the active relief of suffering – rmained intact.

The country ranks ninth out of 175 WHO member countries worldwide.

It comes as an out-of-control driver ploughed into a group of teenagers – knocking them down like skittles across the pavement in Turkey.



The elderly driver, Yakup Mujdat Turer, 73, hurtled towards the group who were strolling on Tibbiye Avenue, Istanbul last week.

The young students were knocked off their feet and sustained various injuries

Horror footage shows the out-of-control car skidding sideways onto the path before smacking into four students.

News.title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford incident, police say
News.content:
A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. Two properties in the area have been searched.

Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said.

"I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation."

Police had initially given the dual UK-Iranian national's age as 27 and said a second man had been questioned under caution, but in a later update said that this was not the case.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site.

The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what it called defensive strikes on Iran.

News.title: Crypto thieves attack man in home and threaten to kill pregnant wife's baby in 'horrific' robbery
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A businessman was beaten with hammers by masked men who broke into his home and threatened to kill his heavily pregnant wife unless he transferred hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency.

Speaking to the BBC, the couple, who want to remain anonymous, described the attack as "horrific" and said they feared for their unborn baby's life.

The attackers left in a car driven by a getaway driver after the man transferred his crypto savings.

Crimestoppers are offering a Â£10,000 reward for information in the attack, which was captured on home security footage and is being investigated by the police.

Experts say it is one of a growing type of violent theft known as a "wrench attack" targeting cryptocurrency investors.

As crypto coins have risen in value, reports of these violent robberies linked to digital assets have emerged in the UK, France and the US.

Once funds are transferred, recovering them can be extremely difficult.

The man, who the BBC is calling James, said three intruders forced their way into their Solihull home before launching an assault which lasted 45 minutes.

"The door gets pushed open, I can see gloves coming in, balaclavas," he said.

James tried to fight the men off but they hit him in the face, head and ribs with hammers.

His wife, who was seven months pregnant, was held down on the sofa by one of the criminals.

"He's got a pillow over her face," James said. "He's literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming, 'I can't breathe'."

The couple still had no idea what the criminals wanted until one of the men demanded James unlock his phone and hand it over.

James said the attackers appeared to know he owned cryptocurrency, but had little understanding of how to access it.

Instead, they were taking instructions from someone else connected via a live video call.

"I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: 'Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he's got'," he said.

News.title: US says Europe should ready fuel supplies as Trump threatens diesel ban
News.content:
Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he mulls a ban on US exports of the fuel amid a global shortage.

The comments followed his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging for Europe to immediately ready and release such supplies. "American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar, he argued.

The US has threatened to restrict diesel exports amid surging costs due to the war in Iran. The issue is top of mind for US voters ahead of the crucial midterm elections.

On Thursday, Britain held talks with European partners about the potential release of diesel reserves in response to any ban.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.

"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.

On Thursday Trump added that he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves, while Bessent said they should do so "immediately".

"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," Bessent said in a post on social media.

The plans come weeks ahead of November elections in the US, where control of Congress will be up for grabs. The president is set to travel across the US campaigning for Republicans in hopes of keeping control of the House and Senate.

Diesel prices in the UK hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.

Britain's Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply.â¯We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.

News.title: Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters
News.content:
The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.

The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

This, clearly, matters for the club, but that is just the start of it.

It matters for Manchester, it matters for the Premier League and so, crucially, it matters for the UK's image around the world â because England's top flight is a colossal global brand. In other words, this matters whether you like football or not.

Added to all of this, Andy Burnham pitches himself as Mr Manchester and is a big football fan.

The man who was the mayor of Greater Manchester a matter of months ago is now the prime minister, and so finds himself caught up in it all at a local level, a national level and a diplomatic level.

Diplomatic, because rows will rage over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state. And the state is a big UK ally.

All of this is why I thought it was in the public interest to put a series of questions to Burnham about it when I spoke to him on Wednesday as the Labour Party conference concluded in Liverpool.

His comments, in his interview with me, followed by no fewer than two attempts to backtrack 24 hours later, amount to perhaps his biggest self inflicted tangle since he arrived in Downing Street in July.

He will have expected to be asked about Manchester City, but he didn't expect sustained scrutiny about it.

One particular exchange prompted a lot of interest. I asked if he was worried that Manchester City's owners from the United Arab Emirates might sell up.

It is worth quoting his answer in full.

"Well, I would be really concerned to lose them. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail, but obviously it's ongoing, and because it's still contested by Manchester City, then I think it's right that I don't say much more."

His answer is revealing on several levels, and was leapt on by many in football and then by the Conservatives, who labelled them "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary".

News.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
News.content:
According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.

Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".

"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.

The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around â¬1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.

Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.

According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.

China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.

That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.

And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.

"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.

But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.

There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.

News.title: Watch: Celebrity Traitors series two kicks off with a wild curveball
News.content:
Warning spoiler alert.

The new series of Celebrity Traitors has kicked off, with 21 contestants including Bella Ramsey, Maya Jama and Michael Sheen.

But only moments after the game's traitors were selected, a huge curveball was thrown when Richard E Grant did something no one has done on the show before.

BBC culture correspondent Noor Nanji discusses his wild admission, as well as the show's latest twist.

More on this story.

News.title: Chaos, coffins and 'Claudiapatra' steal the show in Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

One person in particular may have dominated much of this opening episode, but Claudia Winkleman's gothic arrival still caused a stir.

Carried aloft by druids in a closed coffin, the show's host arrived in a church, to greet 21 anxious-looking celebrities.

"That was quite the nap," she said as she emerged.

"Claudiapatra!" gasped model and actress Jerry Hall - spotting similarities in both grandeur and hairstyles between Claudia and Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen.

Winkleman said at the show's press launch she loved her "iconic entrance", but admitted she'd initially wanted to hide in the castle's suit of armour.

"It's like a sort of GCSE history fantasy - it was either that or the grandfather clock," she said.

News.title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest over funding
News.content:
Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.

Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance of a school in the northern city of Rouen.

Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.

The interior ministry said 1,949 people had been arrested on Thursday, with 305 police officers injured. Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest.

The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".

Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.

In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.

While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.

The blockades and protests at French lycÃ©es - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.

So far, 1,027 lycees have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.

At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.

On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.

News.title: Hundreds of criminals start leaving prison under new early release scheme
News.content:
Hundreds of criminals are being released early from prisons in England and Wales under new rules introduced to prevent facilities reaching capacity.

The first 700 of an expected 4,500 inmates eligible under the scheme were due to be let out on Thursday.

The government has stressed they will remain subject to strict monitoring arrangements, including the expanded use of electronic tagging, and has said action was needed to prevent prisons from becoming full.

But the plan has been strongly criticised by victims and questions have been raised over whether the Probation Service has sufficient resources to monitor thousands more criminals in the community.

Prisons in England and Wales are a matter of months away from reaching capacity, with Ministry of Justice data showing as of Monday 87,499 people were incarcerated, taking prison population levels up to 98.2%.

Thursday's release is the first of 10 scheduled to take place, with the final slated for June 2027.

Prisoners released initially were serving sentences of up to 19 months, with the most serious offenders - serving fixed sentences of more than 12 years - leaving in later waves.

News.title: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case
News.content:
Findings from the Premier League's case against Manchester City require scrutiny from His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the chair of a cross-party group of MPs has told the tax authority.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by Friday.

The club were found to have artificially inflated revenue through "sham" sponsorship agreements with the help of their owners.

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of HMRC, has therefore asked whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates, external which claims City failed to pay as much as Â£12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to Â£24m.

News.title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
News.content:
In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City are expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process", saying it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process, it would be wrong for me to do that."

In response, the Tories accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

Shadow minister for sport Louie French called for the government to "keep politics out of football and ensure the Premier League's independent commission can do its job free of outside influence".

"The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers," the Tory MP said.

"Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues. Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners' well-reported investments in Manchester.

"Football must be governed independently, with the rules applying equally to everyone. Fans deserve confidence that no club or owner is above those rules."

And Lib Dem MP Anna Sabine, the party's spokesperson on sport, said: "Fans of every club deserve to know the rules apply to everyone... Burnham needs to remember he's prime minister for everyone, not just Manchester."

It comes as the chairwoman of the Commons Treasury committee, Labour MP Dame Meg Hillier, wrote to HMRC on Thursday to ask for reassurance that it has "seized of the importance" of the case for any potential tax implications.

News.title: PM warned Rosebank oil field could breach West Bank sanctions
News.content:
The prime minister has been warned that approving a controversial oil field risks contravening his own sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

The government will soon have to make a long-awaited decision on whether to go ahead with Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil field, which sits off Shetland.

Environmental campaigners and Green Party leader Zack Polanski have both separately written to Andy Burnham and the foreign secretary to raise concerns about Rosebank's links to an Israeli company, Delek Group.

Last year Delek Group was included in a UN database of firms which allegedly provide services or utilities to support settlements in occupied Palestinian territories.

A spokesman for the company told the Daily Telegraph, external it no longer had any involvement in Israeli settlements and was wrongly included in the database.

Delek Group controls Ithaca Energy, which holds a 20% stake in Rosebank.

The campaign group Uplift, whose legal challenge against the Rosebank project in 2023 led to the ongoing delay over a decision on exploration, has helped organise a letter to Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

In a letter seen by BBC News, campaigners from Stop Rosebank and Greenpeace, with assistance from Uplift, have asked the government to clarify whether Delek will fall foul of the sanctions announced last month.

Separately, Polanski has also written to Miliband, asking what steps the government would take to make sure revenue from UK oil and gas production did not finance illegal settlements.

He said: "Rosebank is a test of whether Labour's proposed sanctions regime is fit for purpose.

"Companies blacklisted by the UN for operating in the illegal settlements should not be financed by oil and gas revenues from the North Sea."

News.title: Body of baby girl found in Wales may have been in the water for weeks, police say
News.content:
The body of a baby girl found along a north Wales shoreline may have been in the water for up to a few weeks, according to initial indications.

A member of the public found the body on the Menai Strait shoreline near Siliwen Road in Bangor, Gwynedd, on Sunday shortly before 17:00 BST.

In an update on Thursday, North Wales Police said a post-mortem examination revealed the newborn was a girl.

The force is continuing the search for the girl's mother and urged her to make contact with police.

Further tests to find more about the baby are under way, North Wales Police said.

"We understand that the mother may be fearful of coming forward but we urge her to make contact with us," Supt Llinos Davies said, adding that she wanted to reassure her that her welfare and safety was their "utmost concern".

"Anyone with concerns about a girl or a woman you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us," Davies said.

She said all names received would be treated with the utmost discretion and can be eliminated as the mother, without delay.

"I understand that this is a terribly sad incident for the community and I am grateful for the overwhelming support and assistance that we have received so far," Davies said.

Fiona Giraud, director of midwifery and women's services for Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, said her priority remained with the mother.

Addressing her, she said: "Our immediate concern remains to be your health, safety and wellbeing.

"You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone," she said.

"We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death, but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need.

"I am asking you personally, please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you," Giraud said.

News.title: Educating Cardiff teacher admits sexually assaulting teenage girl
News.content:
A teacher who featured in the Channel 4 documentary series Educating Cardiff has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl.

Gareth Ritter, 44, of Bryngwyn, in Monmouthshire, was in the middle of giving evidence in his defence when his barrister asked for the charge to be put to him again.

Ritter, who was also a prominent member of a number of brass bands, was asked to stand up and, when asked how he pleaded, he said "guilty".

He was told all of the charges he had admitted carried a custodial sentence and the court would consider immediate custody.

Ritter had previously denied intentionally touching the teenager sexually without consent when he was in his 30s.

Earlier in the trial, the jury was told that, following an event in Cardiff, Ritter offered to drive the victim home but stopped at a flat he owned in Cardiff Bay, saying he had to check it before a new tenant arrived and invited her in.

Once inside, she said he touched her bottom while they stood on a balcony overlooking the city and later kissed her in the hallway.

The woman, now in her 20s, said: "One hand went around my back, it dropped to my bum and he lent in and kissed me.

"I remember his tongue going into my mouth.

"I remember being against the wall, I couldn't step back, I remember him kissing me. I turned my face away, my hands were on him, I wasn't forceful, I held out my hands on his chest. It was a light push but not forceful."

Asked by prosecutor Andrew Davies if she said anything to him, she replied: "It might seem like a strange comment, but I said 'I'm a good girl, I don't do this. I go to a Christian school'."

The court was told Ritter then drove her home, repeatedly asking her if she was going to tell anyone about what had happened.

"I remember him saying 'Nobody needs to know about this. Are you going to tell anyone about this?'

"What do you say in that situation? Gareth was someone I really looked up to. How do you confront that? I'd never been in that situation."

She said she just wanted to "brush it under the carpet".

The court heard the woman reported the alleged incident several years later after Ritter's phone was examined by detectives following an "unrelated matter" that ended with no charges being brought.

Police had found intimate images of a young woman who was under the age of 18. When she was traced, it was the same woman who was sexually assaulted by Ritter.

The court was told the images had originally been screen grabbed with her consent during an intimate video conversation between the woman and another man.

The images had been stored on his tablet, which had been accessed and shared by the man's housemates, and were later found on Ritter's phone.

The jury were told Ritter had since pleaded guilty to the possession and distribution of unlawful images, as the woman was 17 at the time the images were taken.

The woman said when she was told her images had been found on Ritter's phone she decided to report the incident in Cardiff Bay.

The court was told that when Ritter was interviewed by police in December 2022 he denied knowing about the Cardiff Bay flat, and denied taking the woman there. He also told police he had not given her a lift home.

A year later he was interviewed by police again. When asked if he had given a truthful account in his first interview, he said no.

Ritter was granted bail until sentencing on 4 November.

News.title: Hundreds of jobs under threat at Grangemouth chemical plant
News.content:
Hundreds of jobs are under threat in Grangemouth after an agricultural chemical firm announced plans to cease operations at the site.

Syngenta said it had been unable to make its business at the plant "competitive" in the face of "increasing international competition".

A spokesperson for the company - which manufactures chemicals used for the protection of crops - said it would enter a consultation period over the move, but added a final decision has yet to be taken.

The Economy Secretary, Stephen Flynn, described the plans as "extremely disappointing".

The UK government's Reindustrialisation Minister, Blair McDougall, said they had worked with Scottish counterparts to "explore every possible avenue" for support, but Syngenta had taken the decision on a commercial basis.

A total of 377 workers are set to be affected by the move.

It comes over a year after Syngenta was awarded Â£2.2m from Scottish Enterprise to expand production at the site.

News.title: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Andrew Bailey said the central bank is watching the huge amounts of money being invested in AI "very carefully" and cautioned that "not everybody always wins".

The money that has been spent on and loaned to AI firms over the last few years in the hope of large returns is causing markets to value some of them as multi-trillion dollar businesses.

Asked if he believed an AI bubble could burst, Bailey said: "You could see some correction of asset prices at some point."

He was speaking exclusively to the BBC about what the risks and benefits of AI could be for the UK economy.

Bailey said he believed the technology has "great potential to strengthen growth in our economies", adding that this was something the country needed.

"But it also brings with it substantial risks and so we have to be on top of both of those."

One such risk is what happens if the big bets being made on AI don't pay off.

AI chipmaker Nvidia is currently the world's most valuable listed company, with a market valuation of $5.5tn (Â£4.14tn), thanks largely to investors who believe in the big profits AI could create.

Meanwhile, tech giants Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the technology.

And two of the largest AI companies in the world â Anthropic and OpenAI â are also preparing to sell shares in their firms on the US stock market in moves which many believe will lead to hundreds of billions of dollars more flowing into the industry.

"There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth," said Bailey.

"And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver."

"Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner".

"Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins.

"We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient."

Major League Baseball won't consider staging a game in western Wyoming’s Grand Teton National Park.

Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred sent a letter Thursday to Teton County Commissioner Chair Mark Newcomb, Jackson Mayor Arne Jorgensen and Jackson Hole Chamber of Commerce President Rick Howe, who wrote to Manfred voicing objections on Monday following a report in The Washington Post that Grand Teton was under consideration.

Manfred sent a similar letter to U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico.

“MLB has no formal plan to play a game in Grand Teton National Park,” Manfred wrote. “Our team was conducting initial due diligence on many potential sites when this story was reported and we had made no decision of the feasibility of staging a game in Grand Teton National Park. We also had not reached the stage in our due diligence in which we evaluated the environmental impact or spoke to members of the community to solicit their views — steps that would have certainly been a part of any process should it have moved forward.”

Manfred then said Grand Teton wouldn't remain under consideration.

“Since the story was reported, it has become clear the local community does not want us to continue evaluating Grand Teton National Park as a potential site,” Manfred wrote. “We obviously would not bring a game to a community that has concerns about the venue and will not continue to evaluate Grand Teton National Park as a potential site."

MLB and the players’ association have played a handful of regular-season games away from the 30 big league ballparks in recent years, including in the Iowa cornfields made famous by the movie “Field of Dreams.”

Grand Teton includes a commercial airport — the busiest in Wyoming — and a vast expanse of Jackson Hole bottomlands with spectacular views of the Teton Range.

“We are grateful that Major League Baseball heard the roar of the crowd and rightfully recognized that Grand Teton is already a field of dreams, filled with mountains, forests, wild nature and wildlife that attracts millions of dedicated fans each year," Allison Michalski, Grand Teton senior program manager for National Parks Conservation Association, said in a statement. “The bases were loaded with opposition, and this news is a grand slam for Teton county communities and the enduring legacy of Grand Teton National Park.”

Donald Trump claimed once again that he had the “best numbers” of any president, even as his approval poll ratings continue to slide and Americans are feeling serious economic pains stemming from the war in Iran.

The president was in Denton, Texas, on Thursday at a manufacturing plant on Thursday as part of a two-state swing that will also include a visit to Choctaw tribal lands in Oklahoma. He spoke to a crowd of a few hundred people as he tried — not for the first time this week — to convince voters that it was merely an image problem from which the GOP and his presidency are suffering.

"We have the greatest numbers of any president in the history of our country, and I can't get the word out,” the president complained. “The only thing we’re doing bad at is public relations.”

It’s far from the first time he has said this. Going back months, Trump has insisted that the country’s economic numbers are better than at any point in history, even as interest rates remain high and wages remain just barely ahead of inflation, and not enough for many Americans to deal with surging prices in several key areas, including food prices and gasoline.

The president said at his event on Thursday that Americans worried about affording those commodities were wrong.

open image in gallery Donald Trump spoke about his efforts to revitalize manufacturing in Texas on Thursday ( Reuters )

“They say, ‘yes, but affordability?’ And everyone thinks that the prices are high because of me, but they're not. We're the ones bringing down the prices. I just hope you can know. The one good thing about [the president’s critics] is, they have a great line of bull***t.”

“You know, they came up with the word affordability. So from day one, they said, ‘what about your prices?!’ And then they came up-- you know, they always come up with these words.”

Though the crowd was cheering for his early remarks, it had largely grown silent by the time Trump made his remarks about affordability, in part due to the length of the president’s speech, which began 40 minutes late and lasted a full hour. His remarks were punctuated with calls for voters in the state to support Ken Paxton, a sign that the president sees a real possibility that Paxton will lose his upcoming Senate election against James Talarico, his Democratic opponent. Talarico led Paxton by 51 percentage points to 49 in a Fox News poll released this week, a devastating sign for the Republican candidate in Texas and a worrying sign for the GOP in other areas as well.

Trump faces a 41 percent approval rating in the state of Texas, where Paxton is running to preserve a Senate seat for the GOP that has now cost the party more than $100m in total in advertising and other expenses, thanks in part to the bloody primary fight between Paxton and the Republican incumbent, John Cornyn. The senator has not endorsed his would-be replacement and has already said he won’t campaign or fundraise for him.

open image in gallery Ken Paxton looks on at Donald Trump's rally in Denton, Texas ( AFP/Getty )

Paxton’s own spotty record also makes the race harder to win for Republicans, and those Republicans aligned with Cornyn spent the duration of the primary highlighting those issues for voters. The attorney general of Texas, Paxton, was nearly impeached by the state legislature for abusing his office amid reports of affairs and a messy divorce battle with his wife, Angela Paxton, who is a Republican state senator.

His controversies aren’t the only problem weighing down his candidacy, though, as Trump’s war with Iran has become staggeringly unpopular and by far the least popular of Trump’s stances among his own voters. Three in four Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of relations with Iran in a recent CNN/SRSS poll, and other surveys have shown that Americans broadly doubt that the president has a solid strategy for extracting the U.S. from the conflict.

Trump has pledged to spend much of October on the road campaigning for Republican candidates. Democrats are hoping to win Cornyn’s seat as well as three others to obtain a Senate majority, and polling suggests that the party is competitive in as many as a half dozen or more seats currently held by Republicans.

The average UK home now costs about 7.3 times average earnings, the lowest price-to-earnings ratio in more than a decade, according to analysis by Lloyds.

The bank compared figures for April to June 2026 with the same period in previous years, using data from its house price index and the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Although the comparisons looked at the second quarter of each year, Lloyds assessed all quarters and found that no other quarter had been lower than 7.3 for 11 years.

It said the rate of wage growth has outpaced house price increases over the past year, narrowing the affordability gap.

For first-time buyers, the average home costs just under six times earnings, with a ratio of 5.9, Lloyds said.

Northern Ireland bucked the general UK trend over the past year, with prices rising faster than wages, causing the average house price-to-earnings ratio to increase from 5.8 to 6.0.

The biggest improvements over the past year tended to be in regions where house prices were already relatively high compared with earnings.

The South East of England recorded a significant fall, with the average home costing 9.1 times earnings, down from 9.7 a year earlier.

In London, the ratio fell from 10.9 to 10.3, while in Eastern England it fell from 8.7 to 8.2 and in the South West it decreased from 8.2 to 7.7.

Despite the improvements in affordability, London and the South East remained the two least affordable regions.

Some locations with lower ratios recorded smaller decreases.

In Scotland, the ratio remained broadly unchanged at 5.3. The ratio fell from 5.1 to 5.0 in the North East of England, while in the North West of England it fell from 6.5 to 6.3, and in Yorkshire and the Humber it edged down from 6.0 to 5.8.

The research pinpointed locations where homes are particularly affordable compared with average earnings.

Areas in Scotland topped the list, with homes in Inverclyde and Aberdeen costing 3.5 times wages on average.

Properties in Kingston upon Hull, Blackpool and Dundee cost 3.6 times earnings.

Elmbridge in Surrey was Britain’s least affordable local authority with a ratio of 17.4.

Kensington and Chelsea in London followed at 17.3, while St Albans in Hertfordshire was the third least affordable with an average of 14.1.

Lloyds did not include Northern Ireland in its more localised breakdowns due to small sample sizes.

Lloyds said that despite improvements to the price-to-earnings ratio, mortgage rate rises have pushed up mortgage costs.

The South East of England recorded a significant fall ( Getty )

Andrew Asaam, mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “There are some encouraging signs for people looking to buy a home.

“Wages have continued to rise while house prices have remained relatively stable, helping to narrow the gap between earnings and house prices.

“However, affordability remains stretched for many households.

“Mortgage rates are higher than they were a year ago and saving for a deposit continues to be one of the biggest barriers facing first-time buyers.

“Buyers may have more options than they realise, including mortgages designed for those with smaller deposits.

“While these won’t be right for everyone, they can help some buyers take their first step onto the housing ladder sooner.”

The government recently unveiled a new scheme to help first-time buyers in England on to the property ladder.

The Your First Home initiative will give first-time buyers the chance to buy a new-build property with a 2.5 per cent deposit, with the government lending an extra 20 per cent towards the cost.

Details will be outlined in the Budget and developers will also be expected to make a contribution when signing up to the scheme, to help cover costs.

Mr Asaam said: “For first-time buyers in particular, a small shift in location could make a big difference, not just in getting on the ladder, but in what kind of property is within reach.

“Many parts of Scotland and northern England continue to offer some of the best value relative to local earnings.

“For buyers with flexibility over where they live, that can make a meaningful difference to what they can afford.”

Free NHS flu jabs are being rolled out to tens of thousands of homeless people this week to safeguard them against winter illnesses.

It marks the first time a national scheme has been created specifically for rough sleepers.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the scheme would protect "some of the most vulnerable people from potentially deadly infections".

The jabs will be available to those sleeping on the streets, in hostels, or in night shelters, with NHS England deploying mobile vans and pop-up clinics in high-density areas.

Dr Amanda Doyle, NHS national director for primary care and community services, said: “Winter hits particularly hard for people experiencing homelessness, who can face greater health risks from flu and other respiratory viruses.

“That’s why it’s so important they can get the same protection as other vulnerable groups, with the NHS offering free vaccinations at convenient places this winter.

“So if you’re experiencing homelessness, you don’t need proof of address to register with a GP, you can use a day centre, hostel or the GP practice’s own address. Whatever your health needs, the NHS is there for you.”

The Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) advised in June that NHS flu jabs should be made available to homeless people.=

It is the first time a national programme has been rolled out for rough sleepers ( PA )

A month later, on his first day in Number 10, Mr Burnham also vowed to end rough sleeping.

He said: “Nobody should have to sleep rough, but while people are on the streets, we have a duty to keep them safe.

“This NHS initiative will provide vital vaccinations, protecting some of the most vulnerable people from potentially deadly infections.

“We are delivering for people in crisis now, while changing the system for the long term so everyone has a route off the streets for good.”

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: “No-one should face flu, pneumonia or other serious illness this winter, simply because they don’t have a safe place to call home.

“Vaccinations play a vital role in protecting the most vulnerable in society, and that includes those who are currently homeless.

“Together, we can save lives, support the most vulnerable, and ensure our NHS is there for everyone who needs it this winter.”

Other groups eligible for a flu jab this week include people aged 65 and over, all adults in clinical risk groups, care home residents, carers, and close contacts of those who are immunocompromised.

Restricting how vapes are displayed in shops, standardising device designs, and mandating plain packaging could deter thousands of young people from starting to vape, new figures indicate.

government ministers set out a series of proposals in July aimed at curbing youth vaping, which include standardised packaging and devices, limits on flavour descriptions, and hiding products from view in retail outlets.

As the public consultation on these policies draws to a close on Friday, the government has released a collection of impact assessments examining the potential outcomes.

One analysis focuses specifically on proposed display bans for vaping and tobacco items in shops across England.

Although major retailers have largely placed display cases behind sales desks on their own initiative, nicotine and vape merchandise remains widely visible throughout the UK, particularly within smaller businesses.

Researchers evaluated how reducing this visibility might lower children's exposure and subsequent willingness to try the devices.

They estimate that implementing display restrictions could prevent more than 500,000 teenagers aged 11 to 17 from being exposed to vaping products.

Hundreds of thousands of children in this age bracket would also not be exposed to heated tobacco products or nicotine pouches while in shops, estimates suggest.

There have been growing concerns about the number of children using nicotine pouches – a 2025 report by the teachers’ union NASUWT found 13% of 4,000 teachers reported their pupils using nicotine pouches during school time.

One impact assessment document considers the government’s plan to introduce restrictions on displaying vaping products and other tobacco products in shops in England ( PA )

On experimentation, the authors of the government impact assessment document estimate that restrictions on displays could lead to 38,000 fewer children will try vaping as a result.

The government has also set out plans for vapes to be sold in plain white packaging along with the restriction of flavour names.

The impact assessment states there there is a lack of data specifically on plain packaging for vapes so analysists drew on information from standardised packaging for cigarettes.

“The impact assessment on standardised packaging of tobacco estimated an 11% reduction in the prevalence of ever smoking as a result of restrictions on tobacco packaging,” they wrote.

“If this effect were applied to vaping, and using the 25% prevalence of ever vaping among 11-to-15-year-olds… the prevalence could potentially decrease to 22%.”

Researchers acknowledge that vaping restrictions could also reduce the number of smokers willing to use vapes to quit smoking, but they add: “However, using packaging as an example, preliminary evidence from recent studies, suggests that changes to packaging are unlikely to impact adults’ appeal.”

Leading children’s doctors from the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health have called on the government to go further than the current proposals and limit the types of flavours available, not just their descriptions.

Another measure proposed by the government includes for the vape devices themselves to be black, white or grey. Heated tobacco products should be mandated to be made in a “dissuasive colour, likely pantone 448C”, it has been suggested.

The authors of a separate impact assessment highlight previous research which “supports a potential reduction in the number of people being interested in trying a standardised (white) vape, compared to a branded (coloured) vape”.

England’s chief medical officer, Professor Sir Chris Whitty, has said in the past that marketing vapes to children is “utterly unacceptable”.

President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice is now looking to see if Nixon-era special prosecutors committed misconduct in investigating the Watergate scandal.

An early morning burglary at the Democratic National Committee’s headquarters in the Watergate office complex in Washington, D.C., in June 1972 would become a two-year affair, uncovering corruption inside the White House that would ultimately lead to Republican President Richard Nixon’s resignation.

More than 50 years later, Geoff Shepard, a former Nixon aide who has written books on Watergate, was invited last month to give a two-hour presentation to the DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility, an internal watchdog created out of the Watergate scandal, on allegations that the special prosecutor’s office that investigated the break-in committed misconduct, people familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal.

A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to The Independent that Shepherd gave a presentation to the Office of Professional Responsibility, but said it does not mean an investigation has been opened.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice is now looking to see if Nixon-era special prosecutors committed misconduct in investigating the Watergate scandal ( Daily Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images )

"OPR declined Mr. Shepherd's request to open an investigation in 2022 under the previous administration. Given his expertise and scholarship on Watergate, he was recently invited to give a presentation to OPR, but that presentation does not constitute an investigation,” the spokesperson said.

“OPR remains focused on ensuring that Department attorneys meet the highest professional standards."

Shepard showed DOJ officials internal documents from the Watergate Special Prosecution Force, the Journal reported. Special prosecutor Archibald Cox first led the team and then Leon Jaworski after Nixon demanded Cox be fired.

Shepard claims Cox and Jaworski violated defendants' due process rights in the Watergate investigation by secretly meeting with judges overseeing their cases and suppressing evidence from their legal teams, according to the Journal.

open image in gallery More than 50 years after President Richard Nixon resigned, former aide Geoff Shepard was invited to give a two-hour presentation to the DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility, an internal watchdog created out of the Watergate scandal ( Getty Images )

Nixon resigned in August 1974 while facing impeachment for allegations of obstruction of justice, abuse of power and contempt of Congress — mostly in relation to accusations that his administration tried to cover up its involvement in the Watergate break-in.

Speaking at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library in California in June, Vice President JD Vance drew parallels between Nixon and President Donald Trump, who has been indicted multiple times and claimed it was the result of a witch hunt.

“If you look at the story of how the deep state took down Richard Nixon, it’s not all that different from what the same groups of people, the same institutions tried to do to Donald Trump in the first Trump administration,” Vance said.

He also theorized that if the Watergate scandal were to happen in today’s media landscape, it wouldn’t impact the White House as greatly as it did in Nixon’s time.

“If Watergate happened tomorrow, it would be like a 12-hour news story. The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy,” Vance said.

News.title: What could happen to Christa Pike now after death row killer survives two lethal injections
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Convicted murderer Christa Pike was due to die by lethal injection at a maximum security prison in Nashville, Tennessee, Wednesday night, only to survive and be raced to hospital.

She was in critical condition Thursday and receiving “lifesaving care” at a hospital, her lawyers said.

Pike has been on death row for 30 years after she was convicted over the January 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

Wednesday night, she was given two doses of pentobarbital, but witnesses described hearing her snoring on the gurney she was strapped to in the chamber.

Pike’s attorneys said there were a number of possibilities regarding what went wrong.

The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm.

During the struggle to locate a vein, Pike even suggested where they might find one, he said.

“Please try here, please try here,” Spivey recalled her saying. “She told them over and over, please try higher on my shoulder.”

At one point Pike asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way, though it’s unclear if it was after the first dose entered her body because officials don’t share that information.

open image in gallery Christa Pike was due to be executed late Wednesday, only to survive twin doses of pentobarbital ( Tennessee Department of Correction )

Lawyers for Pike quickly filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and that the situation violated her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. The attempt was ultimately abandoned.

Expert Robin M Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike had experienced was “singular and unparalleled,” pointing out that while medical complications have arisen before, no one has ever survived the drugs they were given.

Had Pike’s sentence proceeded as scheduled, she would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee since 1820 and the 19th woman put to death in the U.S. since 1976.

There are now growing questions over what happens now, particularly as her case had seen calls for clemency even before the botched execution attempt.

Pike’s health remains uncertain

Pike, 50, is currently still in hospital following the failed execution attempt.

“We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,” attorney Randy Spivey said during a news conference. “But we know she is alive right now.”

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine in Atlanta, Georgia, who has been retained by Pike’s legal team, told the BBC she could be left suffering from brain damage.

Pike is unlikely to have received a sufficient quantity of pentobarbital in her blood to cause the apnoea and cardiovascular failure intended for her execution, Zivot said.

“It’s very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury,” he added.

All parties are currently waiting for an update on Pike’s condition before determining how to proceed.

Following the failed attempt, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has suspended the state’s one remaining execution planned for this year, that of convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton on December 3.

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the state’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” Lee said. “I have ordered a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.”

Can she still be executed - and if so when

open image in gallery Kenneth Eugene Smith was due to be put to death in 2022 but executioners could not find a vein ( Alabama Department of Correction )

While the Eighth Amendment to the Constitution bars cruel and unusual punishment, there is no automatic legal mechanism to shield a prisoner from a second attempt to carry out their sentence simply because the first failed, so long as investigators are satisfied that the proper procedure was followed and the subject’s rights were not impeded.

Inmates who survive the death penalty remain convicted felons sentenced to capital punishment and under state custody, their circumstances unchanged despite the advent of a technical fault.

As it stands, Christa Pike’s death warrant expired at midnight Wednesday, meaning the state of Tennessee will have to return to the courts to obtain and set another execution date if it does choose to attempt to execute.

State authorities are yet to say whether they will try again but there is a historical precedent for making a second attempt in cases where the first has not succeeded.

A recent example is Alabama prisoner Kenneth Eugene Smith, who could not be put to death as planned in November 2022 when his executioners could not locate a vein to insert the necessary IV.

He subsequently appealed his case but lost and was finally put to death by nitrogen hypoxia in January 2024.

Dozens of inmates have survived lethal injection

Statistically, lethal injection appears to be the least successful method of execution carried out in the U.S..

Figures from Death Penalty Info say that 75 inmates who were due to die from lethal injection had botched executions, up to 2010.

That represents a 7.2 percent failure rate in the 1,054 lethal injections planned between 1890 and that year, higher than any other method including hanging, firing squad and electrocution.

The average failure rate across all methods is 3.15 percent, so injection is more than twice as likely to be unsuccessful.

Pike’s case is the second time lethal injection has failed in Tennessee this year alone, in a case that sheds light on what may happen next if she survives.

Tony Carruthers was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994 and was set to be put to death in May.

However, it had to be postponed after staff were unable to find a vein to administer his lethal injection.

In that instance, Carruthers was given a one-year reprieve by Gov. Lee and returned to death row, a precedent that could be followed in the Pike case.

open image in gallery Pike was raced to hospital for ‘life-saving measures’ and her condition is currently unknown ( AP )

More legal challenges likely

The failed execution attempt opens up the possibility of further legal challenges from her team.

Pike’s execution had already been delayed by legal battles earlier in the day, having originally been scheduled to take place at 10 a.m., only for the Sixth Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals to vote 2-1 to issue a stay.

That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing, an argument her defense attorneys have long made, insisting that those factors were never taken into account and merited her receiving a life sentence without parole in place of the death penalty.

The Attorney General’s Office appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, saying that halting the execution at the last moment would only further traumatize the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer, and rewarded what it called “abusive delay tactics” by Pike’s attorneys.

Later in the day, the high court cleared the way for the execution to proceed. Its conservative majority did not explain their order, while the three liberal members signed a dissent that said Pike’s claims deserved a closer look.

As criticism grows over the botched handling of the execution, Tennessee’s Department of Correction has defended itself by saying it “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.

“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, ​and ⁠the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening.”
