Virginia State University did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

World.title: College football moves closer to 24-game playoff and the destruction of the best regular season in sports
World.content:
For a sport that spent decades with effectively the same system, structure and configuration, the rate of change in modern college football is jaw-dropping.

The first iteration of the College Football Playoff was in 2014, not too long ago, in the grand scheme of things. Four teams, picked by a selection committee, played two rounds to win a title. For a decade, despite a long list of controversial choices by that committee, it stayed at four teams. Then, the expansion.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

After a wave of criticism from Florida State's exclusion from the 2023 edition and administrators realizing that there was a massive reservoir of revenue available if the sport added playoff games, the sport moved to 12. Just a few years later, here we are and most of the major players involved seem set to blow tradition up further and move to a whopping 24 teams. Seriously.



The execs who control the playoff format met this week outside Chicago, with several new reports saying that the 24-team playoff is all but a done deal.

"We've worked through a lot of the other issues associated with [a 24-team] expansion and those things needed to happen before we started any kind of negotiation [over money]," said executive director Rich Clark, per Yahoo!'s Ross Dellenger.

There's a widespread assumption that the money will be there to make an expansion possible, whether that's with the current network, ESPN or another broadcast partner. And Clark seemed confident enough to publicly explain some details of how the new format would work.

Eight first-round games would start two weeks after the end of the regular season, essentially one week after the current conference championship game window. This would eliminate conference championships, long viewed as a necessary consequence of further expansion. Second-round games, another eight, would follow in late December, "most likely" played at the home stadium of the lower seeded team. Similar to the current first-round format.

Dellenger also quoted a "confident stakeholder," who is adamant that if the money materializes through a TV deal, "we are definitely going to 24."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

There are two ways to react to this news, but a few things seem certain about a 24-team field: traditional bowl games are all but dead, with reaching a 24-team field all that matters. The other? That the college football regular season, long the best in sports, will be irreparably changed.

There’s no question that three-loss teams will be part of a 24-team playoff. It’s a near certainty that four-loss teams will be too. Those close losses between rivals or top programs that were once so meaningful will now just be another week in the schedule, particularly in the era of superconferences, where strength of schedule will guarantee spots for some three-loss teams and four-loss teams.

There is another possibility, as unlikely as it is, that big teams are more willing to schedule each other in non-conference weeks, given that losses are less harmful on an overall resume.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

For example, when the Texas Longhorns lost to Ohio State in 2025 and missed the playoff, head coach Steve Sarkisian went ballistic. He called it a "disservice" to the sport, and ranted about the importance of schedules while threatening to reevaluate future matchups to give the Longhorns an easier path to the tournament. Obviously, he had a different tune after winning in 2026, but the underlying point he made still stands. Easier schedules means a greater likelihood of a 10-2 season and a playoff berth.

But if three losses isn't a death sentence, are programs more likely to risk it with higher-profile matchups?

Particularly with ratings on the decline thus far in 2026, as well as even traditional powerhouses like Penn State struggling to sell out their stadiums, teams could sell season ticket packages on the promise of seeing big games. Even if losing doesn't carry the same penalty as it used to.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Texas didn't struggle to fill up their stadium for the Ohio State game. USC had ~50,000 fans at the San Jose State game in miserable weather at 12 p.m., but sold out against Oregon. With ever-increasing competition for entertainment dollars, rapidly growing ticket prices, and the ease of following and watching games on smartphones, the best way to keep fans in the building is giving them a reason to come in the first place.

That said, even in a sport now infamous for quick cash grabs, this feels like the most blatant of them all. Conference championships and the bragging rights they bring are done. Revenue matters most, rather than competition or truly rewarding exceptional teams. Few fans, if any, have demanded or even wanted a 24-team playoff. But what fans prefer was already at the bottom of the list in terms of importance, and somehow it's sinking even lower.

Get ready for 8-4 Missouri playing 8-4 Wisconsin in the first round of the playoff, coming soon to a television near you.

World.title: Le'Veon Bell accuses Pittsburgh Steelers of racial bias in comparing treatment of Black and White draftees
World.content:
Le'Veon Bell is among the Pittsburgh Steelers most productive running backs of all time, joining a list that includes multiple Hall of Famers. But as an observer of how his former teams do business, Bell put himself in the Hall of Shame on Thursday.

Bell, who played for the Steelers from 2013-17, saw his former team trade cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to the Dallas Cowboys overnight after a contract dispute and decided it was all about race.

Because Porter is Black.

No, seriously.

JERRY JONES GOES ALL IN AS COWBOYS TRADE FOR STEELERS' JOEY PORTER JR IN HOPES OF SUPER BOWL PUSH

"I wish Pittsburgh paid their black superstars they drafted just like they pay their white ones they draft," Bell posted on X on Thursday afternoon.

" ... hate to see porter get traded .. I thought same thing with [George] pickens? TJ Watt is worth every penny tho, so let's not get it confused .. but something needs to change."

Now, Bell has said some wild stuff in the past. But someone needs to jar Bell's memory and adjust his grasp of facts to get him off this race-baiting narrative.

Bell, you see, is not an honest broker. He was drafted in the second round by the Steelers in 2013 and after three 1,000-yard-plus seasons, the Steelers tried to pay him. A lot.

And that led to a contract dispute that ultimately ended his career in Pittsburgh. But before that happened, the Steelers offered to pay him $70 million on a five-year contract before the 2018 season.

That offer from eight years ago, before the NFL salary cap jumped seven times, would be competitive with most running back contracts today.

But Bell, who has admitted he came close to accepting the offer, ultimately turned it down based on his desire for greater guarantees.

Those details aren't primary. What matters is that Bell lived through a negotiation where he, as a Black Steelers draft pick, was offered a lucrative contract by the Steelers. And still on Thursday he's saying the Steelers don't pay their Black draft picks like they do their White ones.

The racist undertones of Bell's post also flies in the face of the fact that the Steelers, at the time of his offer, were coached by Mike Tomlin, who coached the team for 19 years until he stepped away this year.

Mike Tomlin is Black.

The team's general manager now is Omar Khan. He is a first-generation American of South Asian and Hispanic descent, with an Indian father and a Honduran mother.

And those are the people who only want to pay White players?

Pittsburgh's two-highest-paid players today are Watt and quarterback Aaron Rodgers. They are both White. But that has nothing to do with their pay because Watt is the team's best and most accomplished player and Rodgers is the quarterback who has earned the right to be highly-paid after winning four MVP awards ... and, did we mention he's the quarterback?

But Pittsburgh's next seven highest-paid players are Black. And Pittsburgh's next nine of 10 highest-paid players are Black.

The team has shown zero compunction about paying Black players.

Receiver DK Metcalf got a big contract from the Steelers. He's Black.

Defensive back Jalen Ramsey got a big contract extension from the Steelers. He's Black.

Linebacker Patrick Queen got a big contract from the Steelers. He's Black.

Receiver Michael Pittman has gotten two big contract extensions from the Steelers. He's Black.

Someone challenged Bell about these facts beneath his post. And the former running back, who may be suffering from too many blows to the head, shot back that none of those players were drafted by the Steelers.

Except, running back Jaylen Warren got a big contract from the Steelers, as did defensive lineman Keeanu Benton, as did tight end Darnell Washington. All were drafted by the Steelers. All are Black.

All got paid.

World.title: Sleeper Senate race emerges as unexpected headache for Republicans ahead of midterms
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Republicans fully acknowledge they are facing political headwinds going into the midterm elections in November, and those winds are swirling in a race that has become quietly competitive as Election Day nears.

Kansas has, for nearly a century, consistently elected Republicans to the Senate.

But in a midterm election year when voters are unhappy with the Trump administration’s actions and its impact on the economy, the race between Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and megachurch Pastor Adam Hamilton has tightened more than some in the GOP would have liked.

Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., the Senate GOP’s campaign chief, acknowledged that the race is close but remained confident Marshall would hold on.

WOKE MEGACHURCH PASTOR, DEM NOMINEE CALLED ON CONGREGATION TO REPENT FOR DRIVING, EATING BEEF

"Listen, I think if you look at Kansas, it's a very competitive state, more competitive than I'd like to see it. But the fact of the matter is that we're gonna win in Kansas," Scott said.

Republicans are trying to maintain and expand their 53-seat majority but face many toss-up contests across the map and voters that are frustrated with high fuel prices, tariffs and the war in Iran, which could threaten that grip on power.

Kansas isn’t in that toss-up category, but it was recently downgraded by "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican" by the Cook Political Report and in Fox News’ election power rankings.

"No one should be surprised that Adam’s message of leading from the middle and working together is resonating across Kansas," Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton told Fox News Digital.

KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’

"Roger Marshall has spent the past 18 months hiding from his constituents, voting to slash health care and supporting and endless war that’s led to skyrocketing gas and grocery prices," he continued.

"Kansans are ready for something different, and that’s why we’ll vote to elect Adam in November."

Still, Scott gave Marshall and others some advice that could be the recipe for success, even in close contests.

"I told Roger Marshall the same thing I told all the candidates nearly two years ago: "You do one of two things. You either run afraid or you run unopposed,’" Scott said. "And, frankly, it's not unopposed.

"And, therefore, you can't run to the tape. You have to run through the tape. I believe that Kansas is a competitive state," he continued. "I will, however, say that, as I look at all the data, it tells me that Roger Marshall will be successful."

GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS

He has already gotten reinforcements in the form of Vice President JD Vance, who earlier this month rallied for the lawmaker and pitched to voters that Marshall, a former obstetrician, was a man who devoted his life to delivering babies and making sure that moms and children from every walk of life were safe and had the healthcare that they need."

"Let’s stand for Doc Marshall and send the crazy people packing, ladies and gentlemen," Vance said.

He will get more backup soon, too. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital as he exited the Senate late Wednesday night he planned to travel to Kansas. When asked if Republicans would keep the majority, Thune said, "Of course we are."

Marshall is eying a second term in the Senate against Hamilton, a political newcomer who was previously registered as a Republican now running a centrist-aligned campaign. Marshall was first elected to the upper chamber in 2020, cruising to an 11-point victory while Republicans across the country took hits as Trump’s first term came to an end.

Since then, he has aligned himself with Trump as many Republicans did during their time in total control of Washington.

But in recent weeks and months, Marshall has started to distance himself from the administration, like pushing for ICE to coordinate with local law enforcement as agents descended upon southern Kansas or vowing to fight for jobs at Bombardier, a Canadian aircraft maintenance center that employs nearly 1,500 Kansans as Trump’s trade wars ensues.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Hamilton has his own headaches, too. Marshall has consistently painted Hamilton as a "woke" pastor who has delivered sermons to Kansas’ largest United Methodist congregation on Black Lives Matter and climate change, among others.

"As voters continue to learn more about Democrat Adam Hamilton, they are realizing his views are just a carbon copy of every other woke liberal in Washington," Brent Robertson, a longtime senior advisor to Marshall, told Fox News Digital.



"Voters are turning on this guy quicker than cider."

During one sermon six years ago, Hamilton called on his congregation to repent for eating and producing beef. Notably, Kansas is the third-largest cattle producer in the country.

"Some of the things that we grow, because we like to eat them, like cattle, end up producing more carbon dioxide than other crops that we could grow, other forms of food that we could have," Hamilton said.

"And, so, in all of these ways, we are creating or adding to the amount of greenhouse gases in our world."

World.title: Norwegian soccer star files lawsuit against airline that photoshopped his hair onto an airplane
World.content:
Manchester City's Erling Haaland is one of the biggest soccer stars on the planet, and the Norwegian seems to want to make sure that no one capitalizes on that fame.

And that includes taking his signature hairdo and slapping it on an airline.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

One Norwegian air carrier is reportedly learning that firsthand.

SHOULD ERLING HAALAND GET HONORARY US CITIZENSHIP FOR CRUSHING TEE SHOTS OFF A BOAT AND BLASTING ELLA LANGLEY?

According to Norwegian outlet VG, a lawsuit has been filed against Norwegian Air Shuttle ASA by Haaland and York Promotions Ltd. that has to do with a post the airline made on social media.

The company posted a photo of one of their planes with Haaland's ponytail with shaved sides — which he recently cut — plopped on top and the caption, "We've never looked more Norwegian."

POLICE SEIZE COCAINE BRICKS WITH STICKERS OF NORWEGIAN SOCCER STAR ERLING HAALAND ALL OVER THEM

That post has since been deleted, but there's a hearing scheduled for October 9 in Oslo.

"It is true that we have received a lawsuit that we do not understand," Norwegian press officer Eivind Hammer Myhre said. "We, like almost all of Norway, have been involved in cheering on the national team this summer through a few spontaneous posts based on trends in social media."

This is interesting. I'm far from a trademark law expert — I dabble, though — but I could see this going either way.

On one hand, I get wanting to protect your brand, and that extends to a signature hairdo like the one Haaland has become known for.

Buuuuuut...

Social media has made stuff like this so weird, because trends pop up, and then companies (for some reason, I kind of wish it would stop) feel the need to hop on board and toss up a hastily photoshopped image.

Well, maybe this will put an end to that... at least in Norway.

World.title: Disney chief Dana Walden dodges when asked about Jimmy Kimmel's future as ABC's late-night host
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

LOS ANGELES — A top Disney executive refrained from weighing in on Jimmy Kimmel's future at ABC as his role as a late-night host for the long term remains in question.

Dana Walden, The Walt Disney Company's president and chief creative officer, appeared Thursday at the Bloomberg Screentime summit and was asked by Bloomberg's Lucas Shaw whether Kimmel will be hosting his late-night show "a year from now."

"Well, I'm certainly not going to make that announcement with you here today," Walden awkwardly responded with a grin.

CONAN O'BRIEN COMPARES DECLINING LATE-NIGHT TV LANDSCAPE TO DETROIT

Shaw then asked why it isn't a "no-brainer" for Disney to keep Kimmel on air, pointing to a boost in ratings and his status as a "free speech hero" following his clashes with President Donald Trump and Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr.

"The truth is, it's a very challenging day part, late night," Walden responded. "That's not to say that Jimmy is not doing a phenomenal job, and his ratings are up, but they're up relative to a smaller audience that's watching late night on broadcast television."

"Obviously, there's a YouTube channel. Millions of people are watching On Demand, the parts of that show — that is not a lucrative opportunity for a very premium talk show. So we're trying to make sense of the business while also honoring a deep partnership," she continued.

"I love Jimmy. We have a great friendship," Walden continued. "He's close to a number of the people at Disney. And again, we're trying to work through it and make sense of both what does Jimmy want, what's the right thing to do and what's right thing for our business."

JIMMY KIMMEL RETURNS FROM LENGTHY HIATUS WITH DEFIANT MESSAGE TO FCC CHAIR BRENDAN CARR

There has been unconfirmed speculation that the current season of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" will be its last and officially bow out in 2027. It would come following a tumultuous year for Kimmel, including when Disney briefly suspended his show in September 2025 after he sparked backlash for comments he made about the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk. He also clashed with the White House earlier this year after he joked that first lady Melania Trump had "a glow like an expectant widow."

At the same event on Wednesday, comedian Conan O'Brien lamented the decline in the late-night TV landscape.

"I saw over my 17 years with NBC ... I started to see, oh, this is really changing. This is really changing," O'Brien said. "They're asking us to be much more cost-conscious. And it was for a good reason, which is that, you know, HBO, Cinemax, these are the things [that] are coming up. There's more networks — instead of one late night show, 'The Tonight Show,' there's now 'Tonight Show' and there's David Letterman's show, then there are other shows."

"It's a little like Detroit and automobiles," he added, referencing the decline in the U.S. auto industry as competition increased from Japan and Europe.

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

O'Brien spent decades on late-night television between his stints on NBC and TBS before transitioning into podcasts, now hosting "Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend." TBS ultimately scrapped its late-night programming in 2022 following the cancellation of "Full Frontal with Samantha Bee."

Earlier this year, CBS pulled the plug on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert," replacing it with Byron Allen's syndicated comic talk show "Comics Unleashed." "The Late Show" reportedly was losing CBS $40 million a year and had been running on a whopping $100 million budget per season.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While the viewership of "Comics Unleashed" is a fraction of the audience that Stephen Colbert had, it was reported that CBS now expects to make a $15 million profit in the same time slot due to the massive cost-cutting.

World.title: Christa Pike is in critical condition after failed execution in Tennessee, her lawyers say
World.content:
Christa Pike shouldn’t still be breathing. She survived two injections of lethal drugs in a harrowing failed execution by the state of Tennessee, raising questions about how the procedure was carried out and how it went wrong.

Nearly 24 hours after Pike was set to be put to death for a murder she committed when she was 18, she remains in critical condition and is receiving care, her lawyers said Thursday afternoon. Her prognosis is unclear, said Randall Spivey, one of her lawyers. Neither he nor another lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, who spoke with reporters, said he had seen her in the hospital.

“I’m haunted by last night,” said Spivey, who was there during the execution attempt.

At least seven needles were used to try to administer the lethal injection doses, Pike's lawyer said, adding that at least one of the needles looked bent when it was pulled from her arm. Tennessee Dept. of Correction via AP

Spivey said he counted at least seven needles used in Pike’s left arm alone, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt.”

He added that Pike’s right arm had turned purple after the second round of the drug pentobarbital, a sedative used in Tennessee’s execution protocol, was dispensed. Pike’s lawyers said they also learned of “blistering and burning around the sites of the injection.”

The description sheds additional light on what occurred inside the execution chamber as the execution team tried to put Pike, 50, to death. After the curtain to the chamber was opened at 7:26 p.m., a media witness said, Pike complained that “my arm feels like it’s about to burst open.”

Other media witnesses said that Pike moaned that one spot was “really throbbing” and that she was kicking so often that she knocked a sheet that was laid on her.

She continued to make snoring sounds, groan and move after the drugs were presumed to have taken effect, the witnesses said.

Five minutes after the second dose, “it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing,” Spivey said.

00:48 Where is Christa Pike now? 00:00 00:00

He said that he didn’t see any lifesaving care being provided to Pike when he was able to witness the events but that there was a time before the witnesses were led out when no one could see what was happening. Medical care was administered in an ambulance that was called at 8:50 p.m. to the prison in Nashville where executions are held.

“Last night was not just inefficient; it was cruel and it was torturous,” Spivey said.

Medical experts told NBC News that Pike’s injuries could be consistent with the drug’s failing to go directly into her bloodstream but ending up in surrounding tissue because of incorrect insertion or leaking.

If that happened, it would mean less of the drug got into her circulatory system, keeping her breathing and moving rather than becoming deeply comatose before death, said Dr. Jonathan Groner, an emeritus professor of clinical surgery at the Ohio State University College of Medicine.

Burning around the injection site could also be evidence of the drug’s not getting properly injected into a vein, he added.

“I’ve seen partial-thickness burns look red or purple,” Groner said.

Ferrell said he thinks a “number of factors” could explain the execution failure, but he said that based on what medical experts told their team about Pike’s difficult veins, it seems the intravenous line may have infiltrated.

That occurs when a misplaced needle deposits medication into the arm instead of the bloodstream. That, he said, would be consistent with Pike’s complaints that her arm was hurting during the process and that it felt like it was “about to explode.”

Spivey described venous issues that Pike has had throughout her life, noting problems with typical blood draws. It’s part of the reason she feared this method of execution and why she requested a different method, the lawyers said.

“I do know that that really was her biggest fear,” Ferrell said. “It was not a fear of dying. It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death, and that’s what happened minus the death.”

Spivey said that he was given an emergency number for the Tennessee Supreme Court to call if something went wrong with the execution but that when he called it, it went to voicemail.

Pike’s attorneys have since appealed her execution. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has stayed her execution until a third-party investigation uncovers what happened Wednesday.

Emergency vehicles at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tenn., after Pike's execution was halted Wednesday night. George Walker IV / AP

“This is a tragedy. There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened,” Lee said at a news conference Thursday morning.

He declined to give details of Pike’s condition and said he would be hiring a team to look into the circumstances surrounding the failure.

Spivey said of Lee: “I do hope he cares, because this is as a citizen of Tennessee. This is something that was done in all of our names.”

It’s the second time an execution didn’t go as planned in Tennessee this year. Tony Carruthers, convicted in three 1994 killings, was granted a one-year reprieve after executioners in May couldn’t find a vein for a backup IV.

Many questions remain in Pike’s case: Was she in pain when it was occurring? Will she remember what happened? Will there be long-term damage? Ferrell said he doesn’t have the answers.

“We may never know what all she was suffering through, either because she can’t remember it, she can’t tell it, or it overwhelms her in such a way that, you know, sometimes pain and suffering affects people that way,” he added.

Pike’s conviction stems from a 1995 murder case. Pike and two other teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, Knoxville police said at the time. Pike was convicted in Slemmer’s death and sentenced to death; she was on death row for decades.

A number of last-minute efforts to stop the execution were unsuccessful. Pike was set to be the first woman Tennessee has executed in more than 200 years.

World.title: Supreme Court to decide lawfulness of Trump’s immigrant detention policy
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court said Thursday it will consider whether immigrants subject to deportation can be held in detention indefinitely while their cases are adjudicated.

The eventual ruling could endorse or end a key feature of President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration crackdown.

The case was among three the court took up ahead of the justices’ return to action Monday for a new nine-month term following a summer break. Rulings in all three are due by the end of June.

The focus in the first case is whether such immigrants should have a chance to argue at a bond hearing that they can be released while the deportation process moves forward, which was standard practice under previous presidents.

The justices will hear a Trump administration appeal in the case of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a man from Brazil who originally entered the United States in the mid-2000s.

He was detained following a traffic stop in Norwood, Massachusetts, in September 2025. He sued, and a federal district judge ordered that he be released. The New York-based 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld that decision on appeal.

Lower courts have been divided on the issue, although the majority have sided with immigrants who have argued that the federal law the Trump administration cites to hold them without a bond hearing only applies to people detained near the border.

Since last summer, the Trump administration has sought to apply that federal law to anyone deemed to have entered the United States illegally, even if they are nowhere near the border and have lived in the country for years.

Several cases on the issue are pending at the Supreme Court.

“Try as it might, the government cannot twist the law to detain immigrants for months or even years on end without a bond hearing. Not only is it cruel and inhumane; it is unlawful,” Michael Tan, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union representing various detainees, said in a statement.

In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer, representing the Trump administration, called the issue a “critically important question of immigration law.” The policy removes a “perverse incentive” whereby people who evade detention when they enter the United States get treated more leniently than those detained at the border, he added.

The litigation, Sauer said, is “disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law.”

Thousands of people have already been detained under the policy, which could apply to millions of immigrants if expanded, and many of them have contested it. The case does not concern immigrants who have been convicted of certain crimes. Under federal law, they can be detained until they are deported, although separate lawsuits have raised questions about whether they should be eligible for bond hearings, too.

ACLU lawyers said in court papers that the Trump administration policy is a “radical reinterpretation” of immigration law, pointing out that some of those being detained were young children when they crossed the border.

Those challenging their confinement are not a flight risk or a potential danger to the public, ACLU lawyers say.

World.title: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
World.content:
Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

The disgraced hip-hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.

Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs.

They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages.

“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”

NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which include video of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone.

00:17 Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison 00:00 00:00

After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source.

A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved.

“For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said.

TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary.

Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say.

“We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s.

Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones.

“A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said.

Food that was prepared at Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey by inmates who were cooking special meals for Sean "Diddy" Combs and others. Obtained by NBC News

Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or gray sweatpants and shirts.

Meals are delivered in trays, but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink.

“It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said.

It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate.

He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday.

The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.)

“These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement.

Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein.

Combs’ trial last year centered on drug-fueled orgies he organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers and his former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)

The trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on the more serious charges of sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.

World.title: What we know about the pilot hailed as a hero for averting crash of Israel-bound plane
World.content:
He is being hailed around the world as a hero for helping stop a passenger plane bound for Israel from plunging into the ground, despite his own severe injuries.

Images of Capt. Smit Machchhar covered in blood have gone viral after he fought his fellow pilot, who, according to Israeli officials, stabbed him and attempted to nosedive the plane carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

While bleeding profusely, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing other passengers and the Emirati crew to overpower the other pilot and take control of the aircraft. The flight was diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely.

The Mumbai native’s actions have “shown the world the highest form of courage” and “prevented another 9/11-like attack from happening,” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Thursday, after speaking with Machchhar’s family. “The whole world is proud of him,” he added.

Machchhar spoke previously of getting the “aviation bug” at 19 while pursuing a management course to grow his family’s textile business.

He worked for years at a low-cost Indian airline before joining Flydubai and had nearly 10,000 hours of flying experience before Wednesday’s incident.

Machchhar is being treated in a hospital in Tabuk city in northwest Saudi Arabia, with his condition described as “stable” on Wednesday by the Indian Embassy in Riyadh. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News he was “very badly wounded.”

Deepak Mittal, India’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, said on X he met with Machchhar’s family on Thursday in Dubai and “conveyed full support of the Government of India in ensuring welfare and wellbeing of the Indian Hero.”

Flydubai Capt. Smit Machchhar. via Israel Foreign Ministry

The chaotic scene aboard the Flydubai plane as a man covered in blood receives treatment in a still image taken from video verified by NBC News. via Telegram

Netanyahu called Machchhar “a true hero.”

“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” he said.

Machchhar’s former employer, the Indian budget carrier SpiceJet, said on X that he flew for the airline for 10 years. According to his LinkedIn profile, Machchhar joined the Emirati low-cost carrier Flydubai in 2022 after flying for SpiceJet since 2011.

On Wednesday, the veteran captain was flying a Boeing 737 Max 8, the newer variant of the 737 plane that Machchhar had nearly 10,000 hours of experience flying, according to his profile and a YouTube podcast interview he gave last year.

“My first aircraft was a Boeing, and it’s always been that aircraft all my life,” he said.

Machchhar said he had flown challenging routes, dodged bad weather and handled medical emergencies in the air before.

Passengers from the Flydubai flight arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv on Wednesday. Ariel Schalit / AP

His mother was “scared” when he first told her of his plan to become a pilot, he said in the 2025 interview, but his supportive father agreed to cover the steep fees for aviation training.

Between 2008 and 2009, Machchhar trained for 18 months at an aviation college in New Zealand. It was the first time he had been outside India, he said, and he had been on only a “couple of flights” as a passenger before learning to fly.

He “stood out” among those training and did well with his studies, Mainland Air chief executive Philip Kean told New Zealand’s 1News, adding: “We’re all very proud of him here.”

In his early days as a qualified pilot, he took whatever flight routes he was assigned.

“When I started flying ... the only thing I wanted to do then was fly,” Machchhar told the podcast. “I didn’t want to sleep, I didn’t want to go anywhere, and they loved me for it.”

“For a pilot to gain that experience and to refine your skills is what a pilot is,” he added.

But his attitude changed when he got married and started a family, he said.

“Now I would say I try when I get out of the cockpit or the aircraft, I don’t want the other guy to know that I’m a pilot. I don’t want to discuss aviation,” he said.

“Now the kids are there,” he said. “They want to play with you.”

In the interview, Machchhar also spoke about the “rigorous training” that pilots and cabin crew undergo, which includes safety and emergency procedures.

“When we are up there and if something happens, who is going to save you? You’ll be lucky enough to have a doctor on board,” he said.

“They can save your life,” he said, referring to the cabin crew.

World.title: Screaming, panicking, blood: Passengers detail horrifying Israel-bound flight
World.content:
TEL AVIV — A stabbing, an emergency alert, a terrifying mid-air plunge.

Details are still emerging after an Israel-bound flight carrying some 180 people emitted a distress signal Wednesday, raising fears of a possible hijacking when one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit.

Aviatar Alevi, who was onboard the Flydubai flight Wednesday, described people “screaming, running, panicking, blood.”

“At the start I thought it was a plane malfunction, but then I started hearing screaming about the stabbings,” Alevi, 17, told NBC News. “Then I understood the weight of the actual situation.”

“We didn’t know what was going to happen,” he said, adding that the possibility of death “was definitely an option.”

Aviatar Alevi. NBC News

The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, one of its rudders damaged, apparently by the force of its descent.

The passengers, who had been flying from Dubai before the crisis, were mobbed by media and flag-waving fellow Israelis after finally arriving at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

They said they had feared for their lives after the plane plunged more than 14,000 feet in the span of 29 seconds at one point, according to FlightRadar24.

“Imagine sitting on the plane, all scared after you fell down five kilometers. You don’t understand anything,” 16-year-old Peleg Itali told NBC News.

Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia on Thursday as the other pilot, so far identified only as an Omani citizen, was being interrogated elsewhere in the country. Machchhar was widely praised for his efforts to prevent the plane from crashing, opening the cockpit door and allowing passengers and crew to rush in.

Both Machchhar and the pilot who initiated the attack were transferred to Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on Thursday, according to a statement from the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Interior, citing an unnamed “official source” at the ministry.

“The source indicated that initial investigations conducted by the competent authorities in the Kingdom, with the participation of a security team from the sisterly United Arab Emirates, revealed an assault on the pilot by his co-pilot, resulting in both sustaining various injuries,” the ministry said in the statement. “The source confirmed that the pilot and his co-pilot, after their health improved and the medical team cleared them, departed the Kingdom for Abu Dhabi this morning.”

Few details had emerged about the pilot as of Thursday morning. Questions about a possible motive, including whether it was terrorism-related, hang over the attack.

“I don’t think it was a hijacking. It looks like a suicide attempt, simply because of what this hero, Yaniv, has described,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on “CBS Evening News,” as he praised Yaniv Hayun, who rushed into the cockpit and subdued the attacker.

Hayun, who was pictured with his shirt spattered with blood sitting next to Netanyahu, said that he had confronted the pilot who had initiated the attack, according to the Israeli government press office.

“I grabbed the attacker, and choked him, pulled him out first,” Hayun said. “I started pulling the controls.”

“Thank God, we pulled it off. We really put our heads together and worked as a team,” Hayun said, adding: “It was between fear and a sense of a do-or-die situation.”

“We had to win. We had to pull through and come out on top,” he said. Hayun told Netanyahu that he had acted based on what he’d seen on a TV show and helped stabilize the plane.

Flydubai said on-duty crew who were onboard the flight were able to land the plane.

Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and Yaniv Hayun, a flyDubai passenger who helped subdue the attacker during the incident on Wednesday. GPO via Reuters

Motive under investigation

Netanyahu said it was still too early to determine why the pilot apparently stabbed his colleague and appeared to try to take over the Flydubai flight, and whether there was any Iranian involvement.

“We’ve had signs that Iran, in particular through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad,” he said. “But I think it’s too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here.”

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, meanwhile, branded the incident a “jihadist terrorist attack attempt,” without expanding on how he reached that conclusion.

President Donald Trump also weighed in, calling it “an incredible story.”

“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job, and he stabbed the pilot,” Trump told reporters.

On Thursday, Trump told reporters at the White House that the pilot who initiated the attack could be linked to Iran.

“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes. But we’re working on it right now,” he said.

Asked if the pilot could have been radicalized or working with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, Trump replied, “Could have been, yeah.”

Trump also told reporters on Thursday that there would be renewed strikes against Iran if it was behind the attack.

Asked if the U.S. would retaliate against Iran if it was involved in the attack, Trump said, “Oh they’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry.”

“You just ask them,” he added. “They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”

All the passengers were Israeli, according to Netanyahu’s office. Four were dual American-Israeli citizens, two U.S. officials told NBC News.

With few details on the suspect or on any potential motive surrounding the incident, Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for Netanyahu’s office said there was a “strong opinion” that the incident was a terror attack “but we can’t be sure until we debrief everybody.”

A still image taken from video verified by NBC News shows a chaotic scene on the Flydubai plane as a man covered in blood receives treatment. via Telegram

An investigation by Saudi authorities is ongoing, David Mencer, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, separately said.

A senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation and a Saudi official also briefed on the probe said the stabbing increasingly looks like an act of terrorism based on early findings.

The United Arab Emirates’ Attorney-General, Dr. Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, separately ordered an investigation into the incident.

His office said the probe would seek to “gather information and evidence, establish the facts and circumstances of the incident, and determine the underlying motives,” in addition to examining “whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved any prior planning or direction.”

Hessa Alyahya, spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in the U.S., said authorities were waiting to determine whether the attack was a dispute between the pilots or whether it was an act sponsored by Iran or the Houthis.

Israel and Saudi Arabia do not have official diplomatic relations.

World.title: How 16 undecided voters are weighing their 2026 election options
World.content:
James Morton isn’t sure which party he’s going to support in November’s elections, and he doesn’t like his options.

Morton, a 67-year-old retired truck driver in Colorado, said Democrats have “gone too far to the left towards socialism,” while Republicans are “globalists” who “don’t care about the working-class people in this country.”

Morton, an independent who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, is leaning toward backing third-party candidates in races for the House and the Senate this year. But he said his decision will come down to the high cost of living.

“The No. 1 thing is getting the cost of things back down, inflation under control, and pretty much that’s it,” Morton said. He noted that he and his wife have been buying different groceries as they navigate high prices.

Morton is among the 5% of voters surveyed last month in a national NBC News poll who said they weren’t sure which party they wanted to see controlling Congress after this year’s elections. NBC News spoke with 16 of those undecided voters as they weigh their votes this fall, some of whom declined to share their full names discussing politics.

These voters feel little loyalty to either party — and many of them said that’s in part because they aren’t sure either party understands what’s important to them. Almost every one said high costs are top of mind.

In the NBC News poll, 50% of voters said they wanted Democrats to win control of Congress in the midterms, while 45% said they wanted Republicans to have control. How the undecided voters in between resolve their strong, sometimes conflicting feelings could ultimately decide what Congress looks like in 2027, from who controls the majority to how many seats that party holds.

Costs dominate

Voters’ focus on making ends meet has been standing out in recent polling. In the latest NBC News survey, voters ranked cost of living and inflation as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption and threats to democracy.

“I don’t like how expensive things are, and I don’t think anyone does,” said Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old security worker in Texas, who said he hasn’t decided whom to support in his state’s hotly contested races for governor and the Senate.

Joanne, a 72-year-old Vermont independent who works for a heating company, said she plans to sit out her state’s governor’s race, and she hasn’t decided whom she’ll support farther down the ballot.

“I just want somebody to bring some of these prices back down,” she said. Joanne said her husband relies on multiple medications, including insulin. “It’s pretty expensive and leaves nothing for anything else.”

Luke Melanson, 49, of Louisiana, who is retired from construction work, said the rising cost of groceries has changed how he shops.

“I’m not eating as much. I’m eating less food because I can only afford so much,” he said.

Melanson doesn’t identify with either political party, instead considering himself a libertarian, and he declined to say where he was leaning in the midterm election. But he is frustrated with both parties and wants to see new candidates emerge who can personally relate to his financial position.

“I want a plumber. I want someone that ran a smaller business, like a Kroger’s,” he said. “A teacher. I take anybody that isn’t a lawyer or someone so ultra-rich that the pay gap is so far they would never understand what I’m going through.”

Meanwhile, South Carolinian Darien Thompson, a 25-year-old unarmed security guard at a mall, sees gas as the biggest financial woe of the moment. The cost of his commute is only going up.

“It does take a mental load when it’s like, well, it’s going to cost this much to get to work and back, and I’m only making this much,” Thompson said.

It doesn’t bode well for his long-term hopes of owning a home, and he doesn’t see any current politicians stepping up to tackle the issues in a way that has earned his support.

“Politicians are getting into these petty squabbles,” he said. “But it’s, like, none of us can afford houses.”

Thompson doesn’t see himself voting for a Republican in November, but he’s still undecided. He has leaned Democratic before, voting for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but his vote this year will depend entirely on the specific candidate Democrats run in his area.

Ibraham, a 42-year-old truck driver in Ohio who isn’t registered with either party, said he plans to back Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown in the Senate race in his state. Ibraham supported Harris in 2024 and said his vote this year is driven almost entirely by the surging price of diesel and a higher cost of living.

“I’ve been driving for nine years. I’ve never seen anything like it. Never. Never, ever. Even during Covid, it didn’t get that high,” Ibraham said, noting that his weekly diesel costs have jumped from $2,000 to $3,500 or $3,700.

“I’m spending an extra $1,500 on diesel every week. Just think about it — it’s a fortune,” he said.

Down on both parties and Trump

Ibraham described his support for Brown as more about opposing Republicans than endorsing Democrats, blaming the GOP-controlled White House and Congress for the current economic struggles.

“It’s not about Brown,” Ibraham said of his Senate vote. “It’s just voting against the Republicans for what they’re doing. That’s it.”

Other voters who were undecided but leaning toward Democrats expressed similar views, expressing caution and saying their potential support for Democrats was motivated more by reining in Trump and Republicans.

Several voters — including those who backed Trump two years ago — specifically voiced concerns about Trump’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran.

“I will probably support [a] Democrat this time around just so there’s some check and balances in place,” said Aaron L., a 30-year-old California independent who works in tech. He didn’t vote in 2024 while he was moving, but he said he most likely would have voted for Trump. But nearly two years into Trump’s second term, Aaron said, the economy is “a mess.”

“It seems like the party, the Republican Party, just follow whatever Donald Trump says,” Aaron said.

Like other undecided voters, Aaron said the economy and the war in Iran were among his top issues. Dissatisfaction with the war was high, including among Trump voters.

“One of his platforms was no more useless wars, and here we are — we’re back,” said Kevin, a 35-year-old civil engineer in Massachusetts. Kevin, a Democrat, voted for Trump in 2024 hoping he would boost the economy.

This year, he said, he is leaning toward supporting Republican Mike Minogue in the Massachusetts governor’s race, hoping he could shake up the state, and leaning toward backing Democratic Sen. Ed Markey for re-election.

“It goes back to the checks and balances,” Kevin said of the possibility that he could split his ticket, saying he wants to see a Democratic-controlled Congress end the war in Iran.

Kaleb Saracino, 21, of Nevada, doesn’t like how many resources are being poured into the Iran war or the idea that the U.S. is fighting there in behalf of Israel. He said he wants the government to cut off support for Israel, bring down costs and refocus on issues affecting everyday Americans.

“The cost of groceries, the cost of gas, the cost of living have all gone up because of these endless wars,” Saracino said.

Saracino knows he doesn’t want to support Trump, so he’s leaning toward the Democrats this year. But he doesn’t have warm feelings for either party.

“They’re looking out for themselves, their careers, because they’re career politicians, not so much the betterment of the American people,” Saracino said about both Republicans and Democrats.

Alexis, a 20-year-old college student in Florida, also expressed frustration with both parties in Washington.

“They’ve made a bunch of promises that haven’t been fulfilled, and you know why? It’s because people cannot talk to each other these days. Congress is so divided,” she said.

Alexis, an independent who voted for Harris in 2024, isn’t sure whom she’ll support in the Florida Senate race. She said more could get done “when we start allowing younger candidates who are more open-minded to vouching for the American people as a whole, rather than their own specific party.”

Essen Zali, a 46-year-old IT consultant from Texas, voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but backed Trump in 2024 after he became frustrated with Biden during the conflict in Gaza. Now, the Iran war has again left him frustrated.

“He went two steps forward with the whole war thing, and now we are all over the place,” he said. On top of that, Zali said, Trump seems focused on the wrong things.

“All the construction work that was going on in Washington, that was not ever required. All the beautifications and everything, that’s secondary. The tariff war without a reason,” Zali said. “It seems like he is burning all the ships.”

Connor Woodring, a 22-year-old independent from Colorado, also supported Trump in 2024. He was another voter who felt disdain for both parties.

“They’re one on the same side of the same coin, basically. Republicans are the warmongering side of it. Democrats are the side that try to pull at your heartstrings,” he said. “Either way, they’re going to vote and do the same thing they’ve done for the last 50 years, so it doesn’t matter which side you vote in.”

Woodring is a registered independent and doesn’t like any candidates in his area. His preference is to vote for someone not in either major party.

But, he said, “there’s a lot that can happen between now and November.”

World.title: Crew docks at space station with astronaut who'll miss birth of 3rd child
World.content:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket took off on a flight to the International Space Station Thursday carrying two NASA astronauts, a cosmonaut and a Canadian crew member whose wife plans a launch of her own later this year, giving birth to the couple's third child while her husband is in space.

Strapped into a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule, Crew 13 commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk blasted off from pad 40 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 11:10 a.m. EDT.

The launch originally was planned for mid-September, but the flight was delayed to replace a valve in the Crew Dragon's propulsion system.

A SpaceX Falcon 9 carrying a crew of four lifts off on a mission to the International Space Station on Oct. 1, 2026. SpaceX

Watkins, who holds a Ph.D. in geology, flew to space aboard a Crew Dragon in 2022. Her crewmates are space rookies — the 296th, 297th and 298th astronauts to fly aboard the ISS. Delaney and Kutryk are both former military test pilots while Teteryatnikov served in the Russian submarine force before becoming a cosmonaut.

L-R: Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov ahead of launch on Oct. 1, 2026. NASA/Joel Kowsky / Handout / Getty Images

Kutryk and his wife Heather have two children, ages 5 and 7. They're expecting their third child around Thanksgiving, about two months into the Crew 13 mission. They will become the fourth couple in the history of space travel to have a child born while one parent was off the planet.

"Leaving these three (plus one on the way) is the hardest thing I've ever done," he wrote in a pre-launch post on X.

"But that has always been the nature of exploration. Words from Fridtjof Nansen, describing his departure for the North Pole, resonate in my mind," he continued. "'Behind me lay all I held dear in life. And what lay before me? Happy child, little do you know what life is - how strangely mingled and how full of change... and now, a farewell to home. It was the darkest hour of the whole journey.'"

During a launch pad visit, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, his wife Heather and their two children enjoyed an up-close view of the Crew Dragon ferry ship that will carry him to the space station. Joshua Kutryk

Despite President Trump's recent animosity toward Canada, the Canadian Space Agency continues to play a major role in the U.S. space program. Along with supplying the robot arms that helped build the space station, CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon on NASA's Artemis II mission. Kutryk is the 17th Canadian to fly in space.

"When I think about the space station, I hope the legacy is that people see this beacon in the sky going around Earth, one of the most complex things humans have ever, ever created, and they see it for all of its technical marvel and all the science and discoveries we're making there," said Kutryk.

"But (I hope) they also see it as sort of this beacon for what we can do when we make good decisions, when we work together and we collaborate and we prioritize things. It's testament to what we've done, what we can do, and really to what we hope the generations that follow can do."

A camera mounted on the Falcon 9's second stage captures a spectacular view of the Crew Dragon spacecraft separating to fly on its own, setting off on an 8-hour trip to the International Space Station. SpaceX

After boosting the Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon capsule out of the dense lower atmosphere, the Falcon 9's first stage flew itself back to a pinpoint landing at the Space Force station while the rocket's upper stage continued the climb to space. Minutes later, the second stage engine shut down and the crew capsule separated to fly on its own.

"What an epic ride!" Delaney radioed. "What an epic ride it was! Today, we proudly continue the streak of humans living and working in orbit, building on the legacies of yesterday to pave the way for future of space exploration. Huge thanks to the phenomenal teams at NASA, SpaceX, and all of our partners. ... Deepest appreciation to my family and friends who stood by me throughout this entire endeavor. Thank you. I love you guys. And to the Marines back on Earth, Semper Fi."

Flight to space station

Like all flights to the International Space Station, piloted and unpiloted alike, the Crew 13 launch was timed for the moment Earth's rotation carried the pad into the plane of the station's orbit. That's a requirement for rendezvous missions because no current rockets have the power to overcome their orbital momentum and change their direction of travel when moving at nearly 5 miles per second.

While a Falcon 9 cannot change orbital planes, the Crew Dragon capsule can change its altitude as required, flying lower — and faster — to catch up with its quarry and higher to slow down the approach.

In this case, it took the Crew 13 capsule just 8 hours to catch up with the ISS, moving in for an automated docking at the forward port of the station's Harmony module shortly after 7 p.m. ET.

"I personally am looking forward to returning to the ISS as well as flying on Dragon a second time, and really looking forward to experiencing those experiences through the eyes of my crewmates," Watkins said.

"We expect a very busy mission with lots of station maintenance, both internal and external, with a few EVAs (spacewalks) on the docket as well as visiting vehicle capture and stowage operations, lots of science ... and plenty of outreach."

Standing by to welcome Watkins and company aboard will be the crew they are replacing: Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir, pilot Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. They're wrapping up a 235-day mission that began with launch atop a Falcon 9 rocket on Feb. 13.

Also on board: Soyuz MS-29/75S cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and NASA astronaut Anil Menon, launched on a Soyuz 2.1a rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on July 14. They're in the midst of an eight-month stay, returning to Earth in early April 2027.

The Crew 13 fliers will be joining seven crew members already aboard the space station. Clockwise from center left: Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir, pilot Jack Hathaway, Soyuz cosmonaut Anna Kikina, cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, astronaut Anil Menon, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and cosmonaut Pyotr Dubrov. NASA

After an expedited "crew handover," during which Meir and her crewmates will show their replacements the ins and outs of station operations, Crew 12 will board their own Crew Dragon capsule and return to Earth. Undocking is planned for Oct. 5 with splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the Southern California coast just past noon EDT on Oct. 6.

"I think the thing that I'm looking forward to most is seeing my 3-and-a-half-year-old daughter," said Meir, a two-flight veteran with seven spacewalks to her credit. "I'm so looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves, experiencing all those things that we don't have up here.

"But I will very, very much miss being weightless all the time and the incredible views that we have."

Said Hathaway: "Going home and being able to take a nice long hot shower will be very relaxing and very nice. And, of course, I'm looking forward to seeing my family. But a hot shower is near the top of my list."

Crew 12's departure will free up the Harmony module's space-facing port for the arrival of a SpaceX Cargo Dragon on Oct. 13 that will be loaded with crew supplies, science gear, spare parts and two roll-out solar array panels. The Crew 13 fliers also expect to welcome a Northrop Grumman cargo ship in December, along with two Russian Progress freighters in November and February.

European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot takes in the view of Earth from the space station's multi-window Cupola compartment. NASA

The roll-out solar arrays going up on the next Dragon Cargo ship are the final sets in a major upgrade to the station's original solar power system that began with initial installations in June 2021. The final two sets will be installed during spacewalks late this month and early November.

But the major goal of the flight, like all NASA missions to the station, is conducting research in the microgravity environment of space. Scores of experiments and technology demonstrations are running at any given moment with fresh studies going up on virtually every flight.

The Crew 13 fliers will face the same challenges.

"During the mission, the crew will help us fight heart disease and Parkinson's disease by studying human stem cell-derived tissues that will help improve medicine, disease modeling, and pharmaceutical testing," said Dana Weigel, director of NASA's low-Earth orbit mission directorate.

"They will also explore crop production that's important for longer-duration spaceflight missions, and they'll help us better understand blood flow abnormalities that we see in space, along with testing new diagnostic medical equipment for monitoring crew health. That's just a couple of the highlights of the research the crew will be doing on board."

All in all, Hathaway said, the crew is looking forward to an action-packed stay in space.

"For me, between the science, the spacewalks and everything else that the expedition is going to have, it's looking to be a great time," Delaney said. "Excited to launch with this crew, join the expedition, and integrate as an extension of NASA and all the ISS team members. So exciting times ahead!"
