World.title: Montreal hospital isolates patient exhibiting Ebola symptoms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Montreal hospital has isolated a female patient presenting with symptoms of Ebola, a deadly virus, officials said.

The patient arrived at the Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM) late Thursday afternoon exhibiting signs of the disease.

Irène Marcheterre, a spokesperson for the CHUM, said that as soon as the suspicious symptoms were identified, the hospital immediately enacted its required isolation protocols.

The hospital reiterated that all necessary safety measures have been put in place and stressed that there are currently no concerns regarding public exposure.

The suspected case comes amid an ongoing and deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where thousands have died in recent months.

Marcheterre could not confirm whether the patient had recently travelled from the region, stating she did not know the woman's travel history.

World.title: Tsawwassen First Nation identifies 2 elders killed in crash outside mall
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Tsawwassen First Nation has identified the two elders who were struck and killed outside the Tsawwassen Mills mall on Wednesday while a National Day for Truth and Reconciliation event was taking place.

In a social media post, the nation identified the victims as wilapiya (Barb Joe) and Virginia Splockton.

The nation described Joe as a "cultural pillar, knowledge keeper and matriarch" who was responsible for reviving the hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓ language.

Splockton is being remembered as beloved family member and pillar of the community with a deep love for crafting, drumming, singing and who "was always willing to lend a helping hand to those in need."

The elders' families, in the social media posts shared by the First Nation, thanked the community for the outpouring of support they have received in the wake of the tragedy.

WATCH | 2 elders killed in Wednesday crash: 2 Tsawwassen First Nation elders killed after driver crashes into crowd | Duration closed caption 3:08

The deadly collision occurred around 10:25 a.m. PT on Sept. 30, when police say a vehicle struck four pedestrians outside the mall.

Two were killed, while two others were taken to hospital.

The driver of a the vehicle received medical attention following the crash and has since been released from hospital.

In an update earlier Thursday, police say the two people taken to hospital remain in critical condition, with "serious, life-altering injuries," according to Delta Police Department Staff Sgt. Mike Whiteley.

WATCH | Police provide Thursday update: Police provide update on fatal Tsawwassen Mills collision | Duration closed caption 7:19

The two people who were injured are not members of the Tsawwassen First Nation, Whiteley added.

"This was a very tragic event," Whiteley told reporters at a news conference on Thursday afternoon.

"It was very difficult for our first responders, but also for our community, and especially for the Tsawwassen First Nation."

While the crash happened while a Truth and Reconciliation Day Walk was taking place elsewhere on the mall property, police say there is no evidence linking the collision to the event.

Police said Wednesday that the male driver of the vehicle may have suffered a medical emergency in the moments leading up to the crash. They did not elaborate on what that medical emergency was.

"At this time, there is no information to suggest the collision was intentional," Delta Police said in its Thursday news release.

First responders are seen at Tsawwassen Mills mall in Delta, B.C., on Wednesday after the crash. (Johna Baylon/CBC)

Video from the scene of the crash on Wednesday shows a pickup truck with the logo for the company Alpine Building Maintenance printed on its side.

In a statement Thursday, the company confirmed one of its vehicles was involved in the collision.

"We are co-operating with the appropriate authorities to support their investigation. Our thoughts are with everyone affected," it said.

WATCH | Delta councillor offers condolences to Tsawwassen First Nation: Tsawwassen crash a tragic turn of events for community: councillor | Duration closed caption 3:42

No charges have been sworn as of Thursday afternoon, police said.

"If the evidence warrants us forwarding charges to Crown counsel, then we'll be doing that," Whiteley said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and leaders on the B.C. election campaign trail — David Eby, Emily Lowan and Lorne Doerkson — expressed their condolences to the families and the First Nation after the crash on Wednesday.

The Indian Residential School Survivors Society said in a post on social media that the loss of the two "beloved" elders is devastating, while the Huu-ay-aht First Nations on Vancouver Island said it feels the tragedy deeply as an elder who died was a grandparent of one of its citizens.

A statement from the Tsawwassen First Nation said its offices would be closed on Oct. 1 and 2, as it works to support the families of those affected in the crash. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

In a statement issued Thursday, the Tsawwassen First Nation requested privacy as it grieved the loss of the two elders, adding that its offices would be closed on Oct. 1 and 2.

"Two beloved [elders] from our community lost their lives. Our hearts are with their families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss. We are also holding close in our thoughts those who were injured and everyone who witnessed this tragedy," the statement reads.

"We recognize the profound impact this tragedy has had on our community as a whole. During this incredibly difficult time, we are grateful for the care, compassion, and support that has been extended to Tsawwassen First Nation."

World.title: Trump's trade rep sounds pessimistic about deal with Canada, saying issues are 'quite difficult to resolve'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he regularly speaks with his Canadian counterpart, but the two sides have reached an impasse on some trade irritants and there's no sign of a resolution any time soon.

Speaking to reporters at the G20 meeting of trade ministers in Milwaukee, Greer sounded pessimistic about the prospect of a deal with the Canadians saying while "technical talks" are ongoing between trade experts from both countries there are some fundamental disagreements.

"The reality is there are a handful of outstanding issues that are quite difficult to resolve," Greer said.

Greer said the Trump administration's policy of imposing tariffs on foreign manufactured goods to try to "reindustrialize" America is a universal one and not "focused on one country."

Canada, meanwhile, maintains that punishing tariffs on industrial products like steel, aluminum and autos make no sense given just how integrated the two economies are after decades of free trade.

The federal government has strenuously opposed U.S. tariffs designed to decimate those key Canadian sectors, saying it's no way to treat a supposed ally. Plus, Canada is America's biggest customer, purchasing more American-exported goods than any other country.

U.S. losing manufacturing jobs

Still, Greer said Canada and other countries treat the United States as "a dumping ground" for their products and the U.S. just wants to produce more of what it consumes domestically. He added that these policies shouldn't be read as "threats against Canada" alone.

Despite Greer's claims that these tariff policies are boosting industrial employment, data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics compiled by the Economic Policy Institute shows that some some, 62,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost since Trump took office for his second term in January 2025.

WATCH | Carney laughs at Trump's claim that Canada will apologize to U.S.: Carney laughs at Trump's claim that Canada will apologize to U.S. | Duration closed caption 0:45 Asked by CBC News about U.S. President Donald Trump's comment on Monday that Canada will soon apologize to get a trade deal, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada 'stands ready to negotiate in good faith' for a deal that 'respects both our countries' sovereignty.'

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, who is responsible for non-U.S. trade, met with Greer while in Wisconsin.

The conversation was focused primarily on wider world trade issues like ending forced labour and the phenomenon of some countries like China dumping heavily state-subsidized products into market economies.

But the Canada-U.S. dispute did come up, Sidhu said in an interview with CBC News.

He said he stressed to Greer that the two countries need to "find a way to work together, especially for our auto supply workers."

"I think there is energy from both sides," Sidhu said, calling it a "very cordial conversation."

"But we want a good deal," he said. "We won't accept anything less."

Greer downplays Trump's deal comments

Speaking earlier Thursday to Bloomberg News from the summit, Greer seemed to downplay President Donald Trump's assertion this week that the Canadians would come calling for a deal and that something could come together within a month.

"You've heard the president talk about this. Most recently he said, 'Well, we may have a deal with Canada in a few weeks.' I'd emphasize the 'may' in that part of the situation," Greer said.

Greer reiterated that the U.S. is open to a deal with Canada, but he suggested Prime Minister Mark Carney and his negotiators can't accept what the Americans are offering.

"The question is does Canada want to get to 'yes' on some of these things. We have a trade policy where we're not inclined to go to zero tariffs because we're trying to reshore," he said. "Gaps remain between Canada and the United States."

Greer attends the first day of the G20 Trade Ministerial Conference in Milwaukee on Wednesday. (Kamil Krzacysnki/Getty Images)

Those "gaps" became apparent when Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, with Carney pulling his negotiators back from Washington after what he described as a series of last-minute American changes that weren't workable for Canada.

Canada was concerned about U.S. tariffs on medium- and heavy-duty trucks, which could have made a GM plant in Oshawa, Ont., that produces Chevrolet Silverados uncompetitive and imperiled the planned production of Ford F-250s in Oakville, Ont.

Carney also said he couldn't accept language in the proposed deal that could have compromised Canada's sovereignty, namely provisions he described as limiting the government's ability to make trade deals with other countries.

U.S. opposition to Canadian policies designed to promote the "discoverability" of French-language programming on streaming services was also an issue, Carney has said.

While Greer seemingly backed down from U.S. demands on French-language content in an interview with CBC News, no apparent progress has been made on those other issues in the weeks since the bilateral talks imploded.

Carney said this week he thinks it's possible to negotiate a "mutually advantageous trade arrangement" with the U.S. at some point in the future.

"Canada stands ready to negotiate in good faith," he said.

World.title: Joshua Kutryk's launch to the ISS is another example of the important role Canada plays in space exploration
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian Joshua Kutryk is in space, on his way to the International Space Station (ISS) after a flawless launch from Cape Canaveral, Fla.

The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket blasted off at 11:10 a.m., right on time.

He and his crewmates — NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov — are slated to dock with the ISS after roughly eight hours in space.

The launch is Kutryk's first, and he felt it.

"I'm in space. I don't really believe it yet. It does feel weird, though," he said. "It's good to be here."

WATCH | 'It does feel weird': Canadian astronaut on entering space: 'It does feel weird': Canadian astronaut on entering space | Duration 2:06 'I don’t really believe it yet,' says Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, as he enters space. Crew-13 is on its way to the International Space Station (ISS) in a joint NASA-Space X mission. Kutryk joins NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, who make up the rest of the crew on board SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft. The team will join several astronauts already on the ISS to conduct several experiments, some of which are Canadian. The spacecraft's journey to the ISS takes roughly eight hours.

This is a historic moment for Canada. It's the first time two Canadians have launched into space in such a short time. Jeremy Hansen launched as part of NASA's Artemis II mission for a trip around the moon only six months ago.

Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly was at the NASA press site shortly after the launch and noted the important role Canada has played and can play in space.

"It's been a big year, a big year for Canada," she said.

"And now we look forward to seeing how Josh Kutryk's work will continue to obviously participate in international efforts about space exploration and space co-operation, but also to inspire so many young Canadians and older ones that are very much fascinated by space."

Canada's continuing role

Undoubtedly, there have been tensions between Canada and the U.S., but not when it comes to space.

While it's true that NASA has cancelled Lunar Gateway, which would have included Canadarm3, it wasn't due to any political strain between our two countries. Rather, it was a shift in mission priorities brought forth by NASA administrator Jared Isaacman.

Earlier this year, Isaacman announced that NASA was adding a mission to the Artemis Program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface by 2028. And that resulted in the cancellation of the lunar space station and a focus on constructing a lunar base.

WATCH | Blast-off of Crew-13: Blast off for Crew-13 | Duration 1:17 Here is the launch moment of Crew-13 from Cape Canaveral, Fla., on their way to the International Space Station. On board is Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk who is a member of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13. The team will join astronauts who are already on the ISS to conduct several experiments, some of which are Canadian. The crew is expected to live and work on the station for roughly six months.

Asked by the CBC at the post-launch news conference about Canada's collaboration with NASA in its future plans, Isaacman hinted that Canada could play a vital role in the future of a lunar base.

"Canada has immense expertise in robotics, clearly, as demonstrated from the Canadarm performance from shuttle to the ISS," he said.

"As the base becomes operational, it should almost be the last choice to send somebody outside in that very demanding and dangerous environment. And you're going to need extensive robotic capabilities … and we're going to be counting on it as part of the architecture."

It's not only robotics that Canada is looking to contribute, but also lunar rovers.

In December 2025, the CSA awarded four Canadian organizations with contracts totalling $3.2 million for the development of a lunar utility rover that would be used for science, transportation and more to support astronauts on the lunar surface. (Unfortunately, in March the CSA announced the cancellation of another, smaller rover that would have conducted scientific missions on the moon.)

WATCH | Canadian Joshua Kutryk lifts off for a 6-month ISS mission: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk lifts off for 6-month ISS mission | Duration closed caption 6:12 Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov are on their way to the International Space Station aboard a SpaceX Dragon capsule for a six-month mission of scientific research, station maintenance and operations.

"We want to play a bigger part in everything linked to space exploration, but particularly with the moon," Joly said on Thursday. "Being able to have more of a Canadian presence, particularly on the robotic side."

Part of Isaacman's Artemis program restructuring included the speeding up of launches in the Artemis program.

On Thursday, Joly said Canada is ready.

"We know that NASA wants to go further, faster," she said. "We want to do more of that."

World.title: West Coast oil pipeline becomes 1st project designated in national interest
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A proposed pipeline carrying one million barrels of oil a day from Alberta to the B.C. coast has become the first project designated in the national interest, the federal and Alberta governments have announced.

Listing the West Coast pipeline — which will now officially be named the Pacific Link pipeline — on Schedule 1 of the Building Canada Act means the federal government has moved from considering whether it should be built to how it will be built by fast-tracking and consolidating the approval process, including environmental assessments.

"Before the Building Canada Act, proponents would have to spend years and potentially billions of dollars doing this work before even knowing where the federal government stood on the project," Carney said in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Thursday.

"For many builders, the risk was not worth it. So, Canada stopped building. Now, the federal government is making its position clear at the beginning of the process, rather than at the end."

WATCH | Carney designates new pipeline project of national interest: Pacific Link pipeline listed as 'project of national interest,' says Carney | Duration closed caption 1:40 Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Major Projects Office will work to 'finalise conditions' by Sept. 1, 2027 to 'get shovels in the ground' on an oil pipeline to B.C.'s southern coast.

A senior government official told reporters in advance of the announcement that the pipeline is expected to boost Canada's GDP by up to $30 billion annually — $20 billion of that coming from the pipeline itself.

By diversifying Canada's exports away from the U.S., officials said Canada will be able to charge a higher price for the oil it currently ships south of the border, providing what could be an additional $10 billion a year in revenues.

The federal government also said that once approved, the project will create up to 140,000 jobs.

Dominic LeBlanc, the minister of one Canadian economy, has been tasked with completing the conditions document setting out the requirements for the project by Sept. 1, 2027, allowing construction to begin, with a view to having the pipeline up and running by 2032-33.

Carney said the work of crafting those conditions will be supported by the Major Projects Office and the Canada Energy Regulator who will hold consultations with stakeholders to determine environmental protections, oversight, Indigenous ownership and local hiring.

The estimated cost of the project is between $35.2 billion and $43.7 billion, which includes a contingency.

The Alberta government and the federally owned Trans Mountain Corporation would each own 45 per cent of the pipeline, with the Calgary-based Pembina Pipeline Corporation owning a 10 per cent stake through the construction phase.

Once the pipeline is up and running, the Pembina Pipeline Corporation will have the opportunity to purchase an additional 10 per cent stake.

Carney said that Indigenous communities will be offered a minimum 10 per cent ownership stake in the project.

Increasing private sector ownership

While the pipeline is 90 per cent owned by the federal and Alberta governments, a senior official speaking on background explained that there are investors poised to take part.

The official said that those investors are currently watching to see if Canada is capable of fast-tracking the approval and construction of the Pacific Link by 2032-33.

Workers lay pipe during construction of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion on farmland, in Abbotsford, B.C., in 2023. A new West Coast pipeline will ship one million barrels of oil a day from Alberta to the B.C. coast once it opens in 2032-33. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Those investors are cautious, the official explained, because of how fraught the approval process was for the Trans Mountain Pipeline and how long it took to build.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told CBC's Power & Politics that she views government involvement in this pipeline as a way to encourage private investors to take the lead on future projects.

"I think in order to give the industry confidence that we can get these kinds of major projects built, we have to walk every step of the way with them until it's completed," she told host David Cochrane.

WATCH | Pipeline's public-private ownership gives industry confidence: Alberta premier: Pipeline's public-private ownership gives industry confidence: Alberta premier | Duration closed caption 13:06 As Alberta's proposed pipeline to the West Coast becomes the first project to be designated in the national interest by the federal government, it still lacks a private proponent. With 90 per cent set to be publicly owned — with more potential private investment to come — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says the public-private partnership to build the pipeline will grow industry confidence.

Carney said Thursday's announcement — where Alberta, B.C. and Indigenous communities are all involved in the project — and that Canada's effective tax rate for investments has been cut to less than a third of the G7 average are reasons private investors will be attracted to the project.

"This is the best country in the world, major economy in the world, to invest. And I'm sure those companies and companies across the country will take that into account," he said.

Higher emissions, lower intensity

Thursday's announcement was welcomed by business groups such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which commended the Liberal government for providing up-front regulatory backing for the project.

"Getting our resources to Asia-Pacific markets is a path to more production, prosperity and a brighter future for workers, their families and communities," said the chamber's Bryan Detchou in a statement.

Environmental organizations like Greenpeace and the Pembina Institute, however, said Canada shouldn't be pulling more oil out of the ground.

"New oilsands and pipeline projects will drive emissions even higher," the Pembina Institute, which is not affiliated with the pipeline corporation, said in a post on X.

"Every fraction of a degree matters. Canada should be investing in cleaner, more resilient energy solutions."

WATCH | Carney says Pacific Link pipeline demonstrates 'power of Canada': Ahead of Alberta referendum, Pacific Link pipeline demonstrates 'power of Canada': Carney | Duration closed caption 2:51 Prime Minister Mark Carney said designating the Pacific Link pipeline in the national interest shows 'Canada is working,' when asked what message Albertans supporting a separation referendum should take from the announcement.

A government explanatory note says that while the pipeline "does not directly contribute to Canada's greenhouse gas emission reduction targets," it is a key part of plans to reduce emissions intensity, or emissions per barrel of oil produced.

That plan includes the Pathways Project, a carbon capture and storage initiative that Carney said will absorb as much as 16 million tonnes of carbon emissions annually and store them underground.

Rick Smith, president of the Canadian Climate Institute, told Power & Politics that Canada is nowhere near on track to meeting its emission reduction targets. He said the government will need to follow up with further climate policies in light of this new project.

"You're only going to reduce pollution from this increased oil production if you actually fix some of Canada's broken climate change policies," he told Cochrane. "But it's a work in progress."

Carney said that the Pathways Project is only part of his government's environmental mitigation plans which also include $1.2 billion in federal funding for ocean protections announced on Tuesday.

Carney said choosing a southern route, instead of a route through northern British Columbia, will ensure the project does not cross "highly sensitive ecosystems, including the Great Bear Sea."

The 1,200-kilometre pipeline will carry bitumen through Alberta from Bruderheim to a deepwater port near Delta, B.C, where infrastructure at the Roberts Bank terminal will be expanded.

Carney said his government's new oceans funding will include "a series of measures to protect the habitats of killer whales" during the expansion of Roberts Bank.

The federal government's explanatory note says an agreement in principle with Alberta to reduce methane emissions by 75 per below 2014 levels by 2035 is a key component of "Canada's plan to strengthen its position in global energy markets, as customers across the world prioritize low-carbon oil and gas."

NDP and Conservatives weigh in

NDP Leader Avi Lewis accused the Liberal government of rushing the project through the approvals process "while sweeping aside environmental protections."

"It is an offence to Canadian science, public health, collective safety and common sense. And it is a gift to an oil industry already on track to make $100 billion in wartime profits this year alone," he said.

"This project leaves Canadians bearing all the risks of a bad investment without any of the rewards."

Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about Prime Minister Mark Carney's plan to fast-track major projects and how that plan would affect environmental protection? Send us your questions before our Oct. 3 show.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party strongly supports a pipeline and congratulated Premier Smith for championing the project.

"It has taken Mark Carney almost a year and a half to put one proposal on a national interest list. We need a pipeline in the ground, not just on a list," he said.

"The federal government needs to get out of the way and let builders build, investors invest and workers work."

World.title: Edmonton man charged for alleged death threat against Mark Carney: RCMP
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Police arrested an Edmonton man accused of threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney, RCMP say.

Dwight Peter MacIntyre, 44, has been charged with uttering a death threat against Carney, following alleged social media activity last month, according to a Thursday news release from the RCMP Federal Policing Northwest Region’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team (INSET).

“People should not assume they can make threats online without consequences. When online comments cross the line into criminal conduct, police will investigate and take appropriate action to hold those responsible accountable,” Supt. Matt Johnson, officer in charge of national security with RCMP Federal Policing Northwest Region, said in the news release.

“Criminal online actions have real-world consequences, regardless of whether they are made behind a screen.”

Police said INSET started investigating on Sept. 4, after RCMP became aware of a user on X, formerly known as Twitter, who had allegedly posted threats targeting the prime minister. RCMP didn't provide additional details about the alleged threats.

On Sept. 9, five days after the investigation started, INSET officers arrested and charged MacIntyre in relation to the incident, RCMP said.

Police didn't say where the arrest happened. But in Thursday's statement, INSET officials thanked the Edmonton Police Service and the Alberta RCMP’s Parkland detachment for their support in the investigation.

MacIntyre is scheduled to appear at the Alberta Court of Justice in Edmonton on Nov. 25.

In Thursday's statement, RCMP warned " this is a time for increased vigilance," as the security environment in which public figures operate continues to evolve within Canada and abroad.

MacIntyre is not the first person to have allegedly threatened Carney since he took public office more than a year ago.

A Calgary man was arrested and charged last month, in connection with allegations he threatened to kill Carney. Two men in Quebec were also arrested earlier this year on similar allegations.
