World.title: Kyrylo Budanov: European security without the US would be ‘very dangerous’
World.content:
Russia’s intensifying aerial attacks on Ukraine are aimed at exhausting and intimidating the civilian population, Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, told Euronews in an exclusive interview.

 

“Civilians are being killed - women, children, elderly people, veterans of the Second World War,” Budanov said. “It is all truly terrible, especially when children are killed.”

Budanov described Russia’s approach as “classic terrorism”, saying its purpose was not only to inflict damage but to frighten the population.

Asked whether Moscow believed sustained attacks could exhaust Ukrainians and ultimately increase pressure on the government to make concessions, his answer was unequivocal: “Yes, they do believe that.”

But Budanov rejected the suggestion that Russia was adapting faster than Ukraine as Moscow deploys faster jet-powered drones, changes flight routes and carries out complex combined attacks.

“I don’t believe that Russia, in principle, is adapting faster than we are,” he said.

Instead, he said Ukraine was working to develop and deploy technological solutions to reduce the impact of Russia’s attacks, adding that protecting the civilian population the “number one task” in this effort.

Race to scale up new drone interceptors

One of those solutions is a new generation of Ukrainian interceptors designed to counter Russia’s faster jet-powered drones.

Budanov said the technology had moved beyond conventional testing and was already undergoing experimental use in combat.

“The issue is scaling up this technology,” he said.

“There are still engineering improvements to be made. They intercept Russian jet-powered drones in most cases, but there is still work to do. And then there is the question of mass production.”

Budanov said he believed Ukraine could reach the necessary scale before the most difficult period: the coming winter.

His confidence, he said, was based on having personally seen both the technology and its production.

“I have seen these developments, and I have seen the production,” Budanov said. “I am watching how the technological cycle is developing. They will make it in time.”

Deeper defence cooperation with Europe

Ukraine’s new defence technologies could also become part of deeper industrial partnerships with European countries.

Several countries have already signed cooperation agreements with Kyiv under Ukraine’s so-called Drone Deal framework.

Asked whether Ukraine’s latest technology for intercepting jet-powered drones could eventually form part of those agreements, Budanov said: “Anyone who has made such agreements with us has the right, so to speak, to continue negotiations on specific products.”

But he stressed that Ukraine’s own requirements would come first.

“We will be able to meet the demand of other countries when, first and foremost, we have met our own country’s needs for such products,” he said.

Budanov said future defence-industrial cooperation with European partners could take different forms, including joint ventures and, in some cases, production facilities abroad with Ukrainian engineers and shared ownership.

Such production could make sense where it offered advantages and where Ukraine remained the priority customer, he said. But some critical technologies, he argued, should remain inside the country.

Asked what Ukraine could bring to European defence partnerships that its partners could not develop as quickly themselves, Budanov pointed to two advantages: “The speed of implementing innovation, the speed of scaling production — in other words, mass production.”

‘Very dangerous’ for Europe without the US

Looking beyond defence-industrial cooperation, Budanov said it was still too early to define Ukraine’s place in Europe’s future security architecture because the framework itself had yet to take shape.

“What will the future security architecture of Europe actually be?” he said. “There is no answer to that question at the moment, but everyone is working on it.”

Once it was defined and formally agreed, he said, the role of each participating country would become clearer.

Asked whether such a system could work without the United States, Budanov was more explicit.

“I think those who will be developing this doctrine have to take absolutely different options into account,” he said. “But it seems to me that this is a bad option. A very bad one, very dangerous for Europe.”

Ukraine’s financing needs and economic future

Budanov also addressed Ukraine’s immediate financial requirements, saying Kyiv could already see how the greater part of its needs could be covered.

“We can see where the greater part can definitely be covered,” he said, pointing to ongoing negotiations between Ukraine, the International Monetary Fund and the European Commission.

He said Ukraine’s financial requirements would continue to change as the war evolved.

“Look at what is happening now with Russian missile and drone strikes,” he said. “Obviously, more is needed somewhere, but on the other hand, less is needed in other areas. All of this balances out.”

But Budanov drew a distinction between Ukraine’s immediate need to finance the war and the broader question of what its economy should eventually look like.

Longer term, he said he favoured a liberal, free economy with limited state intervention, alongside predictable tax policy and domestic stability.

“But right now, we have to survive,” Budanov said. “That is our main task - to survive here and now.”

He said the defence sector would require a different approach, particularly when it came to military-technical cooperation and arms exports.

“In any civilised country in the world, weapons are not simply sold left and right,” he said. “And Ukraine will not be an exception. There should simply be strict, transparent and understandable conditions for everyone.”

For now, he said, Ukrainian defence exports remained limited because of the country’s own wartime requirements.

Asked what success for Ukraine would look like years from now — economically, in attracting investment and bringing Ukrainians back home — Budanov offered a brief answer:

“A place in the world rankings that is not the one we have now.”

World.title: José Sevilla resigns as Unicaja chair and declines to remain at the bank
World.content:
José Sevilla, chairman of Unicaja, has announced his decision to stand down at the end of his term without seeking re-election, which is scheduled for next April. His departure, which will be formalised at the ordinary general meeting of shareholders, opens a new chapter in the leadership of the Málaga-based listed bank.

 

Sevilla took over the chairmanship on 5 April 2024 with a clear mandate: to restore calm within the institution and put behind it the turbulent governance crisis triggered by the merger with Liberbank. After two years focused on institutional stability, the executive has informed the bank’s highest governing body that he will complete his current term without aspiring to renewal.

In a market announcement filed with the Spanish National Securities Market Commission (CNMV), Unicaja has framed this handover within the usual protocols of its Succession Policy. Until the shareholders’ meeting is held, Sevilla will continue to perform all his non-executive duties at the head of the bank. The board of directors, for its part, has formally recorded its recognition and gratitude for the "valuable services" rendered by the executive throughout his tenure.

Agreed handover after internal peace

The announcement ushers in an orderly transition at the helm of the bank. According to Unicaja, Sevilla’s decision makes it possible to activate the Succession Plan ahead of time, so that the new chairman can be selected with sufficient notice and institutional safeguards.

The arrival at Unicaja of José Sevilla, the former chief executive officer of Bankia, put the finishing touch to the management reshuffle that followed the departure of Manuel Azuaga. His appointment as an independent director stabilised the command structure alongside the chief executive, Isidro Rubiales, paving the way in April 2024 for a smooth shareholders’ meeting that stood in stark contrast to the tensions of the previous year.

The turbulent episode of March 2023, when the "Málaga bloc" aligned with the Unicaja Banking Foundation voted down the ratification of two independent directors in order to regain control of the institution, now remains as the last major internal jolt.

With the tandem formed by Rubiales and Sevilla, the listed bank managed to straighten out its governance after the complex integration with Liberbank, ushering in a period of executive calm that it now hopes to prolong through this planned handover.

World.title: France: Media outlet publishes new antisemitic screenshots attributed to Jordan Bardella
World.content:
French media outlet Mediapart has published new material in the case of the antisemitic messages attributed to Jordan Bardella.

 

The investigative outlet on Thursday published screenshots of Facebook Messenger conversations involving him from 2013 and 2014, whose authenticity it says was established through a data extraction supplied by Meta and certified by a court bailiff, as Edwy Plenel, the outlet's co-founder, explained on Twitter.

Jordan Bardella's Antisemitic Writings: The Evidence of the Lie. Since our revelations, the Rassemblement National has violently challenged the work of « Mediapart ». Here are the documents at the heart of the investigation and the method used to authenticate them.

The investigation, conducted over several months, draws on dozens of written conversations and interviews with 18 people. The exchanges from 2013 and 2014 were passed on to Mediapart by two separate sources, both from Jordan Bardella's entourage. The outlet has stated the two sources are entirely separate and are not linked.

Jordan Bardella, who has denied from the very start of the affair that he is the author of these messages, filed a defamation complaint against Mediapart after the publication of the initial investigation.

The National Rally leader has so far rejected the accusations and on X denounced "crude fakes" and an operation designed to destabilise the presidential campaign. Within the RN, several senior figures have come out in support of him.

Beyond the far right, reactions have been more critical. On Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron described the remarks attributed to Bardella as "extremely serious and unacceptable", calling on the RN to clarify the situation.

World.title: Europe went all in on soft power for too long, Belgian defence minister says
World.content:
Both when it comes to defence capabilities and industry capacities, Europe is in a very difficult position, Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken told Euronews. He pointed to the bloc's decades-long prioritising of soft power as one reason for this.

 

His comments come as the European NATO members are ramping up defence spending and Brussels is rolling out policies to bolster the defence industry. While Francken sees progress being made, he warned Europe does not have all the capabilities it needs.

"Europe has been very good at investing in soft power, in social security, and it's beautiful to have a pension system, to have social welfare systems," Francken said in an interview at Euronews' Defence and Space Summit.

"When somebody gets sick, when somebody has lost his job, we have everything. But when there's war or when there is a hybrid threat, we don't have anything."

He noted that when it comes specifically to defence spending, Belgium has long been the bad apple.

"We neglected this for so long, we were like the worst pupil in NATO class," Francken said, again, referring to the emphasis put on soft power.

"We are the founding father of NATO; we're the founding father of the EU. I think that we always were there for diplomacy, for soft power, but when we talked hard power in Belgium, everybody was looking in the other direction."

Belgium reached NATO's 2% GDP defence spending threshold for the first time in 2025, rising from a low of 0.97% in 2014.

NATO wants that percentage to reach 3.5% by 2035; however, the country will remain at 2% until 2029 due to its challenging budgetary climate. Belgium currently has one of the worst budget deficits in the eurozone.

"Now we doubled the budget; we reached 2%. I know that we add two more, but it's quite a process. We're doing so much, but I cannot undo in 18 months of being a minister what has been neglected for 40 years."

Watch the interview with Theo Francken at the Defence and Space Summit here.

World.title: French protests over school conditions spread as students set fires and put up blockades
World.content:
A protest movement in France's high schools intensified on Thursday, with students setting fire to bins and erecting blockades outside schools in an increasing number of cities.

 

The students have been protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.

Several school principals have been injured, harassed or assaulted at high schools, according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.

Police have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycées, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France. There have been multiple reports of high school students being injured.

University students have now also joined the protest movement, and have blocked access to around 30 campuses across the country.

A security source said there had been 900 blockades or related incidents across the country on Thursday, with more than 160 schools shut down in Paris, Marseille and other cities.

In neighbouring Belgium, there were protests and damage at a handful of schools in the eastern city of Liege, police said.

Protesters demand better conditions

At a Paris high school where students barricaded an entrance, one 18-year-old student said protesters want to target “overloaded schedules, the system, the teachers, people who don’t listen to us, the university application process.”

High school students in France often start classes at 8 am and remain at school until late afternoon.

“Older people say, ‘Kids, go to school from 8 am to 6 pm every day.’ But you don’t know what that does mentally,” said another Paris high school student.

Clashes in Lille and Paris

In Lille, the protest led to particularly tense scenes. Bins were tipped over onto the road, projectiles were thrown and street furniture was damaged. Police intervened to disperse the demonstrators, charging into them and firing tear gas.

In Paris and in several communes in Île-de-France, clashes also broke out between young people and police. The movement had already led to several hundred arrests since the start of the week, mostly of minors.

Three investigations have also been opened by the IGPN after injuries sustained during blockades. In Tours, a student injured in the head on Wednesday was taken to hospital. According to the public prosecutor, his injuries were consistent with those of a non-lethal rubber bullet.

University students join the movement

After a first nationwide day of action on Tuesday, university students joined the movement on Thursday. Around 30 campuses were blocked, according to the France's leading students' union. Lower secondary schools were also affected in some regions.

Seconday and high school student organisations are calling above all for greater resources, replacement teachers and better teaching conditions. They say they intend to continue protesting, while the government now tries to contain the violence and keep access to schools open.

Political reactions

The government as well as far-right politician Marine Le Pen have accused the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the protests.

But LFI's candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Melenchon, said on Wednesday that his party "called for non-violent methods of struggle".

World.title: Palermo, first coffee grown and harvested in Italy: warmer climate is changing farming
World.content:
A plantation on the outskirts of Palermo has for the first time produced Arabica coffee beans grown and harvested entirely in Italy. The result, achieved on the Morettino family estate, has been made possible by climate change, which has effectively brought tropical temperatures to southern Italy.

 

While global warming had already enabled southern England to produce champagne-style sparkling wine, pushing the traditional growing areas of France and northern Italy further north, the jump made by coffee from equatorial zones to the Mediterranean is clearly even greater.

As the daily newspaper La Stampa reported on Thursday (source in Italian), the Sicilian plantation in the San Lorenzo ai Colli area, a few hundred metres above sea level, is currently producing around 100 kilograms of drupes (the fruit of the coffee plant, also known as cherries), which yield just over 15 kilograms of roasted beans.

The project, which involves the University and the Botanical Garden of Palermo (source in Italian) in studying how tropical crops adapt to the new Mediterranean climate, is still far from large-scale commercial production in terms of volume, but it already has considerable scientific and symbolic value.

Typical coffee makers used in Italy, on display at a 2013 exhibition in Milan by historic manufacturer Bialetti (AP Photo/Luca Bruno)

Where coffee is grown: the world’s main producing countries

Traditionally, coffee is grown in the planet’s tropical and equatorial regions, where high temperatures, humidity and steady rainfall favour its growth.

For this reason, the world’s main producers and exporters are largely concentrated in Latin America, Africa and Asia, with the Arabica variety, which delivers higher quality, grown at higher altitudes than Robusta.

The leading producer countries include Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Costa Rica in Latin America; Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania in Africa; and Vietnam and Indonesia in Asia.

According to the promoters of the initiative, the coffee produced in Palermo develops distinctive aromatic notes reminiscent of raisins, a feature that sets it apart from beans grown in traditional coffee-growing regions.

Before the Morettino family’s venture, a local farm had already grown coffee entirely in greenhouses (source in Italian) in Terrasini, also in the Palermo area.

Similar experiments have been attempted in various forms elsewhere in southern Europe.

In Spain, particularly in the province of Granada, experimental projects have been launched to test the resilience of the plants, with results quite different from those in Gran Canaria where, thanks to its more southerly latitude, coffee has been grown since the 19th century, taking advantage of the fertility and humidity of volcanic soils.

On the Azores islands in Portugal, where numerous private plantations have been reported that benefit from the mild climate, the archipelago marks one of the northernmost points where coffee is grown.

Former Italian prime minister and ECB president Mario Draghi sips an espresso during a break in proceedings in the Chamber of Deputies (18 February 2021) (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini)

How coffee consumption in Italy has changed

The growing interest in niche products such as the Sicilian coffee comes in a context in which Italy is the EU’s leading producer of roasted coffee, with over 400 tonnes produced in 2025.

The national coffee industry, although it relies on importing raw material from other producer countries (that is, unroasted beans, or "green coffee"), includes around a thousand roasters and generates an annual turnover of 5.9 billion euros.

The prospect of local cultivation, made possible by global warming, which is unfortunately also bringing more natural disasters, is in step with Italian consumption patterns, which remain robust and are growing, according to several studies published on 1 October to mark International Coffee Day.

According to a survey by AstraRicerche in partnership with the Segafredo brand, 82.6% of Italians consider the quality of the raw material decisive, while 71.8% pay attention to aromatic characteristics and 51.5% want to know the product’s origin and its journey along the supply chain.

Another survey, carried out by the Italian Coffee Committee of Unione Italiana Food and by Altroconsumo on more than 1,200 consumers, shows that three out of four Italians drink coffee regularly and almost one in two see it as one of the symbols of the country’s culture and lifestyle, on a par with pasta.

Among those who drink espresso, 83% have it every day, at home and at the bar, either with a moka pot or with modern capsule machines, which are now neck and neck in people’s habits.

Any commercial prospects must of course be weighed against environmental sustainability when growing coffee outside its traditional areas of origin.

Processing the beans after harvest can require between 50 and 200 litres of water for every kilogram of green coffee and produces wastewater which, if not properly treated, can affect local ecosystems.

And if, instead of the tropical rains that have always sustained coffee plantations, growing moves to areas where seasonal drought is becoming endemic, it becomes essential to match the agricultural challenge of coffee with a technological one, cutting the amount of water needed to grow and process the crop.

World.title: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'
World.content:
It may have taken a little longer than he would have liked, but Jürgen Klopp has finally won a game as Germany coach. Despite a number of debutants, it was a familiar face who stood out in the victory over Serbia.

After 47 days, three matches and 44 squad players, Jürgen Klopp has a first win as coach of Germany's men's fotball team. A straightforward 2-0 victory over Serbia in the Nations League on Thursday meant the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach avoided becoming the first Germany boss to win any of his first three games.

"I'm really happy today," Klopp told German public broadcaster ZDF. "We were outstanding when defending and when we had the ball. We simply played wonderful football."

Klopp had raised a few eyebrows by naming two squads for the four fixtures in this extended international window. But after a somewhat fortunate draw against the Netherlands and a shock loss to Greece with the more senior of the squads, it was left to those lower down the pecking order to get things going Thursday in Munich.

Bischof gets first goal on home turf

That meant a completely new starting XI and debuts to ‌goalkeeper Jonas Urbig ⁠and ⁠winger Derry Scherhant. Such players should "develop without the top dogs" Klopp said before the game. And while Urbig was untroubled by Serbia, his Bayern Munich teammate Tom Bischof made his mark by turning in the opener after Florian Wirtz, one of the sprinkling of senior players, hit the post. It was Bischof's first goal for Germany in only his second national team game.

Florian Wirtz (left) and Tom Bischof were Germay's goalscorers Image: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/AFP

"It's indescribable," said Bischof after the game at Bayern's Allianz Arena. "The stadium was on fire. I let it all out and was overjoyed." Unfortunately, he said, "my knees hurt a little from sliding on my knees. But that doesn't matter."

After a string of tournament failures, the latest new dawn for Germany comes with a little more patience. As well as Klopp's track record, there is a general acceptance from inside the country and abroad that Germany are no longer a top tier side.

"We're not the Bayern Munich of European football," Klopp said prematch. "We're a team that needs to find its footing."

Klopp: 'I liked everything'

While one win against a limited Serbia side will not change that, the emphatic nature of the performance impressed the new boss.

"I liked everything — the opening phase, the middle section, and the end. Our counter-pressing was off the charts," said the man whose Gegenpressing (Counter-pressing) tactic became his trademark at Dortmund. "We can afford to take all the liberties and risks we want when we win the ball back together. Everyone was there during our pressing moments."

The second half brought more debuts for players who may not have made a traditional 26-man squad. Cologne winger Said El Mala and Brentford's Vitaly Janelt made their Germany bows while Celtic's Mika Baur became the country's 1,000th men's international.

It was "surreal," Baur said. "Today was a highlight for everyone, not just for me with my debut."

Wirtz provides spark and hope

While Klopp may have seen enough from a few of the second string to afford them opportunities in the future, the performance of Liverpool midfielder Wirtz, who scored Germany's second goal, may be the most critical of the night.

Wirtz, 23, has struggled to find his best form in the Premier League and has blown hot and cold in his 47 caps for Germany. A cool and composed finish suggested that the player who was so highly regarded at Bayer Leverkusen can be coaxed to life by Klopp.

"It was loads of fun. Every single one of us gave it our all on the field. We stuck to the game plan and did almost everything right," said Wirtz, who took the captain's armband later in the game. "The players around me made it easy for me. We had a lot of movement in the middle. We were all fired up."

The challenge now for Klopp is to work out which of his wide pool of players are the ones he can rely on to take Germany to Euro 2028 and beyond. The next step is a chance for revenge against Greece in Thessaloniki on Sunday.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: UK police make another arrest in RAF Fairford case
World.content:
Counter terrorism police said a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five men arrested on Sunday remain on bail.

Police in the United Kingdom on Thursday said that another man had been arrested as part of the investigation into Sunday's security incident at a US-run air base in Gloucestershire.

The arrest of the dual UK-Iranian national came after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford."

Iran's embassy in London earlier said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation it was involved while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree."

What police have said

Counter terrorism police said that a 27-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was arrested in London "on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006."

They said that a second man who is a UK national was also questioned under caution and that searches of two properties had taken place.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," said Counter Terrorism Policing's Vicki Evans.

"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement. I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation," Evans said.

UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sunday's events at RAF Fairford

Five men in their 20s, all from the London area and with British citizenship, were arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran.

They were wearing face coverings.

Police seized three "suspicious" white vans and evacuated around 85 households in the vicinity, bringing in bomb disposal teams.

Police said a quantity of petrol was but no explosive devices were found in the vans.

The suspects have since been released on bail in a move questioned by US President Donald Trump.

Trump says RAF Fairford suspects known to US authorities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: On October 3, Latvians will elect a new parliament ― with Russia looming large over the campaign
World.content:
On October 3, Latvians will elect a new parliament with Russia looming large over the campaign. Security fears dominate the agenda, but so does a debate over the economic cost of cutting ties with Moscow.

Four German Air Force Eurofighter jets stand ready at Latvia's Lielvarde military air base, just 60 kilometers from Riga. The aircraft are part of NATO's efforts to strengthen Baltic air defenses on the alliance's eastern flank ahead. Germany sent the jets amid repeated drone incursions, which have put Latvia on alert ahead of the country's elections on October 3.

Security fears ahead of elections

Security has become one of the defining issues of this campaign — defense promises appearing on the programs of most of the leading parties in Latvia. And the Latvian public's anxieties aren't unfounded.

In recent months, several drones have entered Baltic airspace. The latest incident occurred on September 15 in Lithuania, when a drone believed to have crossed from Belarus was shot down by an NATO fighter jet.

On top of that there are hybrid threats, including migrant flows that Latvia and its neighbors say are being encouraged by Russia's ally Belarus to pressure the EU and test border security. Intelligence officials of several European countries, including Latvia and the Czech Republic have warned that Russia could seek to test NATO in the upcoming "months, not years."

Guard on the Latvian-Russian border. Image: Gints Ivuskans/AFP

"There are concerns in the West and also here in the Baltic states that Russia might be trying some further actions here in the Baltics," says Maris Andzans, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies in Riga. "If you want to test NATO, there is no better place than the Baltic states."

Near-unanimous agreement on defense

Latvia elects its 100-seat parliament, Saeima, through proportional representation, meaning coalition governments are the norm. Polls currently put the centrist United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs ahead, followed by the populist alliance Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and Latvia First led by Ainars Slesers. The center-left Progressives and the conservative National Alliance are also expected to enter parliament.

Most of these Latvian parties view Russia as a security challenge.

"The biggest threat is our neighbors, Russia and Belarus," says Agnese Kupca of the United List. "Our partners in the EU should understand: it is not only our border with Russia, but also EU and NATO border with aggressor."

Latvia is one of the few NATO members that have committed by law to spending 5% of GDP on defense, and analysts say the country's foreign policy orientation is unlikely to change regardless of which coalition emerges after the vote as there is nearly unanimous consensus on the importance of NATO. Which is backed by their voters: according to Friedrich Ebert Stiftung (FES) Security Radar 2025 Latvians generally have a positive view of NATO.

Unites List election campaign poster featuring Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs before the general election in Riga, Latvia. Image: Ints Kalnins/REUTERS

Economic concerns among voters

But while security policy enjoys broad agreement, the economic consequences of Latvia distancing itself from Russia remain contentious.

Before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia was among Latvia's most important trading partners. Since 2022, Latvia has reduced imports from Russia and Belarus by more than 90% and introduced some of the toughest restrictions in the EU on goods from the two countries. Latvia's economy has adapted, but businesses with strong pre-war links to Russia were among the hardest hit.

"This closeness to the theater of war has strongly influenced the investment climate," says political analyst Filips Rajevskis. "So the big question is how to increase the investments and grow the economy."

Many Latvians reject any economic cooperation with Russia on security grounds. Sixty percent said they want Latvia to reduce dependence on Russia, according to FES Security Radar 2025. "In the current situation, it's absolute nonsense. We can't watch what's happening and still be friends with Russia," one passerby in Riga told DW.

Not breaking up with Russia completely?

At the same time 20% of Latvians, according to FES, favor closer ties with Russia. Calls for a more pragmatic approach towards its eastern neighbor are not uncommon in the political debates.

Julija Stepanenko, leader of Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance, has repeatedly argued against completely severing economic ties with Russia and Belarus.

Earlier this year, it emerged that Stepanenko has received gifts worth roughly €400,000 ($470,000) from her father, a Russia-based businessman whose company manufactures construction materials, including anti-tank fortifications known as "dragon's teeth." But despite that, her party remains in second place in the polls.

When DW met Lyubov Shvetsova, one of Sovereign Power/Union of New Latvians party candidates at a campaign stand just outside the center of Riga, she rejected accusations that the party is pro-Russian.

"Our approach is pragmatism oriented toward the interests of Latvian business," she said.

Economic pragmatism

Another advocate of a more pragmatic economic approach is Ainars Slesers, former businessman and leader of Latvia First.

During an interview on Latvian public television earlier in September, Slesers argued that transit of goods with Russia should continue as long as it is not prohibited by EU sanctions.

His party has focused heavily on economic issues, arguing that Latvia should prioritize growth and investment over what it sees as excessive self-imposed restrictions. And this approach has found support: more than 9% are ready to vote for Latvia First, which is in third place in the polls.

However, discussions about fully restoring trade with Russia are premature, party member Edmunds Zivtins told DW. "As long as the war in Ukraine is ongoing, we cannot talk about it," he said.

Language and identity dividing Latvia

Analysts say such parties may attract some voters who feel alienated by Latvia's increasingly restrictive approach toward Russia.

Golden roofs atop Saints Boris and Gleb Orthodox Cathedral are seen over trees in the centre of Daugavpils, eastern Latvia. Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

The appeal is not necessarily driven by support for the Kremlin. Rather, it often comes from parts of the country's Russian-speaking minority who feel overlooked by mainstream parties and uneasy about policies such as the phase-out of Russian-language school education and the reduced role of Russian in public life.

About one-third of Latvia's population speaks Russian at home.

However, the outcome of these elections is hard to predict. Filips Rajevskis says many voters are hiding not only their party preference, but even their decision to go to vote ahead of elections.

As Latvians head to the polls, Moscow is shaping the campaign in ways both direct and indirect: as a security threat driving support for NATO and defense spending, and as an economic and cultural question that continues to divide parts of the electorate.

World.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties amid Tigray fighting
World.content:
Ethiopia said it was expelling Eritrean diplomats in response to Eritrea's "direct and indirect acts of hostility." Eritrea said it had "no choice but to reciprocate in kind."

Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties on Thursday after Ethiopia accused its northern neighbor of involvement in renewed fighting in the Tigray region.

The Ethiopian Foreign Ministry was the first to announce that it was shutting its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia."

The Ethiopian embassy ​in Eritrea had been reopened in 2018 as ​part of ⁠the rapprochement that culminated in Prime ⁠Minister ​Abiy Ahmed receiving the Nobel Peace Prize.

Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry also declared ten Eritrean diplomats "persona non grata", accusing them of "involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security." The Eritrean diplomats were given 48 hours to leave the country.

Hours later, Eritrea's Foreign Ministry called the move "absurd" and said the expulsion of ten of its diplomats from Addis Ababa had effectively shuttered its embassy there.

Eritrea said it therefore had "no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries ​that this entails."

Reports of earlier blast at Ethiopian military headquarters

The measures came following reports of an explosion overnight at Ethiopian military headquarters in Addis Ababa.

The AFP news agency reported that the explosion took place at the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) headquarters between midnight and 1:00am local time, citing diplomatic and security sources with the information.

The sources could not provide further information relating to the nature of the blast or who was responsible, or if there had been any casualties.

The Associated Press, citing security sources, reported that there had been three blasts that came after the government banned the use of drones in the capital.

It's not clear whether the blasts were related to any attack or whether they had been part of training exercises.

Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Eritrea has denied allegations that it supports an armed alliance — which includes the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) — currently fighting Ethiopian government forces. The coalition is named Alliance for Survival.

Hundreds have been killed and wounded since last week's resumption of heavy fighting in northern Ethiopia.

Clashes have been ongoing and have have taken place along several fronts.

The United Nations has called for de-escalation of the fighting and for talks between the government and the recently formed alliance.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: After 2 years in office, how has Claudia Sheinbaum changed Mexico?
World.content:
Two years after taking office as Mexico's first female president, Claudia Sheinbaum can take credit for a lower homicide rate and improved social benefits. But violence and corruption persist.

Since Claudia Sheinbaum first took office in 2024 as Mexico's first female president, she has largely adhered to the political agenda of her mentor and predecessor, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador.

But she has also had to contend with several problems that go far beyond Mexico's borders: violence inflicted by drug cartels, tens of thousands of missing persons and the growing political pressure from US President Donald Trump.

Fewer murders — but more missing persons

Sheinbaum has been able to report some progress when it comes to the security situation in Mexico. In her second government report, presented in September, she touted a 51% drop in the daily homicide rate since 2024.

To what extent this progress can be attributed to Sheinbaum's administration is, however, a matter of debate. While the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy has also noted progress in the effort to reduce homicides, the Mexico Evalua think tank has said there isn't enough statistical evidence to attribute the decline directly to measures taken by Sheinbaum.

The number of missing persons has increased by more than 20,000 during Sheinbaum's two years in office Image: Daniel Cardenas/Anadolu/picture alliance

And other indicators highlight a problematic trend. Mexico Evalua, referring to the government's own figures, pointed out that the number of recorded cases of kidnapping and enforced disappearances has surged by 127% over the last decade, "crimes against life" by 197% and femicide by 53%.

As of June 2026, the national register recorded a total of 135,271 missing persons. At the start of Sheinbaum's time in office in October 2024, that figure stood at around 115,000, according to an analysis by Red Lupa, a citizen-led network dedicated to monitoring disappearances.

"There is a lack of political will [to address the issue]," said Edgar Cortez, a project coordinator at the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy in Mexico City. On the one hand, he said, the government sees little political benefit, while at the same time it's lacking the technical expertise to coordinate the varied measures implemented at the state and federal levels.

Displacement — another consequence of violence — is also disrupting the lives of millions across the country. According to the National Institute of Statistics and Geography, violence or crime forced at least one member in 510,000 households — some 1.6 million people — to change their place of residence between October 2020 and October 2025.

Mexicans risk their lives to find missing family members To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Selective crackdown on corruption

Eduardo Bohorquez, director of civil society organization Transparencia Mexicana, told DW he has noted a shift in the government's strategy when it comes to fighting corruption. Two years on, he said the government is now focusing on the links between federal employees and organized crime.

As example he gave Operacion Enjambre, during which more than 100 public officials of varying political affiliation were arrested — including mayors, former mayors and police commanders, according to Mexico's security chief Omar Garcia Harfuch.

Critics, however, have accused the government of taking a selective approach. To date, no incumbent or former governor of Sheinbaum's ruling Morena party has been either prosecuted or detained for corruption or alleged links to organized crime.

Shienbaum has announced a package of reforms to tackle corruption, and Bohorquez said that will show whether or not her administration will actually chart a different course than that of her predecessor.

Placating Trump a top priority

Domestic and foreign policy have been closely linked during Sheinbaum's two years in office. Most of that time has been shaped by Donald Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, and his administration's increasing pressure on drug cartels, migration and trade.

Trump has accused Mexico of not doing enough to tackle the cartels, with Washington classifying several Mexican criminal organizations as terrorist groups. The US president has repeatedly threatened to take unilateral action against the cartels. Sheinbaum, however, has opposed any US military actions on Mexican territory, calling instead for "cooperation without subordination."

Sheinbaum (right) and Trump (center) were all smiles during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, co-hosted by the US, Mexico and Canada, but the relationship is far from easygoing Image: Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS

At the same time, Mexico and the US have been cooperating closely — especially when it comes to migration. Between 2024 and 2025, the number of migrant contacts registered by US authorities along the US-Mexico border dropped by more than 84%, from 1.5 million to around 238,000.

Economic cooperation is also key to the cross-border relationship. Mexico and the US are currently negotiating several trade issues, including the future of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, known as USMCA. For its part, Mexico is hoping to reduce Trump's tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles.

After talks with Trump in September, Sheinbaum said both sides were working toward a trade deal. It remains a tricky balancing act for the Mexican president — developing the closest possible trading relationship with her country's most important economic partner, while at the same time not giving the impression that Mexico is giving up its political sovereignty under pressure from Washington.

What is Mexico's US trade strategy? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Progress on social rights

The outlook is brighter when it comes to economic and social rights, with Cortez of the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy singling out the increase in minimum wage and government benefits for older people and those living with disabilities.

When it comes to other human rights concerns, however, he hasn't seen "any progress or setbacks." Alongside the staggering number of missing persons, Cortez also pointed out attacks on human rights defenders and journalists, along with a failure to sufficiently consult with Indigenous groups and rural communities when it came to major construction projects.

Sheinbaum has announced a plan to introduce a nationwide law against femicide that would align the various regulations on the local and state level, said Cortez. "That could end up being a positive, but the problem will be to put it into practice," he added.

Transparency without 'accountability'

The government's record on transparency remains problematic, according to observers, with Sheinbaum doing away with the National Institute for Transparency, Access to Information and Protection of Personal Data, or INAI. The responsibilities of the independent agency, which had been in place for two decades, have since been divided among several state entities.

"Instead of making things easier, everything has become fragmented," said Bohorquez of Transparencia Mexicana. Anyone looking for information from Congress, the judiciary, the military or local authorities now needs to go directly to the source.

Sheinbaum's daily press conferences are good optics but don't provide 'accountability,' say experts Image: Luis Barron/ZUMA/IMAGO

Bohorquez also gave a mixed reaction to Sheinbaum's daily press conference, saying that while it was "a very effective political communication tool it didn't provide accountability."

For Cortez, that reflects a fundamental question of Sheinbaum's political priorities. New social programs bring "instant political benefits," he said, while advancing on civil and political rights required long-term effort and didn't allow the government to "immediately capitalize on political gains."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Ethiopia: Who could bring the warring sides to the negotiation table?
World.content:
Ethiopia might be facing its most complex armed conflict in contempary times. The fragile 2022 peace deal has collapsed. International mediators have failed. How will the country manage to return to normal?

Just four years after a landmark peace deal officially halted the devastating Tigray war, fighting has escalated once again in northern Ethiopia in recent weeks.

Just days before full-scale fighting resumed, several armed groups which had previously considered each enemies formally announced an alliance with a common goal: To bring down Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.

But this time, the lay of the land looks quite different from the previous conflict: Parties outside the country have been accused of meddling in the situation, with each having their own motives to want to destabilize Abiy's government.

This has raised fears about prolonged instability hitting the Horn of Africa.

Reasons for the collapse of the peace deal

The 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the conflict between the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which cost hundreds of thousands of lives in the course of two years.

Negash Mohammed, a journalist with DW's Amharic department. believes that the deal collapsed for three key reasons — or rather because three key actors in the conflict were largely neglected at the negotiation table.

Mohammed explained that the ultimate agreement didn't factor in the role of Eritrea in the conflict, which had fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF; it ignored the part that Amhara militias — known as Fano — played in the war, who later felt sorely excluded from the negotiations; finally, it ignored harliners within the TPLF who viewed the peace peace as nothing but military defeat.

Tensions between the federal government and the Fano escalated further when Addis Ababa moved to forcibly disarm the militias instead of addressing their grievances.

"The federal government has its own shortcomings," said Mohammed. "Instead of convincing the other side, it went on to aggravate the grievances they [already] had."

Tigrayan rebels in northern Ethiopia seized control of strategic airports while facing off federal troops Image: AFP

An alliance of former enemies

Mohammed also emphasized the fact that this coalition against the federal government includes several groups which have otherwise little to do with each other.

It includes the Oromo Liberation Army, a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front as well as multiple smaller armed groups from the western Benishangul-Gumuz region — in addition to ethnic militant factions from Afar, which borders Tigray.

Eritrea meanwhile appears to have shifted sides in the current situation: While not officially a member of the alliance, the neighboring country is believed to be providing support to the rebels.

The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patricia Rodrigues, a senior analyst at Control Risks, a global intelligence and security consultancy, referred to the level of strategic coordination among these various groups in the current conflict as "quite significant" and "definitely alarming for the federal government."

She noted, however, that cracks might eventually appear: "How long this coalition lasts, because all of them have very different interests and represent very different ethnic constituencies, remains to be seen," she told DW.

Rodrigues added that, based on Control Risks' assessment, the fighting is likely to remain limited to Ethiopia's northern regions, particularly those situated along the borders between Tigray, Amhara, and Afar.

Furthermore, she highlighted that the idea of it spreading across the entire country was rather unlikely due to the difficulty of nationwide coordination, taking into consideration the rough terrain of the nation and the fragmentation of other opposition groups.

Could Ethiopia plunge back into a war-like situation as witnessed just a few years ago? Image: UGC/AP/picture alliance

Could the conflict have been prevented?

Rodrigues also pointed out the failure of sustained international engagement after the end of the crisis in 2022 as a key reason for the current conflict_

She noted that while the Pretoria agreement saw some early proof of implementation — including the TPLF's surrender of heavy weaponry in 2022 and 2023 — international attention had soon shifted to other global crises, leaving both sides free to quietly rearm and conscript supporters.

"It was more of a stopgap or a ceasefire, but people were quickly rearming in the background," she told DW.

Rodrigues also noted that the United States had recently lifted sanctions imposed during the 2020–2022 conflict — a step which, according to Mohammed, diminishes the West's leverage in the conflict to push combatants toward coming to the negotiation table.

Many Ethiopians continue to live in IDP camps as a result of the last conflict in the region Image: Amanuel Sileshi/AFP

The real cost of war

In the meantime, civilians are bearing the cost of the warring parties: People caught up in the crossfire have been fleeing the conflict once more, adding further to a population of internally displaced persons (IDPs) that has not recovered from the previous war.

"Since 2020, they have not returned to their areas. They are still in makeshift IDP centers," Mohammed said, adding that there have also been isolated reports of drone strikes hitting civilian areas and of rebel groups deploying military hardware inside schools and clinics.

Telephone and internet connections have also been cut in parts of Tigray and Amhara, electricity has been disrupted, and flights have been suspended to several cities including Kombolcha and Lalibela.

Despite official assurances from all parties that civilians would be protected, Mohammed says that the reality on the ground tells a different story: "Words and practice are very contradictory."

Limited prospects for mediation

Mohammed also noted that outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres dispatched a special envoy to the Horn of Africa, charged with mediating between the African Union, regional powers, and Egypt — many of the same parties involved in brokering the Pretoria agreement.

However according to Mohammed, meaningful negotiations are unlikely to bear fruit until at least one of the sides involved in the conflict "comes to understand that this violence will not help them to achieve what they want."

Rodrigues agrees, stressing that she cannot be optimistic about "an international or a regional mediation being the solution to the current fighting," adding that "intense, but geographically contained" fighting will continue for the foreseeable future.

Adapted from the AfricaLink Podcast by Silja Fröhlich

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Finland probes suspected break-ins at politicians' homes
World.content:
The Finnish prime minister has not ruled out the possibility of foreign involvement in the suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament.

Finnish police are investigating a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, officials announced on Thursday.

Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo was asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the suspected intrusions, and he replied that it was "very possible... quite possible in these times."

"If someone tries to destabilize Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity," he added.

Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated, "An attack against a member of parliament is an attack against democracy."

What do we know about break-ins?

After the media reported on the alleged intrusions, speaker of parliament Jussi Halla-aho confirmed that parliament had been made aware of a "significant" number of break-ins and attempted intrusions at the homes of several politicians.

"I cannot comment precisely on the number of suspected cases known to us, but in any event, it is significant," Halla-aho said at a press conference.

He added, however, that the known cases had occurred over a longer period of time, with the first believed to have taken place about a year ago.

Halla-aho also emphasized that, at this point, no information is available about the motive or the perpetrator.

Paula Risikko, the deputy speaker who leads the parliamentary security group, said she was informed of the suspicions last week.

She added that the Helsinki police had been tasked with the initial stage of the investigation.

A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

MPs advised to keep an eye out

Earlier this week, newspaper Ilta-Sanomat reported that MPs had been warned of potential break-ins and that the newspaper was aware of at least two home intrusions.

All members of parliament were told to keep an eye out, report any suspicious activity, and file police reports if necessary.

Helsinki police confirmed that a preliminary inquiry had been opened. "The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time," it said.

Since the Kremlin began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Finland has been on high alert. The Nordic country, which shares a 1,340-kilometer (830-mile) border with Russia, abandoned its decades-long policy of military non-alignment and joined NATO in April 2023.

Finland previously accused Moscow of "hybrid warfare" and orchestrating a surge of migrants at their shared border in 2023. The Kremlin denied the allegations.

World.title: Renee Good's family sues Trump admin over fatal ICE shooting
World.content:
The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, has sued President Donald Trump's administration alleging negligence and civil rights violations.

Relatives of Renee Good, the 37-year-old woman shot dead in her car in Minneapolis by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent on January 7 this year, are suing the US government in a civil lawsuit connected to her death that was filed on Thursday.

Good and her wife had been taking part in daily protests in the city against the deployment of armed and often masked federal agents deployed to Minnesota to arrest and identify undocumented migrants for deportation.

The lawsuit alleges "federal conspiracy with discriminatory design and authorized use of force against observers," saying that this resulted in "extreme and unconstitutional force" being exerted against "people exercising their rights under the [US] constitution's Bill of Rights."

Good's killing, followed two weeks later by the death of nurse Alex Pretti, intensified the already-sizeable protests against the deployment of ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents in Minneapolis known as Operation Metro Surge.

The deaths of Renee Good and later Alex Pretti led to widespread protests in Minneapolis, and a winding-down of Operation Metro Surge, which ceased entirely by mid-February Image: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images

What do the lawsuits allege?

The plaintiffs in the twin civil suits from the Romanucci Blandin Law firm, filed on October 1 , are Good's brother Brent Ganger — acting as trustee for her other next of kin including her three children — and her partner Becca Good.

One names the United States of America as the sole defendant.

The other names a series of responsible government and border control officials, including but not limited to the ICE officer who shot Good in her car, White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, and the US Secretary of Homeland Security at the time of the shooting, Kristi Noem.

"Renee's death was not an accident," Romanucci Blandin Law wrote in a statement. "It was the predictable result of a coordinated campaign by senior officials in this administration to target Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic origin and silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest."

Minnesota killing spurs backlash over ICE enforcement To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

They allege that Operation Metro Surge "was built on exaggerated fraud accusations that the White House embraced as a pretext for thousands of masked, unidentified federal agents to rove neighborhoods and stop people based on how they looked."

It said that government officials "told agents to force confrontations with observers like Renee and led agents to believe that they would face no consequences for using force."

The crackdown in Minneapolis, which has a large Somali population, came as part of President Donald Trump's tough stance on migration and border security, and amid his assertions that local authorities in some Democrat-run states do an inadequate job fighting crime and irregular migration.

'She was pure love'

Becca Good, Renee's wife, made her public comments about the shooting at a press conference in Minneapolis on Thursday.

"I'm here today because last January the whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed," she said.

Becca said of her wife: "She was pure love. She was ⁠funny. She ​was smart. She was gorgeous."

"Renee believed in something simple: that being good can change the world," she added. "She believed everyone deserves love ​and compassion, care and dignity, no matter who they were or where they came from."

Becca Good made her first public remarks since her wife was shot dead Image: Ellen Schmidt/AP Photo/picture alliance

Brett Ganger, Renee Good's brother, said, "The hole in my family and myself created by my sister’s passing is hauntingly apparent".

"What happened to Renee was completely senseless and the fact ​that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Ganger said.

"What happened to America? Something must change now," he stressed.
