World.title: What Azerbaijan needs to do to benefit from Middle Corridor: World Bank recommendations
World.content:
Benefits for Azerbaijan from the Middle Corridor

Developing the Middle Corridor through 2040 will require more than $55 billion in investment. However, building new railways and ports alone will not guarantee faster cargo deliveries. A World Bank report published on 28 September also stresses the need to simplify border procedures, coordinate rail and maritime transport, and reform state-owned transport companies.

For Azerbaijan, the key question is how much revenue the country can generate from cargo transit across the Caspian Sea and how it can integrate these shipments into the local economy. According to World Bank estimates, developing the corridor could increase the country’s GDP by 0.43 per cent in the long term, or by about $326 million.

In April, we analysed growing demand for the Middle Corridor and constraints on the Caspian route, while in June we examined 10 priority projects proposed to increase cargo volumes. The new report adds separate estimates of Azerbaijan’s investment needs and the potential economic impact. Our June list did not include any projects directly linked to Azerbaijan, while the World Bank report specifically identifies additional investment in the country’s rail and logistics infrastructure.

The new document builds on the World Bank’s 2023 study. It extends the forecast period to 2040 and covers more countries and types of cargo.

Where does the Middle Corridor run?

The Middle Corridor is a transport network connecting Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Turkey. Different sections of the route carry cargo by rail, sea and road.

One of the main routes runs from China through Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk. From there, cargo crosses the Caspian Sea to the Port of Baku in Alat. It then travels through Azerbaijan by rail along the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars line to Georgia. From there, it continues to Turkey or reaches Europe via Georgia’s ports and the Black Sea. The route through the port of Turkmenbashi connects Turkmenistan and other Central Asian countries to this transport network.

The report covers Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Turkey and Uzbekistan. The Middle Corridor currently does not pass directly through Armenia. The World Bank included the country in its calculations on the assumption that relevant transport links could emerge in the 2030s.

Asian-European trade routes. Solid orange lines show the land sections of the Middle Corridor, orange dashed lines show planned extensions, and blue lines show maritime routes. Source: Alam and Blancas, World Bank, 2026, Map O.1. CC BY 3.0 IGO.

What is the $55 billion needed for?

According to the World Bank, more than $25 billion will be needed by 2040 to develop the core physical infrastructure. This includes railways, ports and transport links between them.

Another $30 billion will be needed for additional investments required to operate the corridor and integrate it with local economies. This includes spending on access roads, logistics centres, inland terminals, locomotives and railcars, cargo-handling equipment and digital systems.

This figure does not represent costs that Azerbaijan will have to cover on its own, nor does it refer to a World Bank loan. It is an estimate of the total investment needed along the entire route.

Of the 16 most important infrastructure projects identified by the World Bank, 75 per cent are already under way, while governments have included the remainder in their plans. The report therefore notes that the main task at the next stage may be to improve service quality and the efficiency of transport operations.

What specific projects are planned for Azerbaijan?

The report identifies three areas for additional investment in Azerbaijan, totalling $1.16 billion.

Completing the ongoing modernisation of the Baku-Alat-Boyuk-Kesik railway line will cost an estimated $260 million. Upgrading power supply and signalling systems should improve the efficiency of the corridor’s main section in Azerbaijan.

The report allocates $300 million to developing a network of dry ports. These inland terminals collect, store and transfer cargo between different modes of transport. The list includes the Boyuk-Kesik border crossing, Baku and a southern transport hub that could serve a proposed route to Kars through Azerbaijan and Armenia.

Another $600 million would go towards further expanding the Baku-Alat-Boyuk-Kesik railway line in the 2030s. The latter two projects remain at the preliminary feasibility study stage. The figures therefore do not represent funding under contracts that authorities have already signed. The list also does not cover all of Azerbaijan’s costs related to developing the Middle Corridor.

Alat port capacity and the Caspian Sea’s declining water level

According to the report, the Port of Baku increased its container-handling capacity from 100,000 to 150,000 TEUs in 2025 by improving the efficiency of its existing infrastructure. TEU is a unit of measurement equivalent to a standard 20-foot container. The port handled 107,000 TEUs that year, using about 71 per cent of its container capacity.

At the same time, the port’s overall cargo-handling capacity stood at 55 per cent utilisation. This distinction matters: spare capacity across the port as a whole does not mean that the container and ferry terminals face no congestion.

The World Bank points to another problem: since the port moved to Alat in 2018, authorities have not carried out dredging in the entrance channel or the approach areas leading to the berths. The falling level of the Caspian Sea requires urgent action. Draft restrictions can prevent ships from loading to full capacity and reduce the port’s actual throughput.

What is slowing cargo transport?

According to the World Bank’s analysis, container cargo spends the most time waiting at ports. One reason is poor coordination between train and vessel schedules.

The report proposes creating a single operator to integrate container services run by the railway companies of Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan and Turkey with Caspian Sea shipping operated by ASCO and Kazakhstan’s Kazmortransflot. This would allow operators to coordinate shipments along the entire route.

Document processing also takes considerable time. According to an example in the report, a container shipment between Asia and Europe may require 10 entry and exit procedures under customs transit regimes, five railway consignment notes and two maritime cargo documents. The World Bank recommends introducing a single digital T3 document combining transport, transit and trade data. To use it, countries would need to recognise each other’s documents, agree on data-sharing procedures and establish carriers’ responsibilities.

What conditions are needed to achieve the expected benefits?

According to the World Bank, investment and better services could more than triple cargo volumes along the route by 2040 and halve delivery times. Deeper trade and transport reforms could quadruple cargo volumes and cut delivery times by two-thirds compared with 2023.

The report estimates that, in the long term, the combined GDP of the nine countries could grow by 3.3 per cent, while employment could rise by 2.9 per cent. For Azerbaijan, the corresponding figures stand at 0.43 per cent and 0.66 per cent.

The report suggests that turning Azerbaijan’s geographic position into an economic advantage requires more than simply moving cargo through the country. Local businesses need access to the route, along with reliable transport and competitive logistics services. Planning should account for infrastructure costs, operating expenses and expected cargo volumes together. The World Bank also stresses that the report does not assess projects as ready for financing.

Benefits for Azerbaijan from the Middle Corridor

World.title: ‘Copper is to us what oil is to other countries’ – expert on Armenia’s mineral wealth
World.content:
Assessment of Armenia’s mineral resources

“Armenia does not have major oil or gas deposits with significant reserves. Instead, it can rely on substantial reserves of copper, molybdenum and gold, as well as rare elements and critical minerals. Gold, silver, copper, molybdenum and polymetals such as lead and zinc are currently in greatest demand. However, so-called critical minerals are gradually becoming increasingly important,” geologist Arshavir Hovhannisyan says.

The head of the Mineral Resources Department at the Institute of Geological Sciences of Armenia’s National Academy of Sciences says the terms “critical minerals” and “rare-earth elements” are sometimes confused in Armenia. He explains that critical minerals are elements, mainly metals, that are particularly important for a country’s industrial development, especially in high-tech sectors.

“Rare elements and rare-earth elements are among critical minerals. Copper, for example, is a critical mineral because neither batteries nor electric motors can function without it, but it is not a rare element,” he told Armenpress agency.

Copper, gold and silver reserves, but copper is key

“Copper is the queen of metals, the most important metal.

“We also talk about the importance of lithium, but it is likely to be replaced in the foreseeable future. Lithium is a rather unsuitable chemical element for use in batteries. It is highly flammable, performs poorly at high and low temperatures and has a limited number of charging cycles, after which it becomes unusable.

“Scientists are now looking for alternatives to lithium. Sodium and potassium are the most likely candidates. China is already producing sodium batteries using extremely cheap raw materials.

“Sodium, along with chlorine, is one of the main components of table salt, and Armenia has vast reserves of it. Yerevan is largely situated on salt deposits. The Ararat Valley, from Armavir to Arzni, lies entirely on salt deposits. If necessary, Armenia would have no difficulty obtaining extremely cheap raw materials.

Gold and silver can also be used in electrical equipment. The only element for which there is currently no substitute is copper.

“Copper is to us what, say, oil is to some other countries.”

Armenia’s copper reserves could last decades

“Reserves will be depleted in around 50-100 years unless we discover new deposits in the meantime. I think new deposits could be found because we have done virtually nothing in this area for about 35 years.

“Deposits that were not considered particularly promising during the Soviet period may now attract interest. First, technologies for extracting metals from ore have advanced. Second, the price of copper on the global market is rising rapidly.

According to Bloomberg estimates, by 2030-2040 global demand for copper will reach a level requiring 10-15 new mines to be brought into operation every year.

“I mean mines comparable in size to the large Kajaran deposit.

“According to various estimates, producing a conventional passenger car requires 10-15kg of copper, while an electric vehicle requires more than 50kg. Tens of millions of electric vehicles are produced each year. Simple arithmetic therefore gives an idea of how much pure copper will be needed for the automotive industry alone, with production volumes expected to continue growing.

“There are also other sectors where copper is essential, including electrification, modern technologies and the infrastructure supporting them.”

Oil and gas not worth considering

“The geodynamic processes that took place over tens of millions of years in the territory where Armenia is now located have left virtually no prospect of large hydrocarbon reserves.

“A large number of deep wells were drilled in Voghjaberd for research purposes, and similar exploration was carried out in Armavir. Some traces were found, including small amounts of gas. These are remnants of deposits that once existed, as well as accumulations formed more recently, over the past 30 million years. Given the geology and location, these cannot be large volumes.

“There is little reason to expect oil and gas deposits to be discovered in Armenia in the future.

Small deposits could potentially be found at great depths. But even finding them would be extremely costly, as numerous wells would have to be drilled.

“Even then, it would not be clear whether the gas discovered would last a month, an hour or a year. In any case, the volumes would be so small that they are hardly worth considering.”

Areas where rare elements could be found

“Demand for rare-earth elements and other minerals has risen sharply worldwide, along with their prices. They are in high demand in modern high-tech manufacturing.

“They attracted little interest in the past, but technologies have changed. We need to understand what resources we have.

We cannot say there is no chance of Armenia having rare-element reserves. There are geological areas in the country that could contain them.

“Further research is needed to establish this. Our institute has a dedicated group studying rare-earth elements, funded by a grant from the Science Committee. The research does not have an industrial or applied research component and is purely scientific, but the fact that it is being conducted is itself a positive development.

“The research covers potential mineralisation of lithium, selenium, tellurium and rhenium. Meanwhile, more than 20 other rare-earth elements have not previously been studied.

“Some have been identified incidentally during other research. As demand for them grows, we will have to explore them, whether we want to or not. If the state does not do so, the private sector will.”

Investment needed to explore new deposits

“Armenia is indeed very rich in mineral resources, both metallic and non-metallic. Kajaran, Sotk, Agarak and Teghut are all located within a relatively small area covering around 30-35% of the country. Moreover, Kajaran is among the world’s 10 largest mines by scale.

“The difficulties are related not to geology but to the terrain. In many cases, mines are located at altitudes of around 3,000 metres, in hard-to-reach areas, and deposits are often relatively small.

The chances of discovering new large deposits comparable in scale to Kajaran or Zod [Sotk] are very low. The chances of finding medium-sized and small deposits are higher.

“Exploration of new deposits will become possible if the state creates the necessary conditions for investment and also invests itself. At the very least, this would give us a clearer picture of the rare elements and critical minerals in Armenia’s subsoil. This would then be followed by detailed exploration and reserve estimates, an even more labour-intensive and costly process.”

World.title: From self-defence to political statements: how former Georgian PM Garibashvili’s ‘prison’ letters have evolved
World.content:
Analysis of former Georgian PM’s “prison” letters

Former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has published his eighth letter from prison, which differs significantly from his previous seven. In the letter, Garibashvili looks back on his political career and presents himself to the public as a successful prime minister. The text effectively serves both as a political report and a statement of leadership ambitions.

In the letter, the former prime minister seeks to show that in 2021 he led the government out of a deep political and economic crisis and improved the country’s situation through his work.

At the end of the letter, he asks the public whether the situation has improved or deteriorated since he resigned. Although he does not directly name current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, the question clearly challenges his administration.

“Almost three years have passed since then [my resignation], and I want to ask the people: has the situation in the country improved or deteriorated, both in domestic and foreign policy?”

About former PM Giorgi Gakharia

Garibashvili begins his account with February 2021, when he returned as prime minister for a second time after Giorgi Gakharia resigned. He says Georgia faced several serious challenges at once: a political crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, a shortage of vaccines, an economic downturn, a large budget deficit, rising public debt and a weakening lari.

In his view, Gakharia abandoned the country and the ruling team under these circumstances. Garibashvili’s position on Gakharia echoes the Georgian Dream party’s narrative:

“Gakharia left the country and the team in the middle of an acute crisis, committing an act of unexpected betrayal by resigning. The government stood on the brink of collapse, the ruling party had lost morale, the team was divided, and the party’s approval rating had fallen to 35–37%.”

Garibashvili portrays his return as, essentially, a rescue operation for the government. He says that after taking office as prime minister, he strengthened the team, stabilised the situation, reopened the country and the economy, secured vaccine supplies and lifted restrictions introduced during the pandemic.

The former prime minister stresses that the government abandoned what he calls a “Covid dictatorship” and gave people complete freedom to choose whether to get vaccinated.

“In the shortest possible time, we restored balance, strengthened the team and stabilised the situation. Together with the team, we took bold, decisive, effective and — at the time — risky steps.”

In his view, these measures secured Georgian Dream’s victory in the 2021 local elections. Garibashvili credits himself not only with helping the party clear the 43 per cent threshold and win 47 per cent of the vote, but also with preventing a potential revolutionary scenario after Mikheil Saakashvili returned to Georgia.

“We prevented destabilisation and an attempted revolution involving Saakashvili, put all destructive forces in their place and brought the political crisis to an end.”

Showcasing economic results

A significant part of the letter focuses on economic indicators. Garibashvili claims that Georgia’s economy grew by 30 billion lari (about $11,516,310,000) during his three years as prime minister. He says the economy recorded double-digit growth in 2021 and 2022, putting Georgia first among EU member and candidate countries in terms of growth.

Garibashvili lists the following among his government’s achievements:

cutting the budget deficit from 9 per cent to 2.8 per cent;

reducing public debt from 60 per cent to 38 per cent of GDP;

stabilising the lari exchange rate at between 2.6 and 2.7;

bringing inflation below the target level;

reducing unemployment and poverty to historic lows;

creating tens of thousands of new jobs;

raising pensions and salaries for public-sector workers.

The former prime minister attributes lower medicine prices to the opening of the Turkish pharmaceutical market and the introduction of a reference pricing system for medicines.

EU candidate status and the issue of being “dragged into war” with Russia

Garibashvili also devotes considerable attention to foreign policy. Here again, he echoes Georgian Dream’s rhetoric. He says Georgia faced intense pressure after the war between Russia and Ukraine began, but his government managed to protect the country from the threat of war and destabilisation.

“From the very first days of the war between Russia and Ukraine, despite enormous pressure, we firmly and uncompromisingly defended our country’s national interests, preventing destabilisation and the real threat of war.”

Garibashvili thus repeats one of Georgian Dream’s key political arguments: after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia faced the risk of being dragged into the conflict.

The former prime minister lists his foreign visits and diplomatic initiatives in the letter. These include applying for EU membership, developing strategic relations with China, signing free trade agreements with several countries, mediating between Azerbaijan and Armenia, and hosting a meeting of the three countries’ prime ministers in Tbilisi.

Garibashvili considers Georgia’s achievement of EU candidate status in December 2023 his main foreign policy accomplishment.

“Without bowing to anyone — either inside the country or abroad — and solely through our uncompromising defence of our country’s national interests and the joint efforts of our team, we secured EU candidate status in December 2023.”

The letter says these results came without political subordination to external forces.

Approval ratings and resignation

Garibashvili claims he left office with high levels of public support. According to him, in January 2024, approval of the government’s performance and support for Georgian Dream both reached 60 per cent.

“Thanks to the results we achieved — and, most importantly, thanks to democratic methods — we politically neutralised the entire radical opposition, leaving no one with any grounds for criticism or complaint.”

Garibashvili presents not only his government’s record but also the neutralisation of the opposition as a political achievement. He effectively equates this “democratic success” with the ruling party’s dominance and the opposition’s removal from the political arena.

The letter does not explain why Garibashvili resigned as prime minister at a time when, according to his own account, the government enjoyed high approval, the economy was growing and the opposition had suffered political defeat.

From self-defence to political statements: analysis of former Georgian PM’s “prison” letters

Garibashvili’s eight letters form a coherent political narrative. At first, he sought to protect himself and his family. He later accused the authorities of orchestrating political persecution. He subsequently began raising questions about the government’s actions and several other issues. In his eighth letter, he defends his political legacy and criticises the current government. Political analysts say the latest letter points to political ambitions on Garibashvili’s part.

The first stage — Ivanishvili loyalty and self-preservation

In his first letters, Garibashvili described the pressure against him as the main source of the conflict. He said he did not plan to return to politics, but the authorities demanded that he admit guilt to new corruption charges, fearing a “one per cent risk” that he might return to politics.

He firmly reaffirmed his loyalty to Bidzina Ivanishvili, while holding him personally responsible if anything threatened his family.

“I am not fighting or battling anyone — I am only defending myself and my family!”

Garibashvili took a defensive position, seeking to show that he had not chosen this confrontation and that the authorities had forced him to defend himself.

The second stage — accusing specific individuals

In his subsequent letters, it became clearer who exactly Garibashvili was targeting with his criticism. His focus shifted from Ivanishvili to Prime Minister Kobakhidze and former regional development minister and former State Security Service chief Mamuka Mdinaradze. Garibashvili accused both of them of organising the pressure against him.

By presenting the situation this way, the former prime minister clearly left the door open to reconciliation with Ivanishvili. He continued to describe Ivanishvili as someone for whom he had “enormous love, respect, boundless gratitude and absolute loyalty”, while placing the blame for what was happening on people around him.

The third stage — systemic accusations

In his fifth and sixth letters, Garibashvili broadened the scope of the conflict. He publicly questioned the circumstances surrounding the death of human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze and linked the incident to other suicides that occurred while Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze held power.

The convicted former prime minister later accused the government as a whole of conducting systematic propaganda, using investigations for political purposes, and trying to link Garibashvili to the United National Movement or foreign agents.

Garibashvili moved beyond his own criminal case, criticising the government’s methods and presenting himself as a victim of political persecution.

The fourth stage — creating an alternative to the current government

In his seventh letter, Garibashvili claimed that the authorities had arrested him to destroy his political future. He accused the government of creating an atmosphere of endless chaos, crisis and impoverishment.

The most significant point came when he compared Georgian Dream with Mikheil Saakashvili’s administration:

“You are already following in Saakashvili’s footsteps and bringing back the methods of governance used by the National Movement…”

For years, Georgian Dream has built its political identity around contrasting itself with Saakashvili’s rule. Garibashvili’s accusation that the current government uses the same methods therefore directly challenges the ruling team’s legitimacy.

Analysts say the eighth letter takes a more political tone than his previous statements in his own defence.

Garibashvili has not officially announced a return to politics. However, the logic of his letters points towards a political comeback.

Analysis of former Georgian PM’s “prison” letters

World.title: ‘Transparent and competitive, but also cause for concern’: PACE report on Armenia’s elections
World.content:
PACE report on Armenia’s elections

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe’s election observation mission has published a report on the parliamentary elections, which took place in Armenia on 7 June.

“The elections were competitive, and citizens had a genuine choice between different political forces and alternatives,” the report says.

Observers also found the process well organised and transparent, with no serious incidents.

At the same time, they identified several serious problems. In particular, they expressed concern over a post-election dispute involving the invalidation of voting results at polling stations 10/51, 35/65 and 12/13. PACE experts believe that if officials had counted those votes, the opposition Prosperous Armenia party could have crossed the four per cent threshold and won seats.

Meanwhile, the Central Election Commission said the annulment of the results at these polling stations did not affect the election outcome. It therefore decided not to hold repeat voting there. However, PACE described the decision as “unsatisfactory, given the significance of its consequences”.

“A perfectly acceptable option would have been to hold repeat voting at the relevant polling stations. The CEC rejected this without providing serious justification. Authorities should base such an important decision on strong, transparent and verifiable grounds. Unfortunately, that did not happen,” said Swiss politician Damien Cottier, one of the report’s authors.

Armenian journalists also noted that MPs from the ruling party and the opposition selectively presented PACE’s assessment to the public. They quoted and highlighted the parts of the document that supported their respective positions.

“Politicians often resort to such tactics. In English, there is an expression for this: cherry-picking. Politicians select and present only the findings that portray them in a positive light, while ignoring or downplaying the negative ones,” Factor TV said in a report.

Main concerns

“Interference by the Russian Federation and foreign information operations in a Council of Europe member state have reached unprecedented levels,” the report says.

According to the PACE mission, Russia used economic restrictions and tough diplomatic rhetoric to influence the election results in favour of the pro-Russian opposition.

The report also identifies the following problems:

abuse of administrative resources,

biased coverage on public television and by key opposition media outlets,

some Karabakh Armenians being unable to vote because bureaucratic delays prevented them from obtaining Armenian citizenship,

unprecedented external interference and geopolitical pressure.

PACE recommendations

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe has called on Armenia to amend its electoral code:

“The law should clearly require repeat voting whenever the fundamental right of a political force to have representation [in parliament] comes into question. It should also establish a clear threshold and procedures for such cases.”

The observation mission also recommends that the Armenian authorities take the following steps:

strengthen the resilience of the electoral process and democratic institutions, particularly by increasing national capacity to identify and counter Russian information operations and economic pressure tools;

broaden the range of people who can challenge electoral disputes in court, extend appeal deadlines and introduce more flexible remedies for violations;

ensure the independence of the process for appointing members of electoral commissions;

fully regulate the use of administrative resources and effectively punish any abuse of them;

end the selective prosecution of opposition figures and guarantee compliance with all procedural rules in election-related court proceedings;

guarantee the right of all political forces to hold peaceful assemblies;

simplify documentation requirements for displaced people and vulnerable groups of voters, and speed up the citizenship and registration processes.

PACE said it stood ready to work with the Armenian authorities to address all these issues.

Ruling party and opposition representatives on the report

Hayk Konjoryan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction and deputy speaker of parliament, emphasised that the report described the elections as “well organised”. He also highlighted the following points from the document:

voters had a genuine choice between political alternatives,

observers gave the electoral process a positive assessment at the vast majority of polling stations they monitored.

Konjoryan also highlighted the PACE observers’ assessment that the elections took place amid major geopolitical transformations. They described the scale of external interference in Armenia’s affairs as “unprecedented and alarming”.

The deputy speaker also pointed to the report’s description of the economic restrictions and political pressure that outside actors imposed on Armenia during the pre-election campaign. The report explicitly says that the goal was to influence voters and encourage them to vote for opposition forces.

“According to the report, the election results show that society demonstrated its democratic resilience despite unprecedented external pressure and the shortcomings identified. The PACE report says that the elected authorities received a clear mandate from the people, which they must now carry out with honour,” Konjoryan concluded.

Narek Karapetyan, head of the opposition Strong Armenia faction, focused on other points in the report. He highlighted the following problems identified by European parliamentarians:

“On unlawful detentions

The number of searches and arrests of opposition politicians, activists and candidates has increased significantly.

The observation mission stressed that these measures undermined electoral fairness and had a significant chilling effect on the opposition’s election campaign.

On administrative resources

The ruling party used official government platforms, public infrastructure and administrative levers to support its campaign. This significantly distorted the campaign environment and prevented opposition forces from competing on an equal footing.

On pre-election bribery

While law enforcement agencies promptly launched high-profile investigations into alleged vote-buying and illegal campaign financing by opposition factions, they dealt with similar allegations and complaints against ruling-party representatives far less thoroughly or more slowly.

On election fraud

“Prosperous Armenia” could have crossed the four per cent threshold for entering parliament, won seats and deprived the ruling party of its three-fifths majority.”

“A one-sided approach”: Factor TV’s assessment

Journalists from Factor TV examined the report itself as well as MPs’ comments.

In their view, Konjoryan and Karapetyan presented diametrically opposed interpretations of the same document:

ruling-party MP Hayk Konjoryan completely ignored the parts of the report that criticise the authorities and highlight abuses of administrative resources and shortcomings in the electoral process.

opposition MP Narek Karapetyan focused only on accusations against the authorities, while ignoring sections that confirm the legitimacy of the elections and document external pressure.

“Both sides present only the half of the truth that suits them. But even combining these two perspectives does not provide the full picture. For example, the report contains statements that criticise both the authorities and the opposition.”

The document says:

“Extreme polarisation in society and mass protests created a tense domestic political environment. Years of confrontation and ongoing [unfinished] legal and institutional reforms have weakened confidence in the possibility of achieving political change through institutions and elections.”

The journalists concluded that each side highlighted passages criticising its opponents while leaving out criticism of its own political force.

PACE report on Armenia’s elections

World.title: Iranian ambassador calls history of Georgian Queen Ketevan “controversial”, sparking criticism in Georgia
World.content:
Scandal over Iranian ambassador’s remarks in Georgia

Iranian ambassador to Georgia Seyed Ali Mojani has announced the publication of his own research on Georgian Queen Ketevan. His remarks about the need to “re-examine” history have drawn criticism from a Georgian historian and MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party. The dispute centres on the ambassador’s references to different historical accounts without specifying which generally accepted facts he is questioning.

What did the ambassador write?

Mojani, a historian by profession, posted a photograph on Facebook showing the facade of the Iranian embassy with an image of Queen Ketevan projected onto it. He wrote that, for him, the image symbolises a historical memory surrounded by “numerous conflicting accounts that persist to this day”.

The ambassador promised to publish the findings of his preliminary research soon. The study will focus on Queen Ketevan and draw on Georgian and Iranian sources. Mojani stressed that it would not represent Iran’s official position but rather his personal perspective as a historian, which could be refined or revised in the future.

Mojani has not yet published either the study itself or the sources he intends to use.

Why did the post spark criticism?

Queen Ketevan was tortured to death in the Iranian city of Shiraz in 1624 on the orders of Shah Abbas I. Historical sources and academic studies document her martyrdom. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates Ketevan as a saint and commemorates her on 26 September.

Against this backdrop, some interpreted Mojani’s reference to “conflicting accounts” as a suggestion that the ambassador was questioning the history of Ketevan’s martyrdom.

Historian and lecturer Giorgi Javakhishvili believes the ambassador’s statement goes beyond his diplomatic mandate. According to him, “Queen Ketevan’s martyrdom is a fact.” Javakhishvili also accuses Mojani of disregarding the methodology and ethics of historical research.

Georgian Dream MPs react

Nikoloz Samkharadze, chairman of parliament’s Foreign Relations Committee, urged the ambassador to “stick to diplomatic protocol and refrain from delving into history”. Samkharadze said he would discuss the incident with Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili when she returns to Georgia.

MP Irakli Kadagishvili said Mojani’s statement had nothing to do with the embassy’s work, stressing that the ambassador should perform his duties within the scope of his authority.

MP Aluda Gudushauri expects the foreign ministry to respond, noting that “no one can change or distort the true course of our history — reality is what it is and what we know it to be”.

The ambassador’s previous statements

Mojani’s posts have sparked controversy in Georgia before. On 31 March, he wrote that “countries that willingly or unwillingly surrender their space and territory to foreign adventurers sooner or later pay the price within their own borders”. The ambassador did not name any specific country, but some analysts and politicians interpreted the post as a threat against Georgia.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 2, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020 in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the war.

- On October 2, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to Al Jazeera. The president once again defended the rightful position of Azerbaijan in the international media and informed the international community about the reasons of the Second Karabakh War and the latest situation in the region.

- On the night and in the morning of October 2, combat operations continued in different directions of the front. In the direction of Aghdara, Azerbaijani troops liberated the important heights around Madagiz settlement (now renamed into Sugovushan) and took control of it. From 00:00 to 07:00 (GMT +4), five Armenian armored vehicles, three military infrastructure facilities and a large number of personnel were destroyed. Armenian volunteers brought from Armenia to Azerbaijani then-occupied territories refused to fight under various pretexts, fearing the intensity of the fighting and the heavy losses.

- Armenia shelled Azerbaijani settlements. The villages of Khindiristan, Alibayli, Ahmadaghaly and Safarli in the Aghdam district came under heavy artillery fire.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry has released new footages of the battles. The Armenian manpower and equipment were destroyed.

- Armenian servicemen inflicted strikes on a kindergarten in Shikharkh settlement near Tartar city.

- Armenian armed forces fired on journalists who were reporting from the frontline. The journalists who were operating in the residential areas fired by Armenian forces came under sudden shooting. Armenians shelled the area where the journalists were.

- Shootout between Armenian soldiers. A shootout took place between the soldiers of the 6th Motorized Rifle Regiment of the Armenian Armed Forces in Madagiz (now Sugovushan), who withdrew during the night fighting.

- Armenian military supplies and combat means were destroyed

- Armenia launched nearly 10 Tochka-U tactical missiles to the Sabirkand settlement of Shamkir district.

- The Azerbaijani Army seized the battle flag of the Air Discount Command Union of the Armenian Armed Forces’ 193rd airborne assault battalion, as well as a large number of weapons and ammunition of the Armenian forces who fled the battlefield, helpless in the face of the strength of Azerbaijani Army. The Armenian field control point, as well as several other Armenian manpower and equipment were destroyed.

World.title: “Power of Unity – 2026” exercise concluded (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 1. “Power of Unity – 2026” joint military exercise in Gizilgaya and Garabaghlar Training Centers in the Garabagh economic region and the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, respectively, as well as in Boyuk Zira Training Area in the maritime zone of the Caspian Sea under Azerbaijan’s jurisdiction, has concluded following the Distinguished Visitors’ Day, the Azerbaijan's Ministry of Defense said.

Closing ceremony was held to mark the conclusion of the exercise, during which the national anthems of Azerbaijan, Türkiye, and Uzbekistan were performed accompanied by a military band.

Addressing the ceremony, the speakers noted that the exercise, which involved military personnel from 3 countries as participants and 9 countries as observers, contributed to the exchange of experience among service members, the enhancement of combat readiness, and the expansion of friendly relations.

It was noted that, while carrying out activities adapted to challenging terrain and realistic combat conditions, the military personnel demonstrated a high level of professionalism, tactical competence, and coordinated action. Throughout the exercise, the service members successfully fulfilled the tasks assigned to them.

Following the speeches, gifts were presented to the distinguished military personnel.

The participating military personnel then conducted a ceremonial march-past in front of the grandstand.

The ceremony concluded with performances by the creative ensemble of the Hazi Aslanov Army Ideological and Cultural Center.

World.title: TasWater to fix issue that saw some customers given 500pc sewerage bill increase
World.content:
Tasmania's water utility is "assessing" changes to fixed sewerage charges that saw some non-residential customers facing a 500 per cent price increase.

TasWater said a number of businesses and community groups, such as manufacturers and sporting clubs, had been affected, and it would make changes to lessen the impact.

Under changes that came in from July 1, TasWater's fixed sewerage charges were based on the size of a property's water pipe connection, not their sewage usage.

"We've heard the feedback from this specific customer group, and we need to own and reflect on that while taking action to rectify the issue," TasWater general manager Callan Paske said in a statement.

"While our charging methodology has resulted in lower charges for many customers, the transition has had unintended consequences for a number of customers whose large water connections do not reflect the comparatively low demand they place on the sewerage system."

TasWater said it was working on a solution for those significantly impacted by fixed sewerage charges associated with large water connections but relatively low water use and discharge to the sewer.

It also said it would adjust pricing for sporting clubs which primarily used water to irrigate.

Both changes will be backdated to July 1.

Tasmanian businesses and sport clubs had said they were hit hard by the changes, with one business stating their bill had risen from $630 to $3,800 a month — a 500 per cent increase.

TasWater explained it had made the now-paused changes because an independent inquiry recommended it move away from its previous sewerage charging method.

Government welcomes changes

In a statement, Premier Jeremy Rockliff welcomed the "pause and rethink".

He said the changes followed discussions between his government, TasWater, the Tasmanian Economic Regulator and the local government sector.

"We called for relief from excessive increases, and TasWater has responded constructively," he said.

"This demonstrates what can be achieved through sensible and mature discussions as we all now focus on securing a fair outcome for the Tasmanian community.

"The pause will provide important relief for affected businesses and community organisations who need our support."

The price rises for water usage, including for households, are not affected by today's announcement.

The economic regulator knocked back TasWater's request to rise water prices by 8.8 per cent over four years.

Instead, prices will rise by an average of 5.7 per cent each year for the next four years.

World.title: Calls growing to fix country town's 800-truck-a-day problem
World.content:
Every day, about 800 heavy haulage trucks roll through Western Australia's Peel region.

Most, if not all, pass through Pinjarra's main street, close to schools, cafes, homes and other businesses.

The town, about 80 kilometres south of Perth and home to 6,000 people, sits close to a number of major mining projects, including Alcoa's enormous Pinjarra Alumina Refinery, which is about 10 minutes' drive from town.

The truck traffic has sparked calls to revive long-awaited plans for a bypass, which have stalled despite millions of dollars of funding being allocated.

Shire of Murray President Douglas McLarty said the vehicles regularly locked down the town centre.

There have been longstanding plans to build a deviation route for trucks to bypass Pinjarra's town centre. (Supplied: David Bolt)

"We have students, parents, caregivers interfacing with heavy haulage every single day trying to access either of those two schools," he said.

"We're talking about loads that are going through the centre of town and nearly touching parked cars on either side of the road … knocking the traffic lights over."

The project, which has been on the agenda since the 1990s, was backed by $50 million in state funding and $200 million from the federal government in 2022.

Despite the federal government stripping its share of funding from the project in 2023, the WA government reaffirmed its commitment to the road.

But three years on and the project remains in the planning and approvals stage.

About 800 heavy haulage trucks drive make their way through Pinjarra everyday. (Supplied: David Bolt)

Safety and lifestyle concerns

Business owner Caris McClements said the trucks were affecting the local lifestyle.

"Often we might have to halt a conversation with a customer because a truck is going past and they're really noisy, or we see a truck slam on the brakes as they come up to the crosswalk," she said.

"Sometimes that main street might get shut for a bit and everyone gets stopped for five, 10 minutes while the big truck rolls through."

Caris McClements said she was concerned the trucks were affecting Pinjarra's liveability. (Supplied: Caris McClements)

Liberal member for Murray-Wellington David Bolt said the situation was becoming dangerous.

"It's an issue with noise, it's an issue with crossing the road," he said.

" But the main issue is the vehicles are increasing in number and at some point, we're going to have a major accident. "

Member for Murray-Wellington David Bolt said the situation was becoming dangerous. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

Bypass concerns

A further complication has been concerns the proposed route would disturb the site of the Pinjarra Massacre, one of the most brutal attacks on Aboriginal people in WA's history.

Scores of Bindjareb Noongar women, men and children killed by white settlers on the banks of the Murray River in 1834.

Bindjareb woman Karrie-Anne Kearing said her family had worked to keep the site protected for generations.

The Pinjarra Massacre is known to be one of the most brutal attacks on Aboriginal people in the state. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"We go over to other countries, and they respect our fallen, I think that should also be seen over here in our own country, as Noongar people, they fought for their country, and they lost lives," she said.

"We need that same respect shown to our ancestors or elder people that actually lost their lives there."

In August, Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said the state government was considering stakeholder feedback, while a Main Roads spokesperson said the massacre site remained a significant planning consideration, with a formal memorial or education initiative being considered.

Scars of the Pinjarra massacre Almost two centuries on, families in WA's south-west are still waiting for proper recognition of one of the state's bloodiest days.

"Further work is required before the preferred alignment can be confirmed and any decisions regarding project timing or construction can be made," a Main Roads spokesperson said.

Some 'love to see them'

For others like Bron May, who works in the centre of Pinjarra, there is a potential downside to the proposed bypass.

"We see a lot of people that are visitors to the town, who, are always taking photos of the big trucks," she said.

"There's little kids, they love to see them coming through."

Bron May said the trucks were a part of Pinjarra. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

Ms May said she was concerned visitors would be diverted away from Pinjarra.

"Are we going to lose them as well because they're going to use the deviation road?" she said.

World.title: Pallister and Short continue winning form at short course title
World.content:
Lani Pallister and Sam Short, Australia's stars of the pool in 2026, have continued their terrific year with more success at the national short course championships in Sydney.

The pair, who had already scooped a hatful of Commonwealth and Pan Pacific titles, made it five Australian titles between them in a week at Olympic Park Aquatic Centre.

They are intent on ending their year with more gold at the world short course championships in Beijing in December.

Pallister, having already lifted the 200 metre and 1,500m freestyle titles, powered to victory over 400m on the penultimate night of racing on Thursday, as did Short, who had already won the 800m.

Forrester breaks 17yo record Jenna Forrester has never competed at the short course world championships, but winning a silver and a gold in the same evening, also beating a 17-year-old a national record, has put her in pole position to do so.

Short was in an imperious mood as he took the 16-lap title in 3 minutes and 35.16 seconds, easily inside the Beijing qualifying time of 3:39.14, which convinced him the world record of 3:32.25 was sure to fall at the famed Water Cube venue that hosted the 2008 Olympic swimming program.

"I think that's gone in a couple of months at [the] world short course," Brisbane star Short said.

"I haven't swum much short course … in some ways it keeps you hungry."

Former short course 400m world champion Elijah Winnington, though, was just outside the time needed, as he clocked 3:39.24 to finish runner-up.

Pallister was in a class of her own as she prevailed in 3:54.55, the fastest women's time ever recorded in Australia, shaving 0.03 seconds off the old mark set by Ariarne Titmus six years ago.

Runner-up Jenna Forrester, who won 400m individual medley gold in a national record, was 0.65 seconds outside of qualifying time.

In the women's 50m, Iona Anderson continued her breakthrough year by completing her sweep of the backstroke events, clocking 25.88 seconds as she got closer to Kaylee McKeown's Australian record of 25.35 seconds.

AAP

World.title: Man charged with violent sexual assault of woman in Sydney park
World.content:
A man has been charged over the alleged stalking, choking and sexual assault of a woman at a park in Sydney's west.

NSW Police said a 23-year-old woman was walking from Flemington Station through Airey Park in Homebush about 11:15pm on September 18 when an unknown man stopped her.

Officers were told the woman was restrained and dragged into nearby bushland, where the man allegedly sexually assaulted her.

She left the scene a short time later.

About 8:50am on Thursday, detectives executed a search warrant in Padstow and took a 27-year-old man into custody.

Police also seized items from the property for forensic testing.

He was scheduled to face Bankstown Local Court on Friday.

World.title: 'Information-rich' generation makes voice heard in politics
World.content:
Not all teenagers find agendas, meetings, bills and speeches interesting, but a group of school students from western Queensland are not waiting until voting age to make a mark on politics.

Travelling from their remote region, eight youth councillors have been advocating for their communities as members of the Queensland Youth Parliament sitting in Brisbane this week

The school-aged Blackall-Tambo Youth Council attended Parliament House and had dinner with the Governor of Queensland. (Supplied: Blackall-Tambo Regional Council)

In her second year on Blackall-Tambo Youth Council, Georgia Duncan, 16, was elected youth mayor by her fellow councillors.

Under her leadership, the youth council has already achieved its vision of a new dog park for Blackall, unveiling Bark Park in the Central West Queensland town.

Youth councillors took "pawtraits" of dogs at the opening of Bark Park in Blackall. (Supplied: Blackall-Tambo Regional Council)

"We've all noticed that there's no place to run your dogs without a leash and a lot of tourists have dogs," Georgia said.

Aged across grades 6 to 11, the youth councillors serve their region 10 hours west of Brisbane.

"We have a meeting every two months … and discuss new ideas we want to see in town," the Blackall State High School student said.

Blackall-Tambo Regional Council helped realise its youth council's plan for Bark Park. (Supplied: Blackall-Tambo Regional Council)

The youth council toured Brisbane's Parliament House and Government House this week, an excursion the young leader said would inspire new initiatives for Blackall-Tambo.

Blackall-Tambo Mayor Andrew Martin said the youth council was an important way to hear from the community.

Andrew Martin and Georgia Duncan have taken part in Blackall-Tambo Youth Council's visit to Brisbane. (Supplied: Blackall-Tambo Regional Council)

He said his council supported the young politicians through funding, as well as staff and transport to meetings which alternate between the towns of Blackall and Tambo.

"What they will have wherever they land is a better perspective on life and they'll be a bigger asset to the community in which they end up residing," he said.

Age not a barrier for youth MP

Ava Haine serves as a youth minister and represents the district of Gregory in Queensland Youth Parliament. (Supplied: YMCA Queensland Youth Parliament)

Ava Haine, 19, is also having her voice heard as one of the YMCA Queensland Youth Parliament's 93 members, aged 16 to 25.

Hailing from Moura, about 600 kilometres from Brisbane, Ms Haine represents the western Queensland seat of Gregory.

"I come from such a lineage of powerful female farmers," she said.

" To have a foot in this parliament and be able to speak about their role as more than just a farmer's wife, but as farmers, is so important to me. "

Serving as a youth minister across a range of portfolios, including disaster and volunteering, Ms Haine hopes the Disaster Resilience Corps Youth Bill, tabled in youth parliament this week, could grab the attention of politicians in state parliament.

Youth parliamentarians have met MPs including Jennifer Howard. (Supplied: YMCA Queensland Youth Parliament)

"Volunteering in Queensland is down 20 per cent and so we needed a way to incentivise volunteers because we know cost of living is a big thing."

Ms Haine said she had been inspired by Queensland's youngest-ever state MP, Ariana Doolan, who was elected to the seat of Pumicestone in 2024 aged 22.

"That is just such a beam of hope that I don't have to wait to get older to participate or have more experience," Ms Haine said.

Youth passionate about meaningful input

Young and Resilient Research Centre co-director Philippa Collin from the University of Western Sydney said today's youth were switched on to the world around them.

"Young people are very interested in being engaged, having a say and trying to shape the issues," Professor Collin said.

"And they're pretty open to the different forms in which that can take."

Philippa Collin has researched young people's changing relationship to politics. (Supplied: Philippa Collin)

She said interest in traditional political institutions had dropped, but young people were highly engaged with issues driven by digital and social media.

"We've never had a generation before that is so information rich, that is as educated and has tools at their disposal to access information but also create it and create those networks."

Professor Collin said while youth engagement programs and government advisory councils had increased over the past 15 years, it was critical participants felt heard.

"Young people … are pretty finely tuned to whether or not someone's taking them seriously and whether or not their involvement … is a token rather than a substantial shift in the ways in which we govern," she said.

World.title: Parents outraged as trees chopped down at central Victorian schools
World.content:
Parents at two central Victorian schools have expressed outrage after trees in school grounds were cut down by state government contractors this week with little or no notice.

On Wednesday afternoon, arborists abandoned their work at Elphinstone Primary School, east of Castlemaine, to clear trees and vegetation ahead of the bushfire season amid protests from parents and media attention.

Parents at one school have threatened to climb the remaining trees to save them from being chopped down.

The Victorian Schools Building Authority said it had halted works until it "talks to" the Elphinstone community.

Helen Officer, one of the parents on site, said the school was not given notice to move or transplant trees away from the school building.

Helen Officer says the school was not given notice to move or transplant trees away from buildings. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

"They tried to pull out the kids' cabbages and strawberries from the kitchen garden," she said.

" It's just outrageous. If we have to climb a tree we probably will. "

Ms Officer said three trees and some young saplings had been removed and a further 4-5 trees were earmarked for removal, leaving little shade for students.

"We take bushfire safety extremely seriously, but we just want some more time to provide the children shade and natural spaces for the rest of the year," she said.

"This is a tiny bush school with 24 kids. If they're going to rush through and remove all these assets, why aren't they also rushing to provide new assets to the school?"

Forty-five minutes west of Elphinstone, Carisbrook Primary School also had trees within 10 metres of the school's buildings removed.

School council president Sheree Lendon said the school community and staff were not aware the trees were going to be removed.

"Within two days, every tree is gone. Families are upset, staff are upset," she said.

"There are families that have been attending this school for several decades, and now they feel that the character of the school and the feel of the school has just been destroyed in two days.

" I've had people in tears. "

Arborists at Elphinstone Primary School on Tuesday. (Supplied)

Among the trees removed was a Lone Pine seeded from Gallipoli and planted in 2015 to mark the centenary of the Anzac landings in World War I.

Ms Lendon said the school would have wanted to be able to replant it or take seeds from it.

'Will not risk' safety

In July, then education minister Ben Carroll announced $8 million shared across 330 schools to clear vegetation around school buildings.

Elphinstone Primary School was allocated just over $19,000, while Carisbrook received $28,540.

The schools are on a Victorian government Bushfire At-Risk Register of 850 schools and early childhood services "considered to be at significant bushfire risk".

Seating in the shade of trees at Elphinstone Primary School. (Supplied)

High-risk schools are required to have a place of last resort for students and staff if evacuation is not possible during a bushfire.

A compliant Shelter in Place requires a 10-metre perimeter around the building "clear of combustible materials such as trees and vegetation".

"We will not risk the safety of students in our care, which is why bushfire safety is so important," an education department spokesperson said.

On Thursday morning, Victorian Schools Building Authority CEO Jo Wadell told ABC Central Victoria the authority would reflect on its practices and that there was consultation with Elphinstone Primary School.

"We do acknowledge that it did occur very quickly, but that is because there is a sense of urgency around these works," Ms Wadell said.

"If these trees aren't removed, what it means is that these schools would need to close on high-risk and extreme bushfire days.

"With these trees removed, these schools can continue to operate because they have a safe building in which to harbour if there is a bushfire."

Ms Wadell claimed the arborist did a walk-through of the school as part of an audit and that the principal was consulted with.

This was disputed by the school community and staff.

The ABC can confirm the school's principal, Brendan Stewart, did not know about the works until Thursday last week, a day before the Grand Final long weekend.

Ms Wadell said that there was no nuance to save some of the trees within 10 metres of the school's buildings, but that it would work with the school community and the arborist about whether the remaining trees marked for removal could be saved.

The ABC understands Langley Primary School, 13km north of Kyneton, was also scheduled for vegetation clearing on Wednesday but arborists did not arrive.

John Lewis says the decision to remove the trees and claim bushfire safety is "silly and dead stupid". (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

Elphinstone CFA volunteer John Lewis said removing the trees did not make sense because children were never placed at fire risk.

"As soon as a bushfire is in the region, all the kids are shipped out, and they always have been," he said.

He said many of the larger trees were fire resistant and others were deciduous shade trees.

"They're not going to catch fire, so come summer where are the kids going to get shade," he said.

Greg Moore says the department had "grossly overestimated the risk" the trees pose. (Supplied)

University of Melbourne senior research associate Dr Greg Moore said the department had "grossly overestimated the risk" the trees pose in a bushfire.

"Very often they [the government] look at these situations and remove all the trees because it's such a simple thing to specify," he said.

As well as providing shade, he said trees cool the air, provide humidity in a dry summer and help with student development.

World.title: A town, a team and a dream come together as Newcastle rises as one
World.content:
All week the scribes have been falling over themselves to come up with the best way to describe what the Knights mean to Newcastle ahead of Sunday's grand final against the Roosters.

The love between the team and the town is easy to valorise and even easier to fetishise as you lose yourself in coalfield cliches and well-worn stories about 1997.

The truth is it's something that's easier to feel than it is to describe. In a league of franchises, they are a club in the truest sense of the word because they are a vessel for the community, for its hopes, dreams and fears, for its joy, sorrow and pride.

From tattoos to blue sausages, Newcastle has gone Knights crazy From fresh tattoos to blue sausages, Newcastle goes all out ahead of the NRL grand final.

They are the prism through which Newcastle feels it's feelings and at their best they become avatars of every quality the Hunter likes about itself — that they are hard-working and loyal to their mates, that they're courageous and daring, that they can walk as tall as anyone and fear nothing.

The Knights make it easier to cry, to dream of better times, to roar with triumph if they arrive and despair if they don't, to tell someone you love them or show them just how much.

The Knights are a way of life. The Knights are home. The Knights will make you believe the words of the club song, that this game is their game as surely as this town is their town.

The Knights are Newcastle and Newcastle is the Knights, and both mean more to the other than they could ever really say.

That meaning was in the tears that dried on the faces of current players, former legends and fans alike as Sandon Smith went on his run to paradise last Sunday.

Cody Hopwood, who will be the youngest prop to start a grand final since Josh Perry did for the Knights in their 2001 premiership at just 20 years of age, is 196cm and 105kg of Maitland iron with a grip like a pitbull's bite and a firm belief that the best way through any rugby league problem is to run directly through it.

Through this semi-final run he's forgotten what fear feels like, if he ever knew at all, and while he's a great chat for a young fella he doesn't even know what to call the thing that rose inside him upon realising Newcastle were through to the grand final.

"I was on the 30-metre line in tears. I just wanted to get down to him and give him a cuddle, even if I wasn't moving the fastest," Hopwood said of Smith.

"I just started crying, I don't know what came over me, all these emotions. I can't really describe the feeling."

The meaning is in the red and blue lights that have shot into the night sky all week from Newcastle City Hall in the middle of town and the paint that adorns houses throughout the region.

Old newspaper article shows Knights blueprint Writing in 1987, Newcastle's inaugural coach spelled out the player that would lead to club success.

It's in the ink that fans are putting on their bodies, which the tattooists can't do fast enough.

It's in the red and blue sausages that aren't quite as hard to find as grand final tickets but are flying off the shelves as quickly as they come in.

A trip to five different butchers earlier this week in an effort to bring some back to Sydney as proof of the terminal case of grand final fever that had broken out ended fruitlessly.

Butchers are normally as good at chewing the fat as they are cutting the meat, but the demand had them harried. On Tuesday morning alone, one had sold 50kg in half an hour.

Selling out Hunter Stadium for a grand final watch party didn't take nearly that long — on Thursday, Knights fans snapped up all 22,500 tickets in four minutes.

That shouldn't be a surprise. Newcastle shows up for their Knights, shining armour or not. This is the team which once went a whole season with only one win to show for it but had its average attendance rise from the year before.

Aside from the COVID years, where crowds were restricted, the Knights have played 449 games in Newcastle since 1988 and only ten of them attracted fewer than 10,000 people.

The Newcastle fans have never abandoned the Knights. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

That's through five wooden spoon seasons and, before this year, just four finals wins since that last premiership in 2001.

In darker days, the club took that support for granted. Their people loved them so much they didn't need their team to love them back.

But they never stopped coming, like they always knew it would work out right and they could start anew.

It's in those crowds that Tyson Frizell, once of the Illawarra but now an adopted son of another steel city, first felt it.

"I got a sense of it when I was out and about but it's not until we got everyone back at our home games that I understood how much of rugby league is in people's DNA," Frizell said.

"It's what they look forward to every week, it can make their week better or worse.

"It felt like home straight away. It's easy for it to feel like home because people are so welcoming.

"It's a country town on a big scale, people know who you are and are willing to do anything for you — they reach out, there's a community feel.

The Knights are on the verge of their first premiership since 2001. (Getty Images via All Sport: Nick Laham)

"There's great people everywhere, but there's nothing like Newcastle people."

If you don't have a ticket to the grand final or the watch party there's still other options.

If you want to go Hollywood style, Tower Cinemas will be showing the game on at least three big screens, like they did for the finals wins over New Zealand and Penrith.

Or, if you're after a wilder crowd, every pub in the area will be heaving, like they have been all week as they've filled with talk about last weekend's heroics and confident assertions that someone like Mat Croker is a dark horse for the Clive Churchill Medal.

The region is a fertile ground for public houses, bowls clubs and various other watering holes and it does them better than some places do cathedrals.

When Fletcher Sharpe, Cessnock's greatest export since the Johns brothers, gets asked what the home of the Goannas will be like on game day he just shakes his head.

"It'll go off, I can tell you that. The Leagues Club will be packed with people who couldn't get tickets to go down," Sharpe said.

"I know it'll be wild."

The Newcastle fans have been going wild all week. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The sense of anticipation hangs in the air like smoke. "Up the Knights" has replaced hello, goodbye and thank you.

It is a conversation starter and ender, and it can fill the gaps in the middle. If you say it in Newcastle, even if it's to someone you've just met, it is proof you're not a stranger.

Plenty of Novocastrians who have gone far and wide are planning to head home for the weekend, just to be there if this becomes a dream from which they never have to awaken.

They have been waiting so long for this. Before last week, Dane Gagai was the only player in the NRL that had played in a preliminary final for Newcastle.

The last man standing from their most recent premiership was Timana Tahu and he's been retired for 12 years. Tony Butterfield, who started up front for them in 1997, is 60 years old and both Johns brothers are past 50.

Some fans were there during those old days and crave a win to make them feel young again as they don faded jerseys with long-vanished sponsors.

Newcastle's past triumphs have been at the forefront all week. (Getty Images via All Sport: Nick Laham)

Some remember it from childhood and only now, a generation later and after going to hell and back, have a true appreciation for what it means.

But for plenty, this is their first time. They have heard all the old stories so many times, they have seen the photos of Joey on the skateboard or heard Matty exhorting that it was better than Lego or watched the tape of the ambush of Parramatta in 2001 until it replaced their own dim memories, until it was more real than their own lives.

This is their first chance to be part of it for true, to live a new version of legends they were raised on, to roll back the nostalgic fog and realise that history isn't always about the past.

To do so, they'll have to beat the Roosters and taking on a team like that is to defy an empire, even if Newcastle have found a way to weaponise attacking miracles.

The odds are against them but given they have been each of the past three weeks it feels like that doesn't matter.

Newcastle out for salvation ten years after horror season In 2016, Newcastle hit rock bottom in a season where they won just one game. Ten years later, one more win can deliver them a premiership.

The team will leave for Sydney on Saturday morning. The bus route has been detailed in the Newcastle Herald and on all the club's socials. There are no secrets left.

The people will line the road for miles, and they will wave their flags and lift their signs and go wild for one last look before their heroes try to bring back a little piece of heaven and for one last chance to prove they've loved them all along.

The Knights will leave for their date with destiny and on Sunday they'll meet their fate armed with everything their people have got, which is all they've ever really needed.

Their fans will dominate the day and they will chant that three-syllable symphony that fills stadiums and hearts as, far from home and at the edge of a dream a quarter-century in the making, team and town will prove once more that they are one.

World.title: Judge denies Lindsay Clancy defence motion to find her not guilty
World.content:
The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case has refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defence motion that argued there was not enough evidence to prove she was responsible for killing her three children.

Warning: This story contains details of a crime that may be distressing for some readers.

During Ms Clancy's first trial, which ended on September 4 with a deadlocked jury, her defence argued that she was not criminally responsible because of a mental illness, specifically a rare condition called postpartum psychosis.

As such, the defence did not dispute the fact that the 36-year-old former labour and delivery nurse carried out the killings at her family's Massachusetts home in 2023.

However, in a hearing earlier this week, Ms Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington tried to persuade the judge that prosecutors had not offered any proof that Clancy did it.

Prosecutors argued there was plenty of evidence, calling Reddington's claim "laughable".

Attorney Kevin Reddington argued the case was based on speculation in the defence's latest motion. (The Patriot Ledger via AP: Greg Derr)

In his ruling, Judge William Sullivan noted that, for the purposes of his decision, he was required to analyse the evidence in the light most favourable to prosecutors — and that it was up to the jury, not the judge, to decide whether to believe expert witnesses for the defence who testified that Ms Clancy was not responsible for her actions because of mental illness.

"There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder," Mr Sullivan wrote.

Defence team pivots after mistrial

At the first trial, prosecutors acknowledged that Ms Clancy had mental health problems that included months of treatment and a stay in a psychiatric hospital, but argued that she knew what she was doing when she strangled the children — the youngest just 8 months old — then tried to kill herself.

Mr Sullivan had declared a mistrial with the jury split 11 to one in favour of acquitting Ms Clancy of murder charges.

In Tuesday's hearing, Mr Reddington suggested the entire case "was based on speculation" and proceeded to list the shortcomings in the prosecution's case.

There was almost no police investigation, he claimed, and significant questions revolving around Ms Clancy's condition outside the night of the killings and her lack of memory of what happened.

At the trial, jurors heard testimony that Ms Clancy said she heard voices instructing her to kill 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy. Her DNA was found on exercise bands used to strangle them.

Before the trial, Mr Reddington himself filed a motion in which he said Ms Clancy was willing to stipulate, in writing, to her involvement in the children's deaths.

"For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this," Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told the judge.

Lindsay Clancy jurors speak out over mistrial Eleven members of the jury were persuaded to find her not guilty by reason of insanity, but one member would not acquit.

"I'd suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this."

Ms Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.

Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to bring the case to trial for a second time.

They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or seek to try her only on lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely.

Ms Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder.

If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility.

Her former husband, Patrick Clancy, who discovered the children's bodies, has said in interviews that he forgives her for the killings.

The live-streamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth.

AP

World.title: WA news LIVE: WA Greens staffer the latest to be banned from Land Forces expo
World.content:
A WA Greens staffer who was fined over a foiled protest at the home of former Woodside boss Meg O’Neill is among the activists to have been banned from the Land Forces defence expo that is set to take over the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre next week.

Matilda Lane-Rose was fined $2000 and granted a spent conviction last year after being arrested alongside other Disrupt Burrup Hub activists as they attempted to chain themselves to a gate and throw paint on O’Neill’s western suburbs home in 2023.

Emil Davey, Matilda Lane-Rose and Jesse Noakes outside Perth Magistrates Court following their sentencing last year over their planned protest outside Meg O’Neill’s house. Jesinta Burton.

The arrest was filmed by an ABC Four Corners crew, which was working on a story about climate activism, and Perth Magistrates Court heard the activists had been captured on CCTV scoping out the home 72 hours before their planned protest.

Lane-Rose, alongside co-accused Jesse Noakes, Gerard Mazza and Emil Davey, all pleaded guilty to attempted trespass and attempted unlawful damage.

World.title: 13-year-long AFP bribery investigation ends with no prosecution
World.content:
The Australian Federal Police have accepted a $9 million settlement to end a 13-year-long bribery investigation into a storied Australian engineering company that still has major government contracts.

As part of the settlement agreement to pay the money under proceeds of crime legislation, SMEC, formerly the Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation, made no admissions of wrongdoing. Police did not refer the matter to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions, citing factors including the company’s cooperation and the length of time since the events under investigation occurred.

SMEC has done work on numerous government projects, including Snowy Hydro 2.0. Jamila Toderas

AFP anti-corruption commander, Andrea Quinn, said the $9 million payment showed that companies would still face significant financial consequences following foreign bribery investigations, even if there was no prosecution.

“Noting the cooperation of SMEC throughout the investigation, companies identifying potential misconduct and engaging early, transparently and constructively with the AFP place themselves in a materially different position to those who do not,” Quinn said. “The AFP is committed to detecting, disrupting and deterring foreign bribery and any related criminal activity.”
