World.title: ‘A toothpick?’ Brisbane 2032 emblems design riddle deepens with new piece
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics ‘A toothpick?’ Brisbane 2032 emblems design riddle deepens with new piece Dominique Tassell October 2, 2026 — 9:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Day four of the Brisbane 2032 Games logo reveal has added another piece, but those following along at home might be frustrated to see yet another squiggle. Paralympic swimmer Alexa Leary and beach volleyball Olympic gold medallist Nat Cook revealed the fourth piece of the emblems – for both the Olympic and Paralympic Games – at Wild Horse Mountain Lookout on the Sunshine Coast. The magenta and gold piece could be interpreted as a leaf, a sun ray, a petal – or a toothpick, according to Leary and Cook. Is it … a toothpick? Nat Cook and Alexa Leary don’t know what to make of it. Dominique Tassell Leary said she couldn’t wait to see the finished product, but admitted Friday’s piece didn’t narrow down the options before the design’s full reveal on Monday morning.



The third piece, a gold and magenta almost-sphere, was revealed by retired track cyclist and Paris Chef de Mission Anna Meares and Paralympian wheelchair sprints athlete Angie Ballard on Thursday in Rockhampton’s Riverside Park. The first two pieces were similar but slightly different squiggles, revealed by swimmers Ian Thorpe and Grant “Scooter” Patterson in Cairns on Tuesday. Then NRL legends Johnathan Thurston and Sam Thaiday unveiled another in Townsville a day later. The third piece of the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games emblems revealed in Rockhampton on Thursday. The multi-day rollout of emblems is stretching down the Queensland coast, landing on the Gold Coast on Saturday followed by a final piece in Brisbane on Sunday. How all six elements come together will be revealed on Monday. The spectrum of theories has spread far and wide, from flames and the sun to native flora and fauna.



There was even a suggestion from the press pack on Thursday that it could be the endangered Fitzroy River turtle, known as the bum breathing turtle. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics ‘You’re thinking kangaroos, aren’t you?’ Thurston, Thaiday try to solve Brisbane Olympics puzzle Looking back at the 16 Games emblems used this century, the most common motifs are people, landmarks and cultural aspects of the host city. Seven different Games emblems included a significant cultural aspect from the host city, such as Sydney 2000’s boomerang, Vancouver 2010’s inukuk stone figures, Beijing 2008 and 2022’s use of Chinese calligraphy and characters, and PyeongChang 2018’s use of the Korean alphabet. Six Games emblems featured people and five featured natural or man-made landmarks. Only two used weather motifs, while Athens 2004 alone used a botanical element (the olive branch) and Paris 2024 alone used the Olympic flame and medal.



London 2012, Sochi 2014 and Los Angeles 2028 used none of these motifs, instead going for stylised fonts of the year or host city. The Paris 2024 logo as displayed on a building. Reuters The Sunshine Coast Stadium will be upgraded and has been earmarked for football preliminary matches, and the Sunshine Coast Mountain Bike Centre is being renovated. An indoor sports centre was proposed then scrapped. The Sunshine Coast Mountain Bike Centre will also be renovated, and a temporary facility for road cycling, marathon, race walks, kiteboarding, paralympic road cycling and marathon is proposed at Alexandra Headland. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Rogue migration lawyers to be targeted in federal crackdown; US sends thousands of additional troops to Middle East as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran
World.content:
International students will have to pay about $1200 for a new visa if they want to change universities under a federal crackdown on visa-hopping.

Most students and graduates will also be barred from bringing partners and children to Australia, with exemptions for PhD students, scholarship holders and people from ASEAN and Pacific nations.

Assistant Minister for International Education Julian Hill announced the changes today, warning the government was targeting migrants who move between temporary visas in an attempt to stay in Australia permanently.

Julian Hill is the assistant minister for citizenship, customs and multicultural affairs. Oscar Colman

Temporary migrants on working holiday or employer-sponsored visas will also be blocked from applying for student visas while in Australia.

The government is seeking to reduce net overseas migration from almost 300,000 a year to 225,000 by 2028.

Hill also outlined tougher measures against migration agents, lawyers and other intermediaries accused of exploiting loopholes in the visa system.

World.title: Texts sent from Jesse Baird’s phone revealed in Lamarre-Condon murder trial
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial Texts sent from Jesse Baird’s phone revealed in Lamarre-Condon murder trial Michaela Whitbourn October 2, 2026 — 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former TV presenter Jesse Baird appeared to send his housemates a series of text messages about moving out the day after he was allegedly murdered by Beau Lamarre-Condon, a court has heard. The text exchange was released by the NSW Supreme Court after it was shown to the jury in former police officer Lamarre-Condon’s trial over the shooting deaths of Baird, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Qantas flight attendant Luke Davies. Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of sending text messages from Jesse Baird’s phone after he allegedly murdered him. Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering Baird, 26, and Davies, 29, in Baird’s Paddington share house with his police-issued Glock pistol on the morning of February 19, 2024. The Crown alleges the accused sent messages from Baird’s phone to a housemates’ group chat on February 20 to give the impression he was still alive.



At 5.56pm on February 19, hours after the alleged murders, a housemate – dubbed Belinda Smith in the proceedings – texted a photo of what she believed to be “rusted water” near surfboard bags and a tarpaulin in the courtyard of the home to another housemate. The second housemate, known as Sarah King in the case, replied: “What the actual f---?” Smith told the court on Thursday that she inspected the backyard again the following day and “saw that the surfboards had been cleared, and the liquid was gone”. Texts between all three housemates, tendered in court, show a series of messages from Baird’s phone the day after his death.



The court has heard Smith and King had asked Baird to move out so that another female friend could join them in the terrace. He was slated to move out on February 20, the day after the alleged murders. “Hi both!! I’ve hired an air tasker to come and collect my things … I might be doing a road trip to Perth with mates on Thursday night so should be flying back Sunday and will 100% have it out by then,” a message from Baird’s phone at 12.28pm on February 20 read. Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon (centre) is accused of killing Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird (right). Smith replied: “Hey Jesse, sorry I’m a bit confused. I thought you said you were moving out today 20th Feb. Your final rent payment ends tomorrow and [the new housemate] starts paying from Thursday.” Smith texted King on February 20: “I’m genuinely scared this dude isn’t moving out today.”



The prosecution alleges Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him that escalated when Baird ended their casual relationship in November 2023. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Housemate’s startling discovery at alleged Lamarre-Condon crime scene Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, was killed to eliminate a witness to the crime, the Crown alleges. There is no dispute that Lamarre-Condon was at the terrace when Baird and Davies died, that they died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol, and that he was disguised as a delivery rider. However, the defence case is that Lamarre-Condon was there to pick up some of his belongings and did not expect anybody to be home. A struggle ensued in which his gun accidentally went off twice, killing Baird, and Davies accidentally shot himself in a second struggle after grabbing the gun, the defence says.



According to the defence, Lamarre-Condon panicked and dumped the men’s bodies in surfboard bags in Bungonia, near Goulburn. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial The 1600-word text accused killer allegedly sent to fake a cancer diagnosis The prosecution has told the jury that Lamarre-Condon cleaned the scene while the housemates were out, including throwing items from Baird’s bedroom into a skip bin in Cronulla. The court has heard that police visited the home for the first time on February 21, after items were found in the skip bin by groundskeepers. Three cleaners were at the home at the time because they had been booked by King ahead of the arrival of the new housemate. The trial continues.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Maddinson and Harper called into Test squad as Green injury confirmed
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Maddinson and Harper called into Test squad as Green injury confirmed Daniel Brettig Updated October 2, 2026 — 6:43am ,first published 10:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nic Maddinson and Sam Harper have been vaulted into Australia’s Test squad to face South Africa, amid doubts about the fitness of Cameron Green and Josh Inglis. Green sent alarm bells through Australia’s camp ahead of the series against South Africa after appearing to suffer an abdominal injury while batting in the final ODI against the Proteas. Nic Maddinson has been parachuted into the Australian Test team. Getty Images Having already dealt with shoulder soreness that delayed his return to bowling, Green reeled away in pain, clutching his stomach after trying to hook a delivery from Corbin Bosch. On Friday night the selectors named wicketkeeper Harper, who made a century for Australia A in India last week, and sometime Test player Maddinson, as dual cover for Inglis (broken finger) and Green, who was confirmed as having suffered an abdominal strain.



Cameron Green was floored by a Corbin Bosch full toss to the groin. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Maddinson made a one day Cup century for NSW against Victoria to start the home season. Last summer he made a comeback to the game after treatment for testicular cancer. His selection was made ahead of numerous Australia A players such as Sam Konstas, Nathan McSweeney and Peter Handscomb. “Sam gives us wicketkeeping cover as Josh continues his recovery while Nic provides flexibility throughout the batting order,” said selection chair George Bailey. Nic Maddinson with his son August following his final treatment.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Scary proposition’: Cummins opens door for Marsh Test comeback It had been a dramatic over in which Green had been struck amidships by Bosch and also flicked a delivery for six, but the apparent muscle strain was bad enough to prevent Green from being part of the bowling attack as Australia won the game on rain calculations. “He was locked in to bowl a few overs today,” white-ball skipper Mitch Marsh said of Green. “He had a nice build and it would’ve been nice for him to have a bowl, but it wasn’t meant to be, and I’m sure that it won’t affect his prep too much, hopefully.” Green attempted to bowl during the innings break, but after sending down a few half-pace deliveries under the watch of the team physio, aborted the attempt and was then off the field for the rest of the game. Australia were also monitoring Test opener Matt Renshaw after he suffered a blow to the wrist in the field, forcing him off for treatment.



“I sound like a footy coach, but I haven’t seen them,” Marsh said. “I know ‘Renners’ got a knock on the wrist, and ‘Greeny’ after being hit, I’m not too sure what was going on there, I haven’t spoken to them yet. But hopefully both are OK.” Loading An injury to Green would be a major blow to Australia’s hopes of winning in South Africa, particularly after he broke through for a first Test century on home soil against Bangladesh in Darwin in August. Marsh, meanwhile, said that he was currently planning to fly home to Perth rather than joining the Test squad, but conceded that skipper Cummins still saw him as part of the Test team’s plans should the need arise. “If Pat says the door’s open then it’s open,” Marsh said. “I don’t think I’ll ever be good enough to retire from Test cricket.”



Asked how he would approach batting in Tests were he ever to play again, Marsh paused. “It’s a great question, I don’t really know,” he said. “I imagine it’ll be similar to my white-ball game if I was to get another crack at it.” Marsh led the team despite Cummins’ return to the line-up for his first ODI in two years, in which he bowled five sharp overs during the Proteas’ unsuccessful chase. Pat Cummins and Mitch Marsh share a close relationship. World.title: 13-year-long AFP bribery investigation ends with no prosecution
World.content:
The Australian Federal Police have accepted a $9 million settlement to end a 13-year-long bribery investigation into a storied Australian engineering company that still has major government contracts.

As part of the settlement agreement to pay the money under proceeds of crime legislation, SMEC, formerly the Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation, made no admissions of wrongdoing. Police did not refer the matter to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions, citing factors including the company’s cooperation and the length of time since the events under investigation occurred.

SMEC has done work on numerous government projects, including Snowy Hydro 2.0. Jamila Toderas

AFP anti-corruption commander, Andrea Quinn, said the $9 million payment showed that companies would still face significant financial consequences following foreign bribery investigations, even if there was no prosecution.

“Noting the cooperation of SMEC throughout the investigation, companies identifying potential misconduct and engaging early, transparently and constructively with the AFP place themselves in a materially different position to those who do not,” Quinn said. “The AFP is committed to detecting, disrupting and deterring foreign bribery and any related criminal activity.”

World.title: ‘A toothpick?’ Brisbane 2032 emblems design riddle deepens with new piece
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics ‘A toothpick?’ Brisbane 2032 emblems design riddle deepens with new piece Dominique Tassell October 2, 2026 — 9:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Day four of the Brisbane 2032 Games logo reveal has added another piece, but those following along at home might be frustrated to see yet another squiggle. Paralympic swimmer Alexa Leary and beach volleyball Olympic gold medallist Nat Cook revealed the fourth piece of the emblems – for both the Olympic and Paralympic Games – at Wild Horse Mountain Lookout on the Sunshine Coast. The magenta and gold piece could be interpreted as a leaf, a sun ray, a petal – or a toothpick, according to Leary and Cook. Is it … a toothpick? Nat Cook and Alexa Leary don’t know what to make of it. Dominique Tassell Leary said she couldn’t wait to see the finished product, but admitted Friday’s piece didn’t narrow down the options before the design’s full reveal on Monday morning.



The third piece, a gold and magenta almost-sphere, was revealed by retired track cyclist and Paris Chef de Mission Anna Meares and Paralympian wheelchair sprints athlete Angie Ballard on Thursday in Rockhampton’s Riverside Park. The first two pieces were similar but slightly different squiggles, revealed by swimmers Ian Thorpe and Grant “Scooter” Patterson in Cairns on Tuesday. Then NRL legends Johnathan Thurston and Sam Thaiday unveiled another in Townsville a day later. The third piece of the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games emblems revealed in Rockhampton on Thursday. The multi-day rollout of emblems is stretching down the Queensland coast, landing on the Gold Coast on Saturday followed by a final piece in Brisbane on Sunday. How all six elements come together will be revealed on Monday. The spectrum of theories has spread far and wide, from flames and the sun to native flora and fauna.



There was even a suggestion from the press pack on Thursday that it could be the endangered Fitzroy River turtle, known as the bum breathing turtle. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics ‘You’re thinking kangaroos, aren’t you?’ Thurston, Thaiday try to solve Brisbane Olympics puzzle Looking back at the 16 Games emblems used this century, the most common motifs are people, landmarks and cultural aspects of the host city. Seven different Games emblems included a significant cultural aspect from the host city, such as Sydney 2000’s boomerang, Vancouver 2010’s inukuk stone figures, Beijing 2008 and 2022’s use of Chinese calligraphy and characters, and PyeongChang 2018’s use of the Korean alphabet. Six Games emblems featured people and five featured natural or man-made landmarks. Only two used weather motifs, while Athens 2004 alone used a botanical element (the olive branch) and Paris 2024 alone used the Olympic flame and medal.



London 2012, Sochi 2014 and Los Angeles 2028 used none of these motifs, instead going for stylised fonts of the year or host city. The Paris 2024 logo as displayed on a building. Reuters The Sunshine Coast Stadium will be upgraded and has been earmarked for football preliminary matches, and the Sunshine Coast Mountain Bike Centre is being renovated. An indoor sports centre was proposed then scrapped. The Sunshine Coast Mountain Bike Centre will also be renovated, and a temporary facility for road cycling, marathon, race walks, kiteboarding, paralympic road cycling and marathon is proposed at Alexandra Headland. World.title: Opinion: Melbourne through the looking glass
World.content:
Sponsored PoliticsVictoriaThe University of Melbourne Opinion: Melbourne through the looking glass Advertorial for The University of Melbourne Professor Mark Cassidy AM October 2, 2026 — 9:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Professor Mark Cassidy, Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Research) at the University of Melbourne. As Melbourne prepares to take its place as Australia’s largest city, we have the opportunity to also become the most innovative, sustainable, culturally diverse and liveable city in the country. Let’s start with innovative. The University of Melbourne’s bold ambition is for Melbourne to become the innovation heartbeat of Australia. And we already have the ecosystem and expertise in place to shape solutions that will see Melburnians thrive. The vital research, collaboration and conversations happening across our campuses and precincts today – in both research and education – will power our city’s growth and prosperity tomorrow. AI is enabling new opportunities for research excellence, collaboration and innovation across the University, Australia and the globe. We are actively working with industry leaders, decision makers and communities with a shared vision for Melbourne to become a world-renowned innovation and AI precinct by 2050. Our city will be compared with the Silicon Valley in California and Kendall Square in Boston – an extraordinary science and innovation hub that has produced 105 Nobel Laureates and counting.



The University of Melbourne aims to transform the city into a global hub for research and collaboration. Our world-class precincts will drive this. Cross-disciplinary collaboration strengthens research impact and innovation. The Melbourne Biomedical Precinct, encompassing more than 40 hospitals, research institutes, universities and major companies, is home to 10,000 researchers. The precinct has delivered medical care, research and education for more than 160 years, driving innovations like the development of the multi-channel cochlear implant, the discovery of the rotavirus and personalised cancer treatments. The tangible impacts of these discoveries have rippled across Australia and the world. With imagination and rigour, the University is bringing its interdisciplinary research strengths to existing partnerships and new collaborations. We are realising discoveries that will advance knowledge, answer enduring questions about the world around us, enable healthier lives and communities and deliver environmental and economic benefits. The University of Melbourne invests about $1.6 billion every year on research. Our researchers explore ambitious questions to advance the boundaries of knowledge. AI is accelerating research discovery and supporting world-leading research. Our researchers are supported through responsible AI guidance, partnerships and capability development. We work in partnership with government, industry and the community to solve big problems at scale.



But we never lose sight of why and for whom our research matters. The Melbourne community – today, tomorrow and future – stands to be the biggest beneficiary. The researchers and educators in the University’s three expanding precincts – Melbourne Biomedical Precinct, Melbourne Arts Precinct and Melbourne Connect – are united in building a bold and robust future for our city. The next generation of medical breakthroughs will continue, in part aided by the opening this year of the Aikenhead Centre for Medical Discovery at St Vincent’s Hospital. The Centre is Australia’s first hospital-based biomedical engineering research translation centre that will lead innovations in medtech, biotech and digital health. The Melbourne Arts Precinct continues to learn more about the ways art and music positively shape society, health and wellbeing. Our researchers are exploring how music therapy can assist people with dementia and how dance can increase social cohesion and resilience in an unpredictable world. But the intellectual property and research excellence within the University of Melbourne must be commercialised for real-world impact. This is the purpose of our innovation precinct, Melbourne Connect, a meeting place to facilitate innovation and translation for the benefit of society.



Melbourne Connect brings together researchers, entrepreneurs, experts, students and industry leaders to share ideas, develop creative solutions to local and global challenges, and fast-track innovations to market. The University of Melbourne launched Australia’s first university-based venture capital fund – Tin Alley – a $125 million investment fund to commercialise and scale up innovative companies emerging from the University. The University recently built a new lab, the Laboratory for Advanced Radiochemical Science (LARS), partnering with Cyclotek, to investigate next-gen cancer treatment and to strengthen Australia’s sovereign capability in radiopharmaceuticals. Meanwhile, five University of Melbourne-affiliated startups are working on minimally invasive implants and redefining how we diagnose, manage and treat conditions like paralysis, epilepsy and Parkinson’s disease. Fluent, for example, is developing a brain computer interface helping people with impaired speech to communicate by using only their thoughts. Building a sustainable city is a shared focus. The Australian Integrated Multimodal EcoSystem (AIMES) is a world-first project by the University of Melbourne with 50 partners across government, transport and tech sectors. AIMES collects computing data from smart sensors and systems across 100km of Melbourne’s inner north. This living laboratory is a platform for government, industry and academia to devise better transport outcomes for Melbourne.



University of Melbourne is committed to solving problems, fostering innovation, AI-enablement and delivering exceptional value and benefit to society. Our precincts are on the lands of the Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung and Bunurong (Boon Wurrung) peoples of the Kulin Nation. We will do this while continuing to embed Indigenous knowledges into our research, and the ways Indigenous peoples have cared for Country. As the University of Melbourne has done for generations, it will continue to strengthen collaborative efforts and partnerships to secure the pipeline of unique breakthroughs and innovations for which Melbourne is renowned. In a world where knowledge is increasingly questioned, we are committed to leading with excellence, ethics and integrity. Melbourne is on an exciting journey – one that will transform our brightest research and innovations into real-world outcomes and ongoing prosperity for Melbourne, its people, and for our global community. Professor Mark Cassidy is Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Research) at the University of Melbourne.

International students will have to pay about $1200 for a new visa if they want to change universities under a federal crackdown on visa-hopping.

World.title: Texts sent from Jesse Baird’s phone revealed in Lamarre-Condon murder trial
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial Texts sent from Jesse Baird’s phone revealed in Lamarre-Condon murder trial Michaela Whitbourn October 2, 2026 — 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former TV presenter Jesse Baird appeared to send his housemates a series of text messages about moving out the day after he was allegedly murdered by Beau Lamarre-Condon, a court has heard. The text exchange was released by the NSW Supreme Court after it was shown to the jury in former police officer Lamarre-Condon’s trial over the shooting deaths of Baird, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Qantas flight attendant Luke Davies. Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of sending text messages from Jesse Baird’s phone after he allegedly murdered him. Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering Baird, 26, and Davies, 29, in Baird’s Paddington share house with his police-issued Glock pistol on the morning of February 19, 2024. The Crown alleges the accused sent messages from Baird’s phone to a housemates’ group chat on February 20 to give the impression he was still alive.



At 5.56pm on February 19, hours after the alleged murders, a housemate – dubbed Belinda Smith in the proceedings – texted a photo of what she believed to be “rusted water” near surfboard bags and a tarpaulin in the courtyard of the home to another housemate. The second housemate, known as Sarah King in the case, replied: “What the actual f---?” Smith told the court on Thursday that she inspected the backyard again the following day and “saw that the surfboards had been cleared, and the liquid was gone”. Texts between all three housemates, tendered in court, show a series of messages from Baird’s phone the day after his death.



The court has heard Smith and King had asked Baird to move out so that another female friend could join them in the terrace. He was slated to move out on February 20, the day after the alleged murders. “Hi both!! I’ve hired an air tasker to come and collect my things … I might be doing a road trip to Perth with mates on Thursday night so should be flying back Sunday and will 100% have it out by then,” a message from Baird’s phone at 12.28pm on February 20 read. Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon (centre) is accused of killing Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird (right). Smith replied: “Hey Jesse, sorry I’m a bit confused. I thought you said you were moving out today 20th Feb. Your final rent payment ends tomorrow and [the new housemate] starts paying from Thursday.” Smith texted King on February 20: “I’m genuinely scared this dude isn’t moving out today.”



The prosecution alleges Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him that escalated when Baird ended their casual relationship in November 2023. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Housemate’s startling discovery at alleged Lamarre-Condon crime scene Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, was killed to eliminate a witness to the crime, the Crown alleges. There is no dispute that Lamarre-Condon was at the terrace when Baird and Davies died, that they died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol, and that he was disguised as a delivery rider. However, the defence case is that Lamarre-Condon was there to pick up some of his belongings and did not expect anybody to be home. A struggle ensued in which his gun accidentally went off twice, killing Baird, and Davies accidentally shot himself in a second struggle after grabbing the gun, the defence says.



According to the defence, Lamarre-Condon panicked and dumped the men’s bodies in surfboard bags in Bungonia, near Goulburn. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial The 1600-word text accused killer allegedly sent to fake a cancer diagnosis The prosecution has told the jury that Lamarre-Condon cleaned the scene while the housemates were out, including throwing items from Baird’s bedroom into a skip bin in Cronulla. The court has heard that police visited the home for the first time on February 21, after items were found in the skip bin by groundskeepers. Three cleaners were at the home at the time because they had been booked by King ahead of the arrival of the new housemate. The trial continues.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Nic Maddinson and Sam Harper have been vaulted into Australia’s Test squad to face South Africa, amid doubts about the fitness of Cameron Green and Josh Inglis. Green sent alarm bells through Australia’s camp ahead of the series against South Africa after appearing to suffer an abdominal injury while batting in the final ODI against the Proteas. Nic Maddinson has been parachuted into the Australian Test team. Getty Images Having already dealt with shoulder soreness that delayed his return to bowling, Green reeled away in pain, clutching his stomach after trying to hook a delivery from Corbin Bosch. On Friday night the selectors named wicketkeeper Harper, who made a century for Australia A in India last week, and sometime Test player Maddinson, as dual cover for Inglis (broken finger) and Green, who was confirmed as having suffered an abdominal strain.



Cameron Green was floored by a Corbin Bosch full toss to the groin. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Maddinson made a one day Cup century for NSW against Victoria to start the home season. Last summer he made a comeback to the game after treatment for testicular cancer. His selection was made ahead of numerous Australia A players such as Sam Konstas, Nathan McSweeney and Peter Handscomb. “Sam gives us wicketkeeping cover as Josh continues his recovery while Nic provides flexibility throughout the batting order,” said selection chair George Bailey. Nic Maddinson with his son August following his final treatment.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Scary proposition’: Cummins opens door for Marsh Test comeback It had been a dramatic over in which Green had been struck amidships by Bosch and also flicked a delivery for six, but the apparent muscle strain was bad enough to prevent Green from being part of the bowling attack as Australia won the game on rain calculations. “He was locked in to bowl a few overs today,” white-ball skipper Mitch Marsh said of Green. “He had a nice build and it would’ve been nice for him to have a bowl, but it wasn’t meant to be, and I’m sure that it won’t affect his prep too much, hopefully.” Green attempted to bowl during the innings break, but after sending down a few half-pace deliveries under the watch of the team physio, aborted the attempt and was then off the field for the rest of the game. Australia were also monitoring Test opener Matt Renshaw after he suffered a blow to the wrist in the field, forcing him off for treatment.



“I sound like a footy coach, but I haven’t seen them,” Marsh said. “I know ‘Renners’ got a knock on the wrist, and ‘Greeny’ after being hit, I’m not too sure what was going on there, I haven’t spoken to them yet. But hopefully both are OK.” Loading An injury to Green would be a major blow to Australia’s hopes of winning in South Africa, particularly after he broke through for a first Test century on home soil against Bangladesh in Darwin in August. Marsh, meanwhile, said that he was currently planning to fly home to Perth rather than joining the Test squad, but conceded that skipper Cummins still saw him as part of the Test team’s plans should the need arise. “If Pat says the door’s open then it’s open,” Marsh said. “I don’t think I’ll ever be good enough to retire from Test cricket.”



Asked how he would approach batting in Tests were he ever to play again, Marsh paused. “It’s a great question, I don’t really know,” he said. “I imagine it’ll be similar to my white-ball game if I was to get another crack at it.” Marsh led the team despite Cummins’ return to the line-up for his first ODI in two years, in which he bowled five sharp overs during the Proteas’ unsuccessful chase. World.title: ACT leader David Seymour doesn't see why AI shouldn't write government Cabinet papers
World.content:
Audio player for " RNZ National " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1680618%2Fact-leader-david-seymour-doesn-t-see-why-ai-shouldn-t-write-government-cabinet-papers

RNZ national

In the lead-up to November's election, Midday Report is speaking with the technology spokesperson for a range of parties about their biggest hopes and fears for artificial intelligence (AI) and the role of the Government in regulating the technology. On Friday, Guyon Epsiner sat down with ACT leader David Seymour.

David Seymour says he can't see why AI shouldn't write government Cabinet papers.

In an interview with Midday Report, the Act Party leader said he'd done dummy runs into what AI can do in government and said it should be aggressively adapted.

Seymour said the Ministry for Regulation had issued guidance on using AI.

"One of the critical things it says is: 'Yes, we should be using AI in government, but keep a human in the loop'.

Audio player for " Seymour reveals AI used in government problem-solving trial " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1680618%2Fact-leader-david-seymour-doesn-t-see-why-ai-shouldn-t-write-government-cabinet-papers

Seymour reveals AI used in government problem-solving trial Midday Report Download MP3 24m

"We haven't, sort of, put the whole thing on autopilot. What we're doing is saying, okay, there's a whole lot of steps in this process. Everything in government is long. What if we just gave a part of that process and see if they can do it faster than the humans?"

He said in the last few years every time there was a suggestion anyone in government was using AI there was an uproar.

"At the last election, a few people used some AI to produce their graphics on social media, and this was going to be the end of the world. I think generally the risk for New Zealand is that we're too slow to adopt this. The public sector was too slow to adopt this."

Seymour said there were a number of dangers with AI.

"I read a couple of months ago about a guy in Sydney who had no real special training, managed to create a kind of CAR T therapy for his dog, which actually cured his dog's cancer. He used AI to develop that CAR-T therapy based on some tests of the cancer cells in his dog. Now, when I read that, I thought, that is possibly one of the coolest things I've read in years, but also one of the most terrifying, because what if he wasn't benign? What if he was a cat person? He might use it for evil. Luckily, he was a dog person.

"But the idea that AI will empower some lone wolf to do something truly awful. All technology has sort of been taking us in that direction."

Seymour said the New Zealand government was "probably not" going to be the leader on AI worldwide.

"I suspect out best play is to be a fast follower as those debates play out overseas.

"I would make an analogy to the social media debate. The idea that the New Zealand government is going to change the marketplace for social media globally, maybe good political point scoring at home, but it's not realistic.

"What we should do in the social media debate is follow these American court cases, the most recent one, Alabama versus TikTok, and make sure that New Zealand kids get the same protections as American kids have, and I would make a similar analogy for the role of the New Zealand government in AI."

He said ACT did not have a position on which department AI should rest in or which minister should be responsible.

World.title: Shop owner relieved Northland road re-opening after 'hell on wheels' closure
World.content:
A shop owner in a Northland town cut off by a slip for more than eight months says the road closure has been "hell on wheels" - so today's re-opening is a huge relief.

On 21 January, after a week of heavy rain, a massive landslide buried Russell Road under almost 100,000 cubic metres of soil, boulders and trees.

The slip severed the main road for coastal communities such as Ōakura, Helena Bay and Whangaruru, forcing residents to take a long detour and a ferry to reach jobs, health services and schools in Whangārei.

The council set up an emergency route via steep, unsealed Kaiikanui Road but that could be used only in guided convoys.

Ōakura Bay Store owner Nena Rogers said her main feeling today was relief.

"It's been crippling. People say, 'Are you excited?' And we say, 'oh no, we're just relieved really'. It's been hell on wheels really. But what can you do? You can't do anything, you just got to shut up and beat it," she said.

"But you know, we've scraped through. We're still cheerful. The community's still cheerful. I think they're very happy that the road's open."

Normally the settlement's businesses survived on the annual influx of holiday makers and bach owners.

Aerial view of the cleared slip on Russell Road’s Helena Bay Hill. Supplied / Whangārei District Council

This year, the summer season came to an abrupt end in January, when the road was wiped out.

Rogers said after another major slip shut the road for four months in 2007, she started putting aside a reserve fund to get her through any future closures.

Nineteen years later, that had kept the business afloat.

She said there were also some upsides to the road closure.

"It's so beautiful and peaceful and the water looks so gorgeous, so it's been quite pleasant in a lot of ways. There's been no traffic and very few people. That's the compensation - every night when I finish work, I can sit with my gin upstairs and there's nobody around."

Rogers said many bach owners were vowing to come back once the road re-opened.

Floodwaters at Ōakura Bay as seen from the air. Supplied / Ngātiwai Trust Board

"People have rung us and said, 'Look, we're not coming up yet, but we will, and we'll bring money with us'. So they've been in touch, and that's fantastic."

The long-range forecast was for a warm, dry summer on Northland's east coast, which could help businesses trying to make up for lost income.

Rogers said the re-opening had taken a long time but that was understandable given the sheer size of the slip.

She said the hillside was still moving and any future storms were likely to affect road access.

"So we just have to wait and see. But you know, we keep our chin up and keep smiling. Laughter is the best medicine."

World.title: NZ Warriors seek to cash in on popularity with new 'Wah-House' retail store
World.content:
Riding a wave of popularity, the Warriors are set to open their own retail store inside the country's biggest shopping mall.

The official team store 'The Wah-House' will open next month at Sylvia Park in Auckland under an initial six-month lease.

Demand for Warriors merchandise has exploded in recent] seasons on the back of historic success, the side finishing second in 2026 and hosting two play-off matches.

CEO Cameron George said sales through their store at Go Media Stadium gave the club confidence to step into the retail environment.

"We've formed a terrific relationship with Sylvia Park's owners, have leased store space and will now work towards opening our own store on 5 November."

The newly established store will result in the current retail outlet at Go Media Stadium closing.

"This is all part of our strategy to continue unlocking the power of our brand and expand our opportunity to reach more fans outside the traditional gameday environment."

There was an unprecedented run of support for the Warriors this season.

They sold out 13 NRL games at four different stadiums throughout New Zealand, culminating in a crowd of 48,511 for their preliminary final, lost to the Knights at Eden Park, eclipsing the record of 47,363 for the Rugby League World Cup final in 1988.

The Warriors set the highest total attendance of 356,235, a 134 percent increase in the home crowd aggregate since 2019.

The Warriors have also entered the hospitality sector, having opened the Full Time Sports Bar and Eatery in Kingsland in 2024.

World.title: Graduate job seeker applies for more than 600 jobs amid tough market
World.content:
Audio player for " Wellington student discusses graduating in tough job market " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/business/1679499%2Fgraduate-job-seeker-applies-for-more-than-600-jobs-amid-tough-market

Wellington student discusses graduating in tough job market Morning Report Download MP3 5m

A recent Wellington graduate says she has undertaken more than 600 job applications and 53 interviews in a year amid a tough job market.

Hannah Tollison got her bachelor of communications in 2023 and has recently graduated with her masters.

She told Morning Report during her job-hunting process she made a spreadsheet to "keep herself accountable".

From July 2025 to July 2026, Tollison said she applied for 661 jobs, had 53 interviews and two job offers.

"It's very tough - applying for roles at times felt like it was a full-time role in itself, ironically."

Tollison found work in the public sector after graduating from her undergraduate degree, but within one month her role was disestablished as part of government cuts.

"It's hard because your identity as a person is not reflected in the number of rejections you get.

"Your determination and drive are a better demonstration of the potential you have in the role than the very skills you've ironically studied and learnt about during your degree."

Tollison said to keep herself going whenever she received a rejection she would say to herself, "They were looking for a sunset and I'm a bright, blue sky."

One of the toughest parts of the application process was it didn't let applicants be known as a person, she said.

"My roles that I've interviewed for really got to know me as a person... can't really be seen during an application process. In person you can build a rapport with them."

While many jobseekers were, Tollison said she wasn't using artificial intelligence (AI) to help write her applications.

"I use the skills that I learned during my degree, I did all of these applications with my own mind and my own hands."

High unemployment, AI and a highly-competitive job market mean many recent graduates were picking up jobs completely unrelated to their degrees - if they were lucky enough to find work at all.

According to employment website Seek, s for graduate jobs made up just over 2 percent of the overall share of jobs on the site last month.

In a statement, it said the unemployment rate in New Zealand was high by historical standards, so grads were competing with other grads as well as those with work experience.

Student Job Search chief executive Louise Saviker said New Zealand's labour market remained challenging, particularly for young people.

World.title: NZ's 'clean, green' reputation at risk, ex-UK envoy warns
World.content:
A former British high commissioner to New Zealand says our country's "100% Pure New Zealand" brand is at stake, following a Dutch environmental group lodging a complaint with the European Commission alleging New Zealand may have breached parts of its free trade agreement with the European Union.

On Thursday, University of Canterbury political scientist professor Bronwyn Hayward told Morning Report if the complaint hadn't come from the Dutch group, it could have come from another environmental organisation, such as ClientEarth.

ClientEarth is led by former British High Commissioner to New Zealand, Laura Clarke.

Speaking to Morning Report on Friday morning, Clarke said the action being taken against New Zealand was very significant.

"I think it goes to the integrity and the credibility of the content of trade agreements.

"New Zealand and the European Union agreed in what is a really gold standard free trade agreement. They both promised not to weaken environmental protection or climate action in order to attract trade or investment.

"What this complaint is doing is really testing that."

She said New Zealand had a strong reputation of "batting above its average" when it came to trade policy.

"I think that's due to the quality of its produce. It's really innovative approaches, including free trade agreements that are standard setting like the EU one and the UK one, but also because it's seen as a reliable partner with strong rule of law that's good for its word."

In a post on LinkedIn, Clarke detailed recent measures undertaken by New Zealand which may breach its obligations in the Trade and Sustainable Development chapter of the EU/New Zealand Free Trade Agreement.

"These measures in question include the recent 'tort bar' legislation that shields major greenhouse gas emitters from liability for climate harm; and moves to reopen offshore oil and gas exploration, lower its 2050 methane target and remove the requirement to align carbon market settings with the Paris Agreement," the post said.

Clarke said the case was a test of New Zealand's reputation in the world as an exporter, saying its 100% Pure New Zealand brand and clean, green image was at risk.

"New Zealand has an outsized influence on the world stage, partly because it can be so brilliantly innovative because its people are loved around the world.

"Particularly here in Europe, we've just come through the most awful summer in terms of climate impact. New Zealand's friends and partners want to see New Zealand taking action on these things, particularly to the South Pacific, where it's existential.

"Climate change, sea level rise are existential. So I think it is a real risk to New Zealand's reputation."

Clarke said the European Union's credibility was also on the line.

"This goes to the heart of so much to do with trade agreements and other legal agreements. They're only ever as good as how they are implemented and enforced.

"It's really important not just that you make a declaration or you make a trade agreement, but actually that operates in practice. And that's what gives businesses and consumers confidence that these things that countries have agreed to will be upheld.

"So absolutely, this test for the European Union to say when it makes these wide-ranging commitments on trade and sustainability, how does it make sure that those are then abided by?"

World.title: Man charged with murder after death in Auckland's Glen Innes
World.content:
Police have charged a man with murder following the death of a man in the Auckland suburb Glen Innes on Thursday.

The 33-year-old was due to appear in Auckland District Court today.

He was taken into custody shortly after police were called to Sunnymead Road around 2.45pm, where a man with critical injuries died.

Police are also seeking information and dashcam footage relating to two vehicles; a black Audi A3 and a silver Toyota Crown seen travelling through Panmure and Glen Innes on Thursay afternoon.

Acting Detective Inspector Craig Bolton earlier said there was no risk to the public and support was being provided to the family of the man who died.

"Police quickly attended and sadly, despite best efforts by emergency services, a man was pronounced deceased at the scene.

"One person was swiftly taken into custody and is assisting Police with enquiries."

Residents are gathered outside the cordon at Sunnymead Road following an incident. Jessica Hopkins/RNZ

The Tamaki Regeneration Company confirmed the incident occurred at a Tamaki Housing property.

The company said it was working with police and whānau.

St Johns responded with one ambulance, one rapid response vehicle and one operations manager.

A scene guard was established and cordons were put in place.

Residents are gathered outside the cordon at Sunnymead Road following an incident. Jessica Hopkins/RNZ

Police said there was not believed to be any risk to the wider public.

"Police recognise the impact an incident of this nature has on the community, and we want to reassure residents that support is being provided to the family of the deceased and those in the wider community.

"Staff will also be conducting reassurance patrols in the coming day."

World.title: Carlton continues push for AFLW top four in win over Hawks
World.content:
Carlton have weathered wet and wild conditions to leap into the AFLW's top four with a 12-point win over Hawthorn.

On a day when profiting from key moments defined the Princes Park clash, four minutes of first-quarter magic set the Blues up for a 5.6 (36) to 3.6 (24) victory on Thursday.

Carlton fired three scintillating goals in unrelenting rain while keeping the Hawks scoreless until midway through the second term.

But the visitors suddenly found themselves firmly in the contest when forward Poppy Stockwell and midfielder Kaitlyn Ashmore kicked back-to-back third-quarter majors to level the scores.

Carlton slotted two goals either side of three-quarter time to put themselves in the box seat for victory.

Midfielder Abbie McKay (33 disposals, six clearances) was typically inspirational for Carlton while Irish star Erone Fitzpatrick posted 26 disposals and two goals to help last season's preliminary finalists (6-2) go third on the ladder.

"[It was] great Irish weather, so the Irish are used to this," Fitzpatrick told Channel 7.

"It was just the kind of game that you just need to keep getting the ball forward, whether it's a handball, a kick on the ground, or just a surge kick."

For the Hawks (4-4), the loss keeps them out of the congested top eight with four games remaining as they struggled to capitalise on their 52 inside 50s.

Regardless, star ruck Lucy Wales shone with 20 disposals and nine hitouts, while midfielder Eliza West registered 22 disposals.

Hawthorn had the first seven inside-50s of the match, but it was Carlton who drew first blood when Sophie McKay scooped up a loose ball and kicked a goal.

Moments later, Blues midfielder Dayna Finn capitalised on a rogue handball from defender Lavinia Cox before Fitzpatrick added another major.

Trailing 19-0 at the first break, the Hawks were finally rewarded when Stockwell kicked a goal to close the deficit to 12 points at halftime.

Hawthorn upped the ante again, giving the Blues barely any attacking ball as they scored two majors before Fitzpatrick grabbed her second of the evening to re-establish the home team's advantage.

With the game in the balance, Carlton's Keeley Sherar poked the ball through the centre sticks and the home team emerged victorious.

AAP

World.title: Australia and India to kick off next year's Cricket World Cup
World.content:
Australia will launch its defence of the men's Cricket World Cup in South Africa next year with a blockbuster opener against India, the powerhouse it defeated to win the crown in 2023.

As the fixtures for the 2027 event in southern Africa were unveiled on Thursday, Pat Cummins's side learned it would take on the title favourite and world number one side on October 7 in its first match in Cape Town.

Australia 2027 men's Cricket World Cup draw India — Thursday October 7, Cape Town, South Africa Qualifier — Tuesday, October 12, Paarl, South Africa Zimbabwe — Friday, October 15, Harare, Zimbabwe Afghanistan — Monday, October 18 KuGompo City, South Africa Pakistan — Friday, October 22 Paarl, South Africa

Both teams will also feature in a potentially explosive group A with Pakistan.

The India-Pakistan clash will take place at Johannesburg ‌in the famed "Bullring" atmosphere of the Wanderers' ground just three days after the Australia match, and that venue will also stage the final on November 21.

Also in Australia's group will be co-hosts Zimbabwe, which it has just beaten 3-0 in an one-day international series at the same Harare venue, as well as Afghanistan and one of two qualifiers yet to be decided.

Its last group fixture will be against Pakistan at Paarl, where Australia will also play the qualifying side.

The other group looks potentially even more challenging, with co-host South Africa, desperately seeking its first men's World Cup, facing England, New Zealand, Sri Lanka and another qualifier.

The best four sides will then go on to the semifinals, which will both be played in South Africa.

Men's 2027 Cricket World Cup draw. (ICC)

AAP

World.title: PNG's NRL franchise faces trademark fight over Chiefs name
World.content:
With just weeks to go before unveiling its logo, Papua New Guinea's NRL franchise is yet to secure rights over its name — the Chiefs.

IP Australia, the government agency that administers rights to trademarks, is yet to be persuaded that the PNG club's brand is clearly distinct from that of the Super Rugby Chiefs, who play out of Hamilton in New Zealand.

The Chiefs have played in the Super Rugby for 30 years, claiming championships in 2012 and 2013. (AFP)

So far, the NRL has received three adverse reports in response to the PNG club's trademark applications, with IP Australia declaring there is a "real and tangible danger" of brand confusion.

An adverse report from IP Australia is a formal notice identifying issues with a trademark application that need addressing before it can be accepted.

If the issues are not resolved within the prescribed period, the application can lapse.

The PNG Chiefs are due to launch their brand on October 21, backed by major sponsors Coca-Cola and Bank South Pacific, which has signed the NRL's biggest sponsorship deal worth $15 million.

They are due to debut in the NRL in 2028, with the help of a $600 million Australian government funding package.

PNG Prime Minister James Marape announced the PNG Chiefs' name in October 2025, but a year on it is still not a registered trademark. (Supplied: NRL)

University of Technology Sydney intellectual property law specialist Sarah Hook said she was surprised lawyers did not advise against using "Chiefs" at the start of the process.

"I would have thought they would have said they need something a bit more distinctive," Dr Hook said.

Sarah Hook says she is surprised lawyers did not advise against choosing "Chiefs" as the team's name. (Supplied)

"If they do launch [the name and logo], it's going to be difficult to go back and rebrand if this does end up in Federal Court."

Sydney Law School associate professor Fady Aoun said receiving three adverse reports from IP Australia was unusual.

"If the PNG Chiefs are to proceed [with that name], it does come with some risk and potential embarrassment if later, they're denied registration rights," he said.

'People will be asking which one'

In New Zealand, chief executive of Super Rugby franchise The Chiefs, Simon Graafhuis, said three decades of brand building would be at stake for his club if the PNG franchise dug its heels in and pushed forward with the name.

He said he hoped a deal could be reached with the PNG club before its launch to avoid potential confusion.

PNG 'proved the critics wrong'. Some say it will do it again in 2028 Observers say Papua New Guinea's decades-long history of rugby league success and passion is on its side as it prepares for the next sporting leap into the NRL.

"If you have a trademark, you've virtually got an obligation to defend it, and the best time to do that is before any damage is done," he said.

While it is uncertain how the PNG's trademark application will play out in Australia, the Super Rugby side believes its standing in its home country is watertight.

Mr Graafhuis said his club's brand had legal protection that would make it problematic for a team of the same name to play on New Zealand soil.

He said if the PNG side stuck to "Chiefs", the team may be forced to take to the field in jumpers that do not carry their logo when they play NRL club the New Zealand Warriors in Auckland.

Simon Graafhuis says three decades of brand building are at stake. (Supplied)

"You talk about the Chiefs and people will be asking which one," Mr Graafhuis said.

"We've spent 30 years developing a brand and a reputation, and our sponsors leverage off that, so any risk of confusion [means] there's a very real chance of costing us commercially."

Dr Aoun said he would not be surprised if some sort of co-existence agreement was "nutted out" between the New Zealand and PNG franchises.

New Zealand Rugby meanwhile penned a letter to the NRL last month, saying the Chiefs was not an acceptable name for the incoming team and asked league officials to reconsider it.

Simon Graafhuis says any brand confusion has a real chance of hurting his club commercially. (Getty Images)

The ABC approached New Zealand Rugby and the NRL for comment.

Brand confusion could spread beyond NZ, expert says

But the New Zealand club might not be the only brand to take issue with PNG's chosen name.

In addition to the clash with the Super Rugby Chiefs, IP Australia also identified seven other companies and businesses across Australia, Hong Kong and the United States that could potentially object to the PNG Chiefs' trademark applications.

Dr Hook said the global nature of sports merchandising meant the potential for brand confusion was not confined to a single market.

Jarome Luai was the first of several big-name players to be signed to play for the PNG Chiefs from 2028. (Supplied: PNG Chiefs)

"We're not talking about a product that's sold in one place or another," she said.

"We're talking about brand merchandising that lots of people around the world might be interested in."

The PNG club's chief executive Lorna McPherson appears confident it will secure rights to the Chiefs name, telling the ABC that "the NRL are dealing with it and the planned launch is set for October 21".

PNG Chiefs club chief executive Lorna McPherson and general manager Michael Chammas. (Facebook: PNG Chiefs)

Dr Hook said that was likely wishful thinking, adding that it was risky for the PNG club to push forward with its trademark application unresolved.

"Even if they were to settle with every single company, that doesn't mean IP Australia will register it if it's still similar to other trademarks," she said.

World.title: 'First time I've smiled': Suspended Swan Heeney wins best and fairest
World.content:
Isaac Heeney has won Sydney's best and fairest award following his club imposed sanction for breaching club standards.

Heeney was absent from the ceremony as he claimed his third Bob Skilton Medal in a row, with teammates Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon also avoiding the event.

The five players were banned from playing for the Swans for breaching club standards over late night partying at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel following a match on August 16.

Police are separately investigating an allegation of sexual assault on the same night, with Heeney, Jordon, Blakey and Warner interviewed by police. No charges have been laid and the ABC is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

The club had announced earlier in the week that the five players would not attend the club's awards night, as Heeney became the 11th player in South Melbourne and Sydney Swans history to claim three best and fairest titles.

Heeney video aired at ceremony

A short video from Heeney was displayed after he won the medal, where the 30-year-old apologised to the club and reflected on the award.

"When I was told about this honour it was the first time I've smiled and felt positive about the future for a long time," he said.

"While I wasn't able to attend the awards I look forward to seeing you all again in person very soon.

"My whole life has centred around my two families. My family in Newcastle where mum, dad, brother, and Steph have always been an incredible support, particularly recently. I love you, and thank you.

"And my other family, which I've been a part of since I was 12 years old, the Sydney Swans. A family I also love and cherish being a part of.

"I want to say to everyone, in particular my teammates, the Swans players, AFLW, and the staff, from the depths of my heart, I'm truly sorry for putting you through the extreme difficulty you've had to endure, as it had a huge impact on our club."

Swans chair clarifies eligibility

In his awards ceremony speech, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham said the reasoning behind the club's eligibility criteria was two-fold — protecting the integrity of votes; and ensuring off-field matters were separate from on-field performance.

"We do not believe it would have been appropriate to retrospectively remove votes that have already been cast owing to the subsequent incident," Pridham said.

"The medals awarded tonight acknowledge on-field performance across the season.

"Erasing a season of football after the fact would, in our opinion, be inappropriate and in excess of a sanction.

"I can assure you that we did not make any decisions we have made in recent times like that.

"I respect that some people in this room and beyond may not agree with where we have landed tonight.

"It has been very, very difficult, but let me be equally clear that these decisions to allow the players to remain eligible does not diminish our concern and respect for everyone involved in this."

Ruckman Brodie Grundy finished second, with key forward Charlie Curnow in third.

In other club best and fairest results on Thursday night, Bailey Smith claimed his first Carji Greeves Medal at the Cats and grand final day hero Will Ashcroft took home his first Merrett-Murray Medal at the Lions.

Want-away Essendon skipper Zach Merrett made history with his seventh Crichton Medal, equalling the record set by Bombers legends Dick Reynolds and Bill Hutchison.

Issac Heeney's full speech at Bob Skilton Medal night First, I want to reach out and talk to the whole club and everyone again. All the players, the staff, the board, our great fans, and sponsors. When I was told about this honour it was the first time I've smiled and felt positive about the future for a long time. While I wasn't able to attend the awards I look forward to seeing you all again in person very soon. My whole life has centred around my two families. My family in Newcastle where mum, dad, brother, and Steph have always been an incredible support, particularly recently. I love you, and thank you. And my other family, which I've been a part of since I was 12 years old, the Sydney Swans. A family I also love and cherish being a part of. I want to say to everyone, in particular my teammates, the Swans players, AFLW, and the staff, from the depths of my heart, I'm truly sorry for putting you through the extreme difficulty you've had to endure, as it had a huge impact on our club. Every single day I was away from the club was heartbreaking, knowing that I couldn't make a contribution. Every single day I think about what could have been. To my teammates, a huge thank you. Your incredible fight at the end of the season was inspiring. I was so proud of you all, and gutted I wasn't there. Your commitment to success is why I love playing alongside you and being part of this group. To Coxy, the coaches, and every single member of the staff involved in our program, thank you for everything you do. The time, care, and effort you put into us as players, and as people, is incredible. I'm extremely grateful for your support. Finally, I just wanted to say how incredibly honoured I am to receive this award. It's named after the legendary Swan, Bob Skilton, and has been won by so many past greats of the club, including Paul Kelly, a hero of mine growing up. It reminded me of my great love of playing football and the Swans, a club which has given me so much throughout my career. I want my actions moving forward to show how much this place and its people mean to me. I'm incredibly excited about what this group can do. I can't wait to get back in training with the boys, get better, and attack next year together. To all the other winners, congratulations on your fantastic achievements. You should be extremely proud, as I'm sure you are. Thank you, I love you all, go Swans.

World.title: Federal Court rules against challenge to SA government's golf course plans
World.content:
Two South Australians have failed in a bid to stop the felling of trees as part of the North Adelaide golf course redevelopment.

Public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna Arabana woman Janette Milera brought the action against the State Government in the Federal Court earlier this year arguing the redevelopment was in breach of federal conservation laws.

The Federal Court trial heard last month that 400 trees had been cut down to date, with the government previously saying 585 would ultimately go.

In reading out a summary of her judgement, Justice Natalie Charlesworth said there was evidence brought before the court during the trial that "more than 70,000 trees will remain" in the Adelaide Parklands.

"The evidence showed that there remained a very large number of trees in the project site and in the parklands," she said.

"I'm not satisfied that the depletion, or proposed future depletion, is such that it has had, will have or is likely to have significant impact on species."

Government moves to fell trees at the North Adelaide Golf Course sparked court action. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Justice Charlesworth added that during the proceedings the government did not diminish the importance of the parklands for the Kaurna people, and that the court's findings shouldn't be viewed that way.

"Nothing in the findings should be understood as diminishing the significance of the parklands for the Kaurna people — that … was not disputed by the respondent," she said.

Applicants raise concerns over impact of costs

Justice Charlesworth ordered that lawyers for the government inform the court by October 22 if they wished to file an order for costs against Mr Kemp Attril and Ms Milera.

Outside court, Mr Kemp Attrill said he and Ms Milera were "absolutely worried" about the government making an application for costs.

"It will probably make us bankrupt, both of us," he said.

"This is a public interest case; we have had nothing to gain and everything to lose.

"The whole case has been a waste of time and money for the government because they failed to provide the information to the public and they failed to have independent assessment of this project.

"All we asked was for this to be referred to the federal environment minister, which is what they are doing for the MotoGP; that's all we're asking for."

Mr Kemp Attrill said they still "maintain the project is damaging the environment".

"This was not a decision of approval by this judge, this was not a decision that supported this project, it was just a technical assessment according to the EPBC Act," he said.

"We didn't win this case, but we didn't lose because we fought … you only lose if you don't fight.

"We're going to continue to fight."

He added that they would make a decision about whether to appeal the judgment once they read it.

Protesters gathered outside the Federal Court ahead of Thursday's decision. (ABC News: Eva Blandis)

Ms Milera highlighted the importance of the parklands in Aboriginal culture.

"The judgment hasn't changed myself, or my position, as a Kaurna person; it will always be Aboriginal land," she said.

"The parklands for me are like Ayers Rock are for them mob up there.

"Ayers Rock's sacred to them and the spiritual place, and the parklands are sacred."

Mr Kemp Attrill and Ms Milera have 28 days to file an appeal against the decision.

Justice Charlesworth ordered that the injunction on the works at the North Adelaide golf course lift immediately despite the 28-day appeal period.

World.title: Chris Fagan headed the ultimate Lions reawakening
World.content:
Chris Fagan said earlier this week: "You don't coach a team to win a popularity contest."

Despite his best intentions, the departing Brisbane Lions three-time premiership winning coach has done just that.

Today, after days of speculation, the 65-year-old has told the club he he will step down.

"Telling the players and football staff today was one of the hardest things I've done in my life," he said.

"We have been on a mission to make the Lions the most entertaining and competitive team in the competition, and we have done that."

In his decade at the Lions, Fagan has broken the mould of what is needed to be an AFL coach. He also leaves as one of the most popular figures in Australian sport.

The reason Fagan took on the difficult job at the Lions back in 2016 was to help the club on its road to redemption.

Safe to say now, a little more than 10 years on, mission accomplished.

Three AFL premierships. In a row.

Chris Fagan and the Brisbane Lions celebrate their third consecutive AFL premiership. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer/AFL Photos)

Fagan is also known as "Fages", or "Papa Fages" to so many of the young men he coached during his tenure. Many have referred to him as a father figure, or another grandfather.

That respect goes both ways, with Fagan often noting that he considered players at the club as his sons, and wanted to "help them develop into the best people they can be".

He finishes his role with 148 wins in 243 games as head coach, the most of any Brisbane Lions coach of all time, and of course those three titles.

Brisbane will never forget the work, effort and glory he has given the team.

But back in October 2016, public opinion on the surprise appointment was mixed.

A goalscoring teacher

Fagan grew up in Queenstown, Tasmania — a far cry from the humidity of Brisbane.

He played 260 games of senior footy in the Tasmanian Football League with Hobart, Sandy Bay and Devonport between 1978 and 1990.

Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan, third from the left at the front, grew up in Queenstown and played for the Lyell-Gormanston football club as a junior. (Supplied: Galley Museum Collection)

Before coaching, Fagan went into teaching, working as a high school teacher in Tasmania towards the end of his playing career. He took on some local coaching roles in Tasmania.

The long apprenticeship from high school teacher to three-peat AFL premiership winning coach began in 1999 when AFL great Neale Daniher brought him to Melbourne Football Club.

He served under Daniher until 2007 before joining as an assistant and eventually general manager of football at Hawthorn.

The Lions hierarchy saw the value in what Fagan had learned and appointed him to replace Justin Leppitsch in late 2016.

Fresh start for Brisbane

After finishing second bottom of the ladder in 2016, the Brisbane Lions were looking for a fresh start.

A five-person coaching selection panel, led by then club chief executive Greg Swann, made the selection to appoint Fagan on October 4.

Chris Fagan speaks to the media after being unveiled as the Brisbane Lions' coach in 2016. (AAP Image: Dave Hunt)

The committee said Fagan was "exactly the person" the club needed.

"Chris is the perfect fit for the Brisbane Lions as we strive to regain relevance — his knowledge, experience, mentoring skills and ability to communicate are all elite," Swann said announcing the appointment.

At the time, Fagan said he felt Brisbane's best football was ahead of them.

Yet in Fagan's first season at the club, the Lions finished rock bottom. The team ended the 2017 campaign with 17 losses.

The Brisbane Lions lost 19 of 22 games in 2016, finishing second-last on the ladder. (AAP: Ben Macmahon)

You would be forgiven if you thought Fagan must have been disheartened after his first season at the club ending in a wooden spoon.

You would also be wrong.

"It's been a great year, I've learned so much about the group," Fagan said in August 2017.

"I think right now, I'm in a good position to know what's required."

Lions coach Chris Fagan (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The 'Gabbatoir' returns

In 2019, Fagan took the Lions to second on the ladder and a semifinal.

They narrowly lost the semifinal to Greater Western Sydney, but it was a marked turnaround from the year prior.

It had been a long time since playing in Brisbane was seen as a difficult away trip, but that year Fagan and his Lions turned the Gabba into a fortress.

Chris Fagan and the Lions turned the Gabba into the "Gabbatoir". (Getty Images: Albert Perez/AFL Photos)

From 2019 to 2023 the Lions won 49 of 53 regular season games at the Gabba. In 2023, Brisbane were unbeaten at home.

Once again, the Lions had turned the Gabba into the "Gabbatoir". He had made them believe.

"There's nothing magical or mysterious about it," he said in 2019 before the incredible home form began, adding the secret would be hard work, staying humble and believing.

He led the club to the Finals series in 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022.

At the end of the 2022 season, Fagan took a leave of absence as Brisbane coach to assist with an external review into the treatment of Indigenous players during his time as an employee at Hawthorn alongside then-coach Alastair Clarkson and former welfare manager Jason Burt.

Fagan, Clarkson and Burt categorically denied all allegations of wrongdoing, and the case was settled out of court. Fagan returned to his coaching duties in late October 2022.

In 2023, he guided the Lions to their first grand final in 19 years. They lost to Collingwood by four points.

Despite the frustrations of falling at the final hurdle, Fagan asked the fans and his players to be patient.

Fagan shakes hands with Collingwood coach Craig McRae after the Lions' grand final loss in 2023. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Daniel Pockett)

"Grand final losses don't have to define you or destroy you, they can make you," he said.

"There's lots of teams in the history of the game that have lost close grand finals and gone on to win premierships in the ensuing years."

Almost as if he knew.

Back-to-back-to-back

In 2024, after a fifth-placed finish in the regular season, the Lions clawed their way through the longer finals path to reach the grand final.

In it, they defeated the Sydney Swans 120-60 in what was an emphatic victory. They became just the third team to win the premiership from outside the top four.

Brisbane Lions players and coach Chris Fagan after winning the 2024 grand final against the Sydney Swans. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"I'm so proud of the group, the resilience that they've shown this year," Fagan told ABC Sport after the win.

"We certainly know how to do it the hard way, but it makes it all that better when you achieve it."

He was right about Lions doing things the hard way. In 2025 the Lions lost their qualifying final against Geelong, 112-74.

Despite that, the Lions eased past Gold Coast Suns in the semifinal and then defeated Collingwood in the preliminary final, setting up a rematch against Geelong in the grand final.

The Lions turned around the qualifying final result and defeated Geelong 122-75 to claim their second premiership in as many years.

Self belief within the group was at an all time high going into the match, Fagan recalled afterwards.

"I always talked about the idea of failing our way to the top," Fagan said after becoming a back-to-back premiership winner.

“We don’t get too upset when we lose. I think everybody has embraced that at the footy club."

Harris Andrews, Chris Fagan and Lachie Neale celebrate the Lions' 2025 victory. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

The 2026 season saw the Lions defeated in the qualifying final once again. This time the Swans humbled Brisbane 144-88.

Brisbane had to do it the hard way for the third year in a row. "We've got work to do," Fagan said.

In the post match conference he posed a question to his players: "How badly do they want it? We'll see."

It turned out they wanted it (a three-peat) badly. The Lions roared past Adelaide Crows, then held off Hawthorn on the way to a fourth consecutive grand final.

In that final, against Fremantle, the Lions pulled off what can only be described as unbelievable to claim their third AFL premiership in a row.

With a little over four minutes left on the clock they trailed by 17 points. The camera panned to Fagan on the sideline, he looked his usual calm self. He believed.

As did his players, just like he had asked them to do for the last 10 years. Believe.

Against the run of play and all logic, the Lions scored four unanswered goals as the clock ran down and won the match by seven points in an instant classic.

Fagan leaves the Lions at the peak of his powers. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Fagan had coached the players to have so much belief in themselves that they would produce results where no one else would think possible. But under Fagan's stewardship it was.

Until his achievements with the Lions, successful AFL coaches had all played at the top level, and typically utilised old school methods of rallying the troops.

But Fagan's coaching ethos has relied on mutual trust, relationships and emotional intelligence to challenge his players. Now, he walks out on top.

Never someone to chase personal accolades, Fagan is leaving the role at the peak of his powers, and opting not to chase the four-peat that would leave him in even rarer air.

Fagan took on one of AFL's biggest assignments at the Lions and leaves a club favourite. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

It was one of the AFL's biggest assignments — saving a flagship club that was depleted on and off the field. Brisbane was not only struggling to win matches, the club was also losing memberships and crowds.
